Using fluorescently labeled polyethylene nanoplastics as extracellular tracers, we further show that they accumulate within the developing tubular lumen, consistent with its formation through neuroepithelial folding and internalization. These findings provide new insights into early human brain morphogenesis and suggest the potential utility of cortical organoids for investigating developmental processes relevant to neural tube defects.

items.title: Can rat cortical cultures predict what comes next, unpredictable or learned?
items.abstract: In humans, physiological activity recorded before an unpredictable stimulus reportedly varies slightly with what the stimulus will be, an effect termed predictive anticipatory activity. Whether reduced neural preparations show it is unknown. We re-analyzed a public dataset in which twelve dissociated rat cortical cultures on high-density multi-electrode arrays performed a hidden-source inference task (DANDI 001611: 27 experiments, 691,200 trials). Two features of the dataset limit what it can test. Each experiment replays one fixed 256-trial source sequence in all 100 sessions, so the upcoming source is unpredictable only in session 1. One stimulation volley per trial arrives on an exact 1-s clock, so every pre-stimulus window lies in the previous trial's after-effects. Two questions were fixed before a confirmatory run on held-out experiments. Q1 asked whether, in session 1, a stimulation-free 250-ms window before each trial's volley carries information about the upcoming sources beyond what trial history explains. Q2 asked whether this information grows over the 100 repetitions, as learned expectation would predict. Q1 (13 experiments, 9 cultures): decoding above a shifted-label null, {Delta}AUC +0.003, 95% CI -0.026 to +0.033, randomization p = 0.73, equivalent to zero within +/-0.059 (the human effect expressed as AUC) and narrowly within +/-0.03. Q2 (12 experiments, 8 cultures): growth {Delta}G +0.004, 95% CI -0.006 to +0.013, p = 0.29, equivalent within +/-0.02. Pre-stimulus activity thus carried no detectable information about the stimulus, and none emerged with repetition.

items.title: Disentangling tonic and phasic dopamine in fiber photometry from single recordings to cohorts
items.abstract: Fiber photometry signals combine fast neurotransmitter transients with slower changes in baseline. However, current pipelines separate the two before measuring either, so errors in one carry over into the other. Here we present PhotoSVI, a multi-scale statistical model that splits a recording into a slow tonic signal and discrete release events, estimated together. For each recording, PhotoSVI returns event probabilities over time, the drug effect on event rate with its uncertainty, and the time course of the tonic response, and it pools recordings across a cohort. In simulations matched to experimental recordings, PhotoSVI detected transients and recovered the shape of the tonic response more accurately than existing methods. In mouse dopamine recordings, it revealed an effect that count-based analyses largely missed: a nociceptin receptor agonist enhances the phasic response to morphine while reducing the tonic one, consistent with lower tonic dopamine relieving phasic release from autoreceptor inhibition.

items.title: Rank Deficiency in Parameter Estimation for Hodgkin-Huxley Type Current Models
items.abstract: The Jacobians of nonlinear least squares residuals play a central role when simultaneously fitting parameters of Hodgkin--Huxley (HH) type models to ionic currents measured through voltage clamp experiments. Their rank deficiency is tied to parameter degeneracy, i.e., the ability to produce the same current response with different parameters, and the Jacobians' null spaces provide insight into the structure of the parameter degeneracy, as well as into which additional experiments can reduce or even remove it. This paper analyzes Jacobian rank structure across HH-type models used for H-, A-type, fast sodium, and delayed rectifier currents. The Jacobians are rank deficient to varying degrees, depending on experimental conditions. Analytical representations of the Jacobians' null spaces are provided. In all models, one source of rank deficiency is the multiplication of the peak conductance and state variables, such as activation and inactivation, inherent to the HH-type model structure. H-current models derived from either whole cell, or cell-attached patch recordings exhibit additional rank deficiencies, implying the local existence of manifolds of parameters that lead to the same current responses. For A-type, fast sodium, and delayed rectifier models there is no additional rank deficiency, although their Jacobians may exhibit characteristics associated with ill-conditioned parameter estimation problems. Descriptions of the null spaces of these Jacobians are used to prove that the rank deficiency can be reduced or even be removed by fixing certain parameters, or by adding additional experiments. The analytical results are illustrated numerically, using data from voltage clamp experiments described in the literature.

items.title: PreSMA population dynamics keep the beat atop the primate audiomotor hierarchy
items.corresponding_institution: Instituto de Neurobiologia, Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico
items.abstract: Humans move in time with musical beats, yet how the brain builds the internal beat that guides movement is unknown. We recorded 4,719 neurons in six nodes of the audiomotor circuit while monkeys tapped in synchrony with auditory metronomes at different tempos. We found a clear functional dissociation in the temporal-frontal axis. Auditory cortex detected metronome clicks and contained local clocks that tiled each interstimulus interval, whereas parietal, striatal, and motor areas, most strongly the pre-supplementary motor area (preSMA), generated movement-aligned neural sequences that rescaled with tempo. Only in preSMA did population activity formed a cone-shaped manifold that jointly encoded tempo in its height, the produced interval in its width, and the timing of each tap relative to the beat in its position along the trajectory. During timing errors, preSMA activity kept conical shape but drifted toward shorter or longer tempos, revealing a hierarchical neural clock for beat synchronization.

items.title: FOLR2 Identifies Functionally Distinct Decidual Macrophage Populations that Coordinate Immune and Tissue Remodelling During Human Labour
items.abstract: The initiation of human labour remains incompletely understood, although mounting evidence implicates decidual macrophages in this process. Despite this, macrophage heterogeneity remains poorly defined, with current macrophage classification systems, including M1/M2, failing to capture their biological diversity. Here, we investigate whether macrophage differentiation state, defined by expression of the tissue residency marker FOLR2, provides a more informative framework for characterising human decidual macrophages at term. RNA sequencing and flow cytometry identified FOLR2- and FOLR2+ macrophages as transcriptionally and phenotypically distinct populations. FOLR2- macrophages displayed features consistent with recently recruited monocyte-derived cells and were characterised by enrichment of inflammatory and leukocyte recruitment pathways, with greater expression of IL-8 and CCL5 than FOLR2 macrophages. In contrast, FOLR2 macrophages expressed higher levels of MHC class II molecules, CCL2, IL-6, MMP9 and MMP19, and demonstrated the capacity to degrade collagen in fetal membrane explants. Monocyte and macrophage numbers peaked during early labour in the decidua parietalis, accompanied by increased CCL5 expression, whereas FOLR2+ macrophage expression of MMP9 was highest prior to labour. These findings suggest that decidual macrophage heterogeneity is best understood through differentiation state rather than M1/M2 polarisation and point to complementary roles for FOLR2- and FOLR2 macrophages in leukocyte recruitment, tissue remodelling and the local adaptations required for labour initiation and progression.

items.title: RPAP3 impairs TRBP-mediated translation of TAR-containing RNAs and FTSJ3 recruitment onto the HIV-1 genomic RNA
items.corresponding_institution: Universite de Lorraine, CNRS, IMoPA, F-54000 Nancy, France
items.abstract: The interaction between TRBP and RPAP3, which is mutually exclusive from that between TRBP and Dicer, revealed a possible role for RPAP3 in the regulation of miRNA activity. Besides miRNA processing and/or function, TRBP is involved in promoting the expression of TAR-containing transcripts, and to impede innate immune system from sensing HIV-1 in infected cells by recruiting the cellular 2'-O-methyltransferase FTSJ3 onto the viral RNA. Here, we show that RPAP3 prevents the TRBP stimulatory effect on the translation of TAR-containing reporters, both in vitro and in cellulo, without affecting TRBP's ability to bind to the TAR. We also observe that virion production is increased in RPAP3 depleted cells. Additionally, we show that TRBP directly recruits the methyltransferase FTSJ3, and that RPAP3 inhibits this ability. These observations open new avenues for possible novel therapeutics strategies aimed at hindering TRBP pro-viral functions, via novel regulation mechanisms involving RPAP3.

items.title: A minimal common core and dynamic protein associations orchestrate nuclear mRNP maturation
items.corresponding_institution: Laboratory of RNP Biochemistry, Institut de recherches cliniques de Montreal (IRCM), Center for Genetic and    Neurological Diseases, Montreal, QC, Canada
items.abstract: How nuclear mRNAs are selectively packaged into ribonucleoprotein particles (mRNPs) is fundamental to elucidating the mechanisms that govern gene expression. Here, we interrogate nuclear mRNP maturation in S. cerevisiae by combining a proteomic (34 baits) and transcriptomic (18 baits) affinity-purification survey with sequential purification of individual MS2-tagged nuclear transcripts at successive stages of maturation. Contrary to the prevailing models in which nuclear mRNAs are extensively coated with a stable complement of proteins, we find that they share a minimal core of Yra1p and Pab1p, together with a more dynamically associated cap-binding complex. Most other factors associate transiently and transcript-selectively, assembling as pre-assembled, stage-specific modules. The minimal core is invariant to promoter, coding sequence and transcript length, whereas intron class, rather than intron presence alone, determines spliceosome composition. The breadth of factor association further tracks promoter class and proximity to chromatin-domain boundaries, linking mRNP biogenesis to genome organization.

items.title: Kinesin-1 selectivity for stable microtubules is mediated by MAP7D1's recognition of expanded lattices
items.abstract: Microtubules are organized into functionally distinct subsets that differ in stability, post-translational modifications (PTMs) and lattice spacing, but what defines these subsets and governs selective binding of motors and microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) to specific subsets has remained unclear. Here, we demonstrate that the preferential motility of the motor protein Kinesin-1 along stable, long-lived microtubules depends on microtubule lattice spacing and MAP7 family members. Using Kinesin-1 truncations and MAP7 family depletions, we show that Kinesin-1 subset selectivity is not specified by its motor domain, but instead requires its coiled-coil 1 region, which mediates MAP7 binding. While depletion of all MAP7 proteins abolishes Kinesin-1 motility, loss of MAP7D1 alone results in non-selective motility, identifying MAP7D1 as the key determinant of selectivity. Using knock-out cells lacking detyrosinated and acetylated microtubules, we find that MAP7D1 enrichment on stable microtubule subsets depends on lattice structure rather than PTMs, whereas in vitro reconstitution assays directly demonstrate that MAP7D1 preferentially binds expanded microtubule lattices characteristic of long-lived microtubules. Together, our results establish microtubule lattice conformation as a key determinant of cellular microtubule subset identity and selective binding of MAPs.

items.title: Palmitic acid promotes glomerulosclerosis via TGF-β1 upregulation in podocytes
items.abstract: Podocytes are terminally differentiated visceral epithelial cells of the glomerulus and play a vital role in renal filtration. Nevertheless, they are vulnerable to several insults in obesity and metabolic syndrome. Obesity-related glomerulopathy (ORG) is characterized by podocyte hypertrophy, reduced podocyte density, and secondary focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS). However, how lipid overload, particularly palmitic acid (PA), whose plasma levels are frequently elevated in obesity, injures podocytes remains incompletely understood. Human podocytes were exposed to PA (100 M for 24 hours), and we assessed lipid accumulation, WT1 expression and promoter activity, TGF-{beta}1 signaling, and cell-cycle regulators. PA induced lipid droplet accumulation and increased WT1 expression in podocytes. Concurrently, PA treated podocytes showed cytoskeletal aberrations, loss of podocyte structural genes (podocin, nephrin and synaptopodin) and TGF-{beta}1/Smad2 axis causes upregulation of fibronectin, collagen, and -SMA. Similarly, mice fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 16 weeks exhibited TGF- {beta}1 activation in podocyte enriched glomeruli together with glomerulosclerosis, impaired kidney function, and podocyte loss. In both models, Cyclin D1, Cyclin B1, CDK4, p53, and p21 were increased. Notably, ~30% of PA-treated podocytes were binucleated, yet podocyte number did not increase. Lipotoxic stress was associated with concurrent induction of WT1 and TGF-{beta}1, loss of the podocyte phenotype, and abortive cell-cycle re-entry accompanied by binucleation and podocyte loss. These findings point to a WT1-TGF-{beta}1-cell-cycle axis as a potential contributor to ORG and a candidate therapeutic target. Whether WT1 directly regulates TGF-{beta}1 remains to be determined.

items.title: STL1267 alters HIF-1α and REV-ERBα localization and transcriptional responses in CoCl2-treated HeLa cells
items.corresponding_institution: Auburn University College of Veterinary Medicine
items.abstract: Background: REV-ERB nuclear receptors regulate gene expression and cellular metabolism, but their role in the response to hypoxia-associated stress remains unclear. We examined how the REV-ERB agonist STL1267 affects protein distribution and gene expression in HeLa cells exposed to cobalt chloride (CoCl2). Methods and Results: Immunofluorescence microscopy and RNA sequencing were used to compare vehicle-treated controls, cells exposed to CoCl2 plus vehicle, and cells exposed to CoCl2 plus STL1267. Representative images showed stronger nuclear HIF-1 staining after CoCl2 exposure. Nuclear staining was less pronounced with STL1267, while REV-ERB showed more extranuclear staining. CoCl2 exposure altered 267 genes, and STL1267 treatment during CoCl2 exposure altered 132 genes at a false discovery rate below 0.05. STL1267 increased ATF4 expression alongside genes involved in amino-acid synthesis and one-carbon metabolism, including ASNS, PHGDH, PSAT1, PSPH and MTHFD2. CTH and CHAC1 also increased, highlighting changes in sulfur-amino-acid metabolism and glutathione turnover. Among the genes induced by CoCl2, CA9, BNIP3 and LDHA decreased with STL1267, whereas HK2, PDK1 and VEGFA did not change significantly. Conclusions: STL1267 selectively reshapes hypoxia-associated gene expression and induces an ATF4-associated metabolic transcriptional program in CoCl2-treated HeLa cells, alongside qualitative changes in HIF-1 and REV-ERB distribution. These findings identify a potential connection between protein compartmentalization and metabolic stress responses, providing a basis for investigating how REV-ERB ligands influence cellular adaptation to oxygen limitation.

items.title: Revealing the platelet transcriptome using Siphon-seq: a sensitive, purity-aware method for RNA-sequencing
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Medicine, University of California, San Francisco, San Francisco, CA, USA
items.abstract: Platelet transcriptomics is limited by the exceptionally low RNA content of platelets and by disproportionate contributions from contaminating cells to bulk RNA-sequencing libraries. We developed Siphon-seq, an approach that deliberately overloads independently barcoded single-cell partitions to increase aggregate platelet RNA input, then computationally identifies and removes partitions containing contaminating RNA after sequencing. Applied to 34 healthy human donors, Siphon-seq increased platelet-marker representation, depleted leukocyte and erythrocyte transcripts, and removed contamination-associated inter-donor transcriptional structure. We defined a 3,436-gene core platelet transcriptome that was strongly related to megakaryocyte expression. However, megakaryocyte transcription did not fully explain the platelet transcriptome, which had specific pathways systematically enriched or depleted that were obscured by leukocyte contamination. These findings were confirmed in an independent cohort and were associated with protein detection in two platelet proteome resources. In a pilot human sepsis cohort, Siphon-seq reduced transcripts associated with leukocytes to reveal increased platelet-associated pathway signals. These contaminating immune pathways were also enriched in samples analyzed by bulk RNA-seq from an independent sepsis cohort, most strongly in the stratum with the highest estimated leukocyte burden. Combined, these results reveal that RNA-level contamination can alter both transcriptome structure and biological inference, and that Siphon-seq bridges the sensitivity-purity tradeoff that has limited platelet RNA sequencing, enabling sensitive, purity-aware studies of platelet biology in health and disease.

items.title: Confocal Live-Cell Imaging Under Ultralow Irradiance Using Superconducting Transition-Edge Sensor
items.abstract: Confocal laser scanning fluorescence microscopy (CLSFM) is widely used for three-dimensional live-cell imaging. However, high irradiance is required to overcome dark counts in photodetectors, often leading to observation bias. In this study, we examine whether a CLSFM system equipped with a virtually dark-count-free superconducting transition-edge sensor (TES) can enable live-cell imaging under low irradiance, thereby mitigating observation bias. Using green fluorescent protein-tagged HeLa cells, we determined the minimum laser power required for live-cell imaging and demonstrated suppression of photobleaching and cell-division arrest during long-term observation. Innate fluorescence signature analysis revealed that TES-CLSFM could discriminate between two oleaginous yeast species with different lipid productivities at ca. 1/400 the irradiance required by conventional CLSFM. These results establish TES-CLSFM as a minimally invasive imaging modality for the quantitative physiological assessment of living cells.

items.title: A conserved dimerization motif squelches transcription
items.abstract: Squelching is an indirect inhibition of transcription that results from redistribution of cofactors away from DNA. Here, we describe a class of Lis homology (LisH)-derived peptides that act as transcriptional squelchers. LisH domains are a highly conserved motif found in 10s of thousands of proteins and are composed of ~30 amino acids in a helix-turn-helix fold. By examining a phylogenetically diverse subset of LisH domains in a synthetic Saccharomyces cerevisiae assay, we identified a small number of hydrophobic residues within the first helix that are required for effective inhibition of reporter expression. In addition, squelching required binding to the general transcriptional cofactor Taf5, a subunit of the TFIID complex. Transcriptome-level impacts were largely correlated in yeast expressing two distinct LisH sequences, consistent with a model that LisH-based squelching results from a shared mechanism of sequestering Taf5. Consistent with that inference, overexpression of Taf5 partially reversed the squelching effect. Given the interest in squelching as a potential area for anti-cancer therapies, we also tested whether our shortest squelching sequence called YC5C-H1 had any effect on the human colorectal cancer cell line HCT-15. In addition to preferentially squelching high expression genes, YC5C-H1 sharply slowed growth of HCT-15 cells.

items.title: Contrasting plasmid-host associations shape the distribution of enterotoxigenic E. coli (ETEC) colonization factors
items.corresponding_institution: 1: Department of Microbiology and Immunology, Institute of Biomedicine, Sahlgrenska Academy, University of Gothenburg, Gothenburg, Sweden; 2: Wallenberg Centre
items.abstract: Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC) causes a substantial burden of diarrhoeal disease, but how its virulence plasmids spread across E. coli populations remains unclear. We generated 479 complete ETEC genomes and combined them with 56 publicly available assemblies to produce the largest plasmid-resolved ETEC collection to date. Clustering of 903 virulence plasmids identified distinct plasmid lineages associated with individual colonization factors (CFs). Some CFs were carried by plasmids confined to a single ETEC lineage, consistent with long-term vertical maintenance, whereas others, including CS23 and CS12, were found on closely related conjugative plasmids distributed across multiple lineages, indicating horizontal transfer. Screening the AllTheBacteria dataset confirmed these patterns and revealed additional plasmid diversity for several CFs. Finally, we identified eight previously undescribed putative adhesion operons on toxin plasmids that may explain CF-negative ETEC isolates. These findings showed that plasmids, rather than bacterial lineages alone, shape the evolution and dissemination of ETEC virulence.

items.title: Stress granule transcript contrasts between colorectal cancer compartments depend on scoring and depth
items.corresponding_institution: The Affiliated Hospital of Guizhou Medical University
items.abstract: Stress granule (SG) gene-set scores summarize transcription associated with stress-response machinery, but their stability across scoring definitions is uncertain. We compared fibroblast-epithelial expression contrasts for four fixed SG lists in two colorectal cancer single-cell cohorts containing 195,527 cells from 85 donors. Analyses used donor pairing, gene-wise standardized expression, within-cell ranks and raw-count pseudobulk summaries, with tissue and sequencing-depth sensitivities. At least 20 tumor cells per compartment were available for 15 and 29 paired donors. Pseudobulk SG-A contrasts were negative in both cohorts: median differences in mean log2 counts per million were -0.383 (95% confidence interval -0.493 to -0.319) and -0.493 (-0.614 to -0.384). Rank-based SG-B contrasts were also negative in both cohorts. In a post hoc comparison using identical depth-retained cells and weights, the second cohort had positive gene-Z estimates and negative rank-based estimates; the positive estimates did not meet the eight-test false-discovery threshold. Spatial comparisons depended on the fibroblast reference subtype, and the CosMx panel measured only 11 of 27 SG-B genes. RNA-protein correlations varied across genes, while organoid depletion calls were more frequent for selected translation-associated members than for the four core members. These findings establish reproducible relative-expression contrasts under specified definitions and show that their direction can change across scoring and depth conditions. Reporting the scoring definition, retained donor population, depth sensitivity and gene coverage together identifies the contrasts that reproduce and provides a defined basis for testing their relationship to SG formation.

items.title: Identifying disease-associated dysbiosis in image-based spatial microbiome via MiSA
items.abstract: Background: Extensive studies have revealed the associations of microbiome dysbiosis with disease through compositional analysis of 16S rRNA amplicon or shotgun metagenomic sequencing data. However, dysbiosis in spatial organization of microbiome inhabiting the body sites and its implication for diseases remain understudied. Recently developed high phylogenetic resolution fluorescence in situ hybridization (HiPR-FISH) is an image-based mapping technology that provides spatial microbiome data at single-cell resolution, which allows for visualizing and quantifying spatial arrangement of microbial cells. Despite the growing availability of such data, no methods have been tailored to studying spatial dysbiosis in image-based microbiome data. Results: Here we introduce MiSA (Microbiome Spatial Aberration), the first statistical framework for identifying disease-associated spatial dysbiosis and the individual taxa that may contribute to it, based on differing degrees of clustering or regularity, i.e., microbial cells being more aggregated or more evenly spaced than expected under complete spatial randomness, between diagnostic groups. In simulations based on a real dataset, MiSA was robust across diverse and noisy spatial configurations, achieving substantially higher statistical power than a method borrowed from spatial proteomics, while controlling type I error at both the individual-taxon and community levels. When applied to an oral biofilm study, MiSA detected peri-implant mucositis-associated spatial dysbiosis at the community level and identified five taxa as potential contributors, including Actinomyces, which showed increased clustering in mucositis. Conclusions: MiSA is a powerful and robust framework for identifying spatial dysbiosis and the contributing taxa in image-based microbiome data, offering new insights into the spatial organization of microbial communities in disease.

items.title: Averaging in gene perturbation benchmarks hides perturbation-strength variation: Consequences for model evaluation
items.abstract: Perturbation-response benchmarks usually represent each genetic intervention by averaging all cells assigned that perturbation label. We inquire what perturbation-strength information is lost by this averaging, and whether current model predictions preserve enough perturbation-specific information for this perturbation-strength variation to be evaluated. Using X-Atlas/Orion CRISPRi screens, we use depth-corrected guide abundance as a cell-level proxy for perturbation strength and examine how transcriptional responses vary within a nominal perturbation. Higher perturbation strength is associated with greater response reproducibility. The effect is present in two human cell lines, HCT116 and HEK293T, but is larger in HCT116. For model evaluation, HCT116 retrieval tests show that observed responses preserve perturbation identity, whereas the evaluated STATE and Cell2Sentence predictions do not reliably recover it, hence the question of within-perturbation strength information cannot be meaningfully evaluated.

items.title: Flux Transformer learns intracellular metabolic fluxes from isotope labeling and measured reaction rates
items.abstract: Cells convert incoming nutrients into energy and biomass via metabolic fluxes. Quantifying these fluxes involves feeding cells isotope-labeled nutrients, quantifying metabolite labeling patterns, and inverting the labeling data to retrieve the underlying flux distribution. Traditional metabolic flux analysis (MFA) is both computationally expensive and frequently requires manual refinement of the cost function to obtain plausible results. For this reason, MFA has remained inaccessible to non-experts. Here we present Flux Transformer, an AI model that uses reaction-specific attention to integrate isotope-labeling data with available reaction-rate measurements, reconstructing mass-balanced steady-state fluxes. The model is trained on simulated data with added noise and identifies the underlying fluxes from these data more effectively than traditional MFA. Provided experimental data from wild-type and mutant bacteria, yeast, plants, and mammalian T cells, it efficiently and accurately recovers expert-curated MFA fluxes. By making flux analysis accessible, Flux Transformer is poised to accelerate metabolic research and engineering.

items.title: Gene set selection for classification with single-cell RNA-seq
items.abstract: Marker genes are important for analyzing and interpreting single-cell RNA-seq (scRNAseq) experiments. They are used to identify and categorize cell types and can also be useful for the design of downstream experiments. We present CellSieve, which tackles the problem of finding effective gene sets rather than distilling markers one at a time. While several "combinatorial" approaches to gene set selection have been proposed, we find that our approach, which leverages a combination of multinomial logistic regression and linear programming, is much more effective at finding small gene sets that can classify cell types.

items.title: ERM proteins antagonistically control cancer invasion and metastasis via mechanosensing regulation
items.abstract: Metastasis requires cancer cells to overcome anchorage dependence and rewire mechanosensing pathways. Here, we identify the ERM proteins ezrin, radixin, and moesin as key but antagonistic regulators of breast cancer metastasis. Expression profiling across matched low- and high-metastatic breast cancer models revealed consistent upregulation of all three ERM proteins in highly metastatic cells. Despite this, ezrin depletion reduced colony formation, invasion, and lung metastasis, whereas radixin or moesin depletion enhanced these phenotypes. Loss of radixin or moesin increased ezrin localization at the cell edge, while ezrin depletion reduced membrane-associated moesin, indicating a dynamic balance among ERM proteins. Ezrin depletion also increased focal adhesion size and number, FAK activation, and force transmission to the extracellular matrix, whereas radixin or moesin silencing produced opposite effects. Cellular force magnitude was inversely correlated with invasion, and pharmacological modulation of contractility reverted the effects of ERM depletion. These findings reveal an ERM-dependent mechanosensing checkpoint that regulates metastasis through control of adhesion dynamics and force transmission.

items.title: Ion channel-enhancing nanoparticles reprogram T cells in vivo for cancer immunotherapy
items.abstract: In head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), immunotherapy is frequently ineffective due to the impaired ability of tumor-infiltrating T cells to sustain calcium-dependent cytotoxic effector functions. Kv1.3 potassium channels in T cells are essential for maintaining membrane potential, which is necessary for Ca2+ influx; however, they are suppressed within the tumor microenvironment, and no pharmacologic Kv1.3 activators are currently available. To address this limitation, we developed lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) functionalized with anti-CD5 antibodies to specifically deliver mRNA encoding Kv1.3 (KCNA3) to T cells, thereby increasing channel expression and function. Treatment of human T cells with KCNA3-LNPs resulted in increased Kv1.3 channel protein levels and activity, leading to enhanced Ca2+ influx and elevated secretion of effector cytokines (IL-2, IL-17, TNF-, and IFN-{gamma}) and cytotoxic molecules (Granzyme A, Perforin, Granulysin, and Fas ligand). In a human peripheral blood mononuclear cell-engrafted HNSCC humanized mouse model, peritumoral delivery of KCNA3-LNPs significantly reduced tumor burden and increased the infiltration of CD8 Granzyme B cytotoxic T cells within the tumor, indicating improved antitumor immunity. Our study demonstrates that in vivo reprogramming of T cells through targeted Kv1.3 enhancement can overcome immunosuppressive barriers within the tumor microenvironment and enhance immune-mediated tumor clearance in vivo. This novel approach offers a scalable and cost-effective alternative to ex vivo T cell engineering and holds promise as a therapeutic strategy to improve immunotherapy outcomes in HNSCC and other solid tumors characterized by Kv1.3-dependent immune dysfunctions.

items.title: β-catenin/TCF signaling represses GUCY2C hormone expression through a p38α-GATA2 axis in colorectal cancer
items.abstract: Guanylin (GUCA2A) and uroguanylin (GUCA2B) are paracrine hormone ligands of the tumor-suppressor receptor guanylyl cyclase C (GUCY2C). In early colorectal tumorigenesis, expression of GUCA2A and GUCA2B is silenced through transcriptional repression by APC-regulated {beta}-catenin/TCF signaling, a pathway activated early in malignant transformation. This repression depends on a locus control region (LCR) 1,000-3,683 bp upstream of GUCA2A. Here, we used dCas9-APEX2 biotinylation at genomic elements by restricted spatial tagging (C-BERST) in colorectal cancer (CRC) cell lines with inducible suppression of {beta}-catenin/TCF signaling to identify {beta}-catenin/TCF-regulated proteins associated with the GUCA2A regulatory region that mediate repression of GUCY2C ligand transcription. Guide RNAs were used to direct dCas9-APEX2 for locus-specific proximity biotinylation of proteins. Quantitative mass spectrometry identified p38 (MAPK14) as a candidate regulator enriched near the GUCA2A promoter following {beta}-catenin/TCF suppression. Loss-of-function and rescue experiments established that p38 supports GUCA2A and GUCA2B induction following {beta}-catenin/TCF suppression. Importantly, GATA2 was identified as a p38-dependent activator of GUCA2A and GUCA2B transcription that remained enriched near the GUCA2A promoter independent of {beta}-catenin/TCF signaling. Indeed, GATA2 S192 phosphorylation was reduced by p38 loss and by active {beta}-catenin/TCF signaling. Thus, a p38/GATA2 axis links oncogenic {beta}-catenin/TCF signaling to repression of GUCY2C hormone expression in CRC.

items.title: A multimodal arrayed Perturb-seq platform for dissecting microglial state dynamics and target identification
items.corresponding_institution: Neuroscience, Novartis Biomedical Research, Cambridge, MA, USA
items.abstract: Microglia are highly dynamic immune cells of the central nervous system that can adopt diverse functional states in health and disease, making them both emerging therapeutic targets and challenging systems for target identification. Here, we developed TF-iMG, a human pluripotent stem cell-derived transcription factor-induced microglia model generated by inducible expression of SPI1 and CEBPA in Cas9-expressing stem cells. TF-iMG rapidly acquired microglia-like transcriptomic, morphological, inflammatory, and phagocytic features while remaining compatible with efficient lentiviral CRISPR knockout workflows that can be completed within one week. We next established an arrayed multimodal Perturb-seq platform that integrates lentiviral CRISPR knockout, multiplexed single-cell RNA sequencing, cytokine profiling, and live-cell imaging. Single-cell analysis showed that TF-iMG recapitulates intrinsic microglial heterogeneity and captures homeostatic, activated, inflammatory, and proliferative signatures. Stimulation with IL1B and IL4 reproducibly induced distinct pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory states, respectively, providing a framework for perturbation-based interrogation of microglial state regulation. Targeting IL1B and IL4 pathway components validated the platform by attenuating expected stimulus-driven state shifts. Profiling of putative microglial regulators and Alzheimer's disease-associated genes further revealed perturbation-specific transcriptional signatures, altered state occupancy, and multimodal phenotypes spanning cytokine release, morphology, and trajectory. Together, this platform enables scalable target identification in microglia.

items.title: Spatial atlas of gut-draining lymph nodes reveals the developmental organization of intestinal tolerance and immunity
items.abstract: Early life offers a window to establish lasting tolerance to dietary and commensal microbial antigens. How developing gut lymph nodes balance tolerance and immunity remains unclear. Using spatial transcriptomics, we map small intestine- and colon-draining nodes during weaning and adulthood, resolving rare immune and stromal populations and their niches, including Thetis cells (TCs), an antigen-presenting lineage critical for intestinal tolerance. We uncover a peri-weaning subcapsular compartment enriched for TC I but depleted of classical antigen-relaying macrophages, coincident with attenuated follicular responses. Peri-weaning colonic nodes are hubs of T cell activation enriched for peripherally-induced regulatory T (pTreg) cell responses. We resolve distinct classical dendritic cell (cDC) and TC niches, including a pTreg-associated niche shared by TC IV and CCR7 cDC2. We further characterize a distinct population of intestinal tissue TCs, and establish TC migration to draining lymph nodes. Together, our atlas provides a framework for understanding how the timing of intestinal antigen exposure intersects with developing lymph node niches to shape tolerance or immunity.

items.title: Continuous generation of short-lived resident effector CD8 T cells sustains alopecia areata
items.abstract: CD8 T cells mediating chronic tissue inflammation have been thought to depend on stem-like progenitors that self-renew and replenish cytotoxic effector cells or exhausted progeny. Here, we show that stem-independent, short-lived resident effector CD8 T (TRE) cells sustain alopecia areata (AA), a common autoimmune disease that destroys hair follicles. AA-TRE cells exhibit TCR-dependent cytotoxicity, undergo rapid apoptosis in the skin, and lack memory or stem-like properties. Following adoptive transfer, donor TRE cells serve only as an initial trigger, whereas the host-derived CD103CD101 pathogenic pool is rebuilt continuously in skin-draining lymph nodes (sdLNs). Single-cell multiome and CUT&Tag profiling revealed that AA-TRE cells epigenetically silence Tox and upregulate RUNX2 to initiate the TRE differentiation program in sdLNs, while RUNX3 and AP-1s sustain it in the skin. Notably, CD8 T cells from patients with AA share this conserved regulatory network. Altogether, these findings define a distinct CD8 T cell differentiation state, offering new therapeutic implications for autoimmune diseases.

items.title: Cell identity and activation state determine the innate immune response to nanoplastics
items.abstract: Autoimmune disease is on the rise, and while no direct connection has been made, evidence suggests environmental toxins such as nanoplastics may be contributing to the increased incidence. A key factor in the onset of autoimmunity is inflammation; yet how nanoplastics impact innate immune function is unclear. Here, we exposed primary human neutrophils, macrophages, and endothelial cells to biocorona-coated polystyrene nanoplastics at physiologically relevant concentrations. All cells internalized nanoplastics without viability loss, but functional consequences diverged. Neutrophils increased myeloperoxidase release as nanoplastic concentration increased. Endothelial cells reduced leukocyte-recruiting mediator secretion and had decreased neutrophil adhesion following inflammatory stimulation. M1 macrophages broadly upregulated inflammatory cytokine secretion (including TNF- and IL-6), whereas M0 and M2 macrophages exhibited no significant secretory changes. Collectively, these findings indicate physiologically relevant nanoplastic concentrations do not universally increase inflammation but rather dysregulate innate immune populations in a manner that could contribute to autoimmunity.

items.title: CCDC81 is a conserved microtubule-binding protein that maintains centriole integrity
items.abstract: Centrioles are microtubule-based organelles that exhibit a highly conserved architecture that is essential for their function. However, the molecular mechanisms maintaining their structural integrity remain incompletely understood. Here, we characterize CCDC81 as a conserved microtubule-binding protein that contributes to centriole organization. Using expansion microscopy, we localize CCDC81 to the A-C linker of Chlamydomonas basal bodies, where it associates with POC11, the homolog of human A-C linker protein CCDC77. We demonstrate that CCDC81 directly binds microtubules through its N-terminal HU domains, promotes microtubule bundling, and stabilizes microtubules by reducing depolymerization and increasing rescue frequency. Cryo-electron microscopy further reveals its association with the outer microtubule lattice. We identify distinct domains mediating CCDC81 interaction with POC11 and propose a molecular organization of this complex within the A-C linker. Importantly, CCDC81 also localizes to human centrioles, where its depletion disrupts centriole architecture and A-C linker organization, with defects exacerbated by co-depletion of CCDC77. Together, our findings establish CCDC81 as a conserved regulator of microtubule organization and centriole structural integrity.

items.title: pH Gradient Drives Redox Reactions in the Nucleolar Caps to Modulate Nucleolar Integrity and Function
items.corresponding_institution: Clinical Research Institute, The First Affiliated Hospital of Xiamen University, State Key  Laboratory of Cellular Stress Biology, School of Life Sciences, Facu
items.abstract: While enzymatic catalysis is the main driver of redox processes in cells, biomolecular condensates exhibit unique electrochemical properties that can potentiate redox reactions. Nevertheless, the regulatory mechanisms governing the electrochemical equilibrium of biomolecular condensates and their influence on the emergent physicochemical functions remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that specific nucleolar stressors induce alkaline nucleolar caps, which generate an interfacial pH gradient and electrical potential that drive spontaneous redox reactions. Non-enzymatic reactive oxygen species (ROS) production depends on positively charged constituents within the nucleolar caps and correlates strongly with the pH microenvironment. Excessive ROS directly modulates the partition and diffusion of proteins rich in redox-sensitive residues, whereas scavenging ROS markedly accelerates the recovery of nucleolar multiphase organization and functionality upon stress removal. Collectively, our findings propose a non-enzymatic redox mechanism operating within cellular condensates and highlight the critical role of physical interfaces in orchestrating the chemical dynamics of biomolecular condensates

items.title: Autophagy induction by cytoplasmic Acinus requires Lrrk activity
items.corresponding_institution: University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center
items.abstract: Autophagy is a critical pathway for maintaining cellular health in ageing and disease but mechanisms matching levels of autophagy to different stress conditions remain incompletely understood. In response to proteostasis stress, autophagy is induced upon activation of Acinus, a mostly nuclear protein previously linked to alternative splicing as a subunit of the ASAP complex. Here, we show that Acinus induces autophagy independently of its function in splicing. Instead, autophagic flux is promoted by mutations of Acinus that either disrupt its interaction with the ASAP complex or otherwise increase its cytoplasmic fraction. Proximity labeling of the proteome preferentially associated with cytoplasmic rather than nuclear Acinus identified Rab32. Genetic analysis revealed that the Rab32 GTPase and its effector Lrrk kinase are required for autophagy induction by activated Acinus, in contrast to Lrrk-independent mTor-regulated autophagy. This specific requirement in Acinus-regulated autophagy has possible implications for Parkinson's disease for which mutants in the human orthologs of Rab32 and Lrrk constitute risk factors.

items.title: pbzarr: cohort-scale storage and analysis of per-base genomic data with Zarr
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Human Genetics and Utah Center for Genetic Discovery, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, UT, USA
items.abstract: Genomic assays now produce per-base signals for cohorts comprising thousands of samples. However, existing genomic data storage formats (e.g., D4, bigWig) were designed primarily for single samples or individual datasets. Consequently, cohort-scale analyses across samples, populations, or species require opening, reading, and merging thousands of files before proceeding to downstream computational analyses. Here, we present pbzarr, a format and toolkit that stores per-base genomic data from many samples and assays as a single Zarr store. Across multiple datasets, pbzarr simplified cohort construction to a single command and created cohort-scale datasets up to 2.1x faster than existing approaches while simultaneously using 5-6x less memory. More importantly, pbzarr compresses signal tracks to only a fraction of the input data size, using only 3.3% of the input size to store per-base coverage for 1,024 short-read genomes. Despite this smaller storage footprint, pbzarr maintains fast access to underlying genomic data: region-based queries complete 61x faster than D4 and 6x faster than bigWig, and full-genome scans are as fast or faster than existing formats. Finally, because pbzarr stores are native Zarr arrays, it integrates directly with widely used array libraries (e.g., Xarray and Dask), allowing cohort-scale analyses to be expressed in a single line of Python code using standard array operations instead of a complex, custom pipeline. Together, our results suggest that pbzarr is dramatically smaller, substantially simpler, and faster than competing formats for biobank-scale analysis. pbzarr is open source and available at https://github.com/pbzarr/pbzarr.

items.title: A toolkit to identify parameter degeneracy and solution manifolds of Hodgkin-Huxley type current models
items.abstract: Countless studies have fitted Hodgkin-Huxley (HH) type models of active currents to voltage clamp data using nonlinear least squares. Yet, little is known about the uniqueness of parameter solutions and the interdependence of HH-type model parameters. Here, we show that considerable insight can be gained from the singular value decomposition (SVD) of a matrix closely related to the objective function used in the fitting procedure. After fitting all model parameters simultaneously using synthetic data originating from a representative range of experimental cases, this reveals that a manifold of solutions is possible depending on the type of voltage clamp data available and on the selected HH-type model. In such cases, we use the SVD to determine which parameters are least identifiable. Next, we develop an SVD-based manifold tracing technique that can efficiently unveil the structure of the manifold of equivalent solutions in the parameter space of the model. Our methods also identify parameter interdependencies and their impact on joint parameter confidence regions. The most salient one consistently observed across our experimental examples was between the peak conductance and reversal potential of active HH-type current models. The SVD-based strategy presented here is expected to be generally applicable to investigate parameter degeneracy and solution manifold structure in biophysical models of single neurons. Thus, our results should prove valuable for understanding the constraints imposed by the biophysics of ion channels on single neuron computation.

items.title: Extracellular vesicles from alternatively activated macrophages remodel the injured hepatic niche and promote repair
items.abstract: Alternatively activated macrophages (AAMs) are in clinical development for acute liver injury, but their mechanisms of action remain incompletely understood. AAM therapy remodels the injured hepatic niche, promoting reparative macrophage states, suppressing inflammatory myeloid programmes and restoring hepatocyte metabolic and biosynthetic programmes. We identify extracellular vesicles released by AAMs (AAM-EVs) as essential mediators of AAM therapeutic activity. AAM-EVs enhance macrophage phagocytosis and induce reparative transcriptional and proteomic responses, including increased TREM2 abundance. Following administration in established APAP injury, AAM-EVs reduce necrosis and neutrophilic inflammation, and promote hepatocellular regeneration, and we observe preferential and rapid association of AAM-EVs with hepatic macrophages alongside reparative phenotypic shift. Moreover, pharmacological inhibition of EV release attenuates parent AAM efficacy and TREM2 macrophage accumulation, while EVs derived from Dicer-deficient AAMs exhibit reduced therapeutic activity, implicating miRNA-associated mechanisms. Comparative single-nucleus transcriptomics reveals overlapping but distinct macrophage and hepatocyte responses to AAMs and AAM-EVs. Together, these findings identify EV-mediated communication as an important mechanism of macrophage-induced liver repair and support the development of AAM-EVs as a cell-free therapeutic strategy.

items.title: Polymer type and surface functionalization determine the impact of nanoplastics on neural crest cell adhesion, migration, proliferation, and apoptosis in primary cultures.
items.abstract: Nanoplastics (NP) constitutes a pervasive source of environmental pollution that contaminates all ecosystems, the atmosphere and freshwater. They are absorbed by living organisms and cross biological barriers, with increasing evidence pointing to their harmful effects both at cellular levels and in whole organisms. The impacts of NPs vary not only depending on their size and concentration, but also on the cell type, the polymer composition and surface charge, requiring a comprehensive understanding of the responses of a wide range of cells to these parameters. Because neural crest cells (NCC) are highly proliferative and migratory embryonic progenitors that contribute to a wide range of tissues, they provide a relevant model for investigating the impact of environmental pollutants on developmental cell behaviors. Using a well-established primary NCC culture system, we show that polypropylene (PP) and polyethylene (PE) NPs are more detrimental than polystyrene (PS) NPs to NCC survival and proliferation in a dose-dependent manner. These effects were particularly pronounced for amine-functionalized NPs, which increased NCC apoptosis compared with carboxylate-functionalized NPs. In addition, amine-functionalized PP and PE NPs shortened NCC production period and strongly decrease cell adhesion and migration through alterations of substrate adhesions. Our results indicate that NPs disrupt key biological processes of NCCs, depending on the polymer type and surface functionalization and might contribute to the pathogenesis of structures derived from the NCCs.

items.title: Isolate relatedness is more strongly associated with host and geography compared with phenotypic variation in a broad host range pathogen
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Plant Pathology, University of Wisconsin-Madison, Madison, WI 53706, U.S.A and Wisconsin Institute for Discovery, Madison, WI 53706, U.S.A.
items.abstract: Determining the drivers of diversity in plant pathogen populations is a critical for developing effective management strategies. Sclerotinia sclerotiorum, a cosmopolitan fungus infecting over 400 plant species, causes considerable yield and economic losses worldwide. However, longstanding questions remain about the association between genetic and phenotypic variation in this pathogen, leaving the drivers of its diversification unresolved. Here, we characterized the diversity of S. sclerotiorum isolates from the United States in a global context and tested the hypothesis that phylogenetic relatedness structures phenotypic variation among isolates. Genome-wide variant analysis resolved US isolates into several distinct lineages, with short within-lineage branch lengths consistent with recent common ancestry or clonal propagation. Population structure analysis confirmed two major global clusters, one composed predominantly of Australian isolates and the other largely of isolates from the rest of the world, including the US. Notably, several US isolates grouped within the Australian cluster, suggesting historical intercontinental movement of this pathogen. Contrary to our expectations, isolate relatedness was more strongly associated with data such as host, geographic origin, and year of collection compared with morphological variation, suggesting that phenotypic variation segregates independently of phylogenetic structure. Instead, the distribution of phenotypic variation primarily reflected two trade-offs: rapid radial growth with shorter sclerotial development versus slower growth with prolonged sclerotial development, and the production of many small sclerotia versus fewer larger ones. Together, our results shed light on the complex relationships between phenotypic, ecological, and phylogenetic variation and bring us one step closer to predicting how diversity is structured in natural populations of a global fungal pathogen.

items.title: Dynamics of somatic L1 retrotransposition in the human brain
items.abstract: The sole source of genomic diversity in the human brain caused by autonomous retrotransposition is facilitated by the long interspersed nuclear element-1 (L1). However, assessing the rate, timing and source elements of this event has been challenging due to the lack of technologies that capture of L1s at sufficient scale in single cells. Here, we introduce LUSTRE, a single-cell assay that enables mapping L1 sites without whole-genome amplification, and profile ~17,600 neurons from the dentate gyrus, cortex, cerebellum of the adult human brain. We report the presence of somatic L1s that define related lineages and conservatively estimate a validation-adjusted rate of 0.1-0.3 somatic events per neuron. Our analyses further indicate two distinct waves of retrotransposition during development and combined with the variability in their polyA tract lengths across single nuclei, suggest the formation of lineage hierarchies marked by new somatic retrotransposition events and cell divisions. Mapping the origin of L1s through 3'-transduction events identify the rare source L1s that are responsible for the majority of retrotransposition events. These results uncover the dynamics of L1-driven somatic mosaicism and establish L1s as endogenous recorders of cellular and lineage history in human tissues.

items.title: CATEomics: model selection and ensembling for heterogeneous treatment effect estimation from high-dimensional omics data
items.abstract: CATEomics addresses the lack of a standardized and reproducible process for choosing among conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimators in high-dimensional omics studies, where their estimation errors cannot be evaluated directly from observed outcomes. The R package accepts a SummarizedExperiment, applies common preprocessing and data partitions across R and Python estimators, compares their out-of-fold estimates using proxy losses, supports model selection and ensembling, and returns the resulting CATE estimates to the original object for downstream omics analysis. Availability and implementation: CATEomics is implemented in R and is freely available under the MIT license at https://github.com/matsui-lab/CATEomics. The software version described here (v0.99.0) is archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.24189754. A vignette illustrates the complete workflow from a SummarizedExperiment to downstream analysis.

items.title: Neural processing of linguistic speech features and their modulation by selective attention in users of hearing aids and cochlear implants
items.abstract: Understanding speech relies on the neural processing of acoustic and linguistic features, which can both be analyzed using Temporal Response Functions (TRFs). While both types of features have been the focus of numerous studies in typical-hearing individuals, much less is known about the neural processing of continuous speech for people with hearing loss, particularly how hearing-impaired listeners process word-level features in noisy environments, where they typically struggle. We recorded EEG from hearing aid (HA, n=29) and cochlear implant (CI, n=24) users, and an age-matched typical-hearing (TH) control group (n=29), while participants listened to audiobook segments in quiet and with a competing speaker, using their personal hearing devices (CI and HA). A hierarchical encoding framework incrementally added word onset, word frequency, and word surprisal as predictors of the EEG signal. Attentional modulation was assessed by comparing encoding scores for attended versus ignored speech. All three groups showed clear neural responses to word onset, frequency, and surprisal for speech in quiet. Surprisal tracking emerged at 400~ms in TH participants, 500~ms in HA users, and 600~ms in CI users, weakest in the CI group. All three groups exhibited attentional modulation of surprisal tracking. Word frequency yielded significant encoding gains in quiet only for TH and HI listeners, not CI users. We show for the first time that CI users exhibit significant, attention-modulated neural responses to word surprisal. More broadly, surprisal tracking was present across all hearing-impaired groups but weakest in CI users, the cohort with the greatest difficulty understanding speech in noise.

items.title: Depletion of LKB1 in cerebellar granule cells affects parallel fiber-Purkinje cell synaptic organization and causes progressive locomotion deficits
items.abstract: integrates sensory and motor information and transmits signals to the muscles via motor neurons. The sole cerebellar output neurons, Purkinje cells (PCs), receive two main inputs from climbing fibers (CFs) and parallel fibers (PFs), which are the axons of granule cells (GCs). The serine/threonine kinase liver kinase B1 (LKB1) regulates GC migration; however, its role in PF synapses remains unclear. We generated a novel strain of mice with a LKB1 conditional knockout (cKO) in GCs during the postnatal period to investigate the presynaptic function of LKB1. LKB1 cKO mice exhibited progressive declines in motor coordination, whereas general locomotor activity was preserved. Morphological analysis revealed shrinkage of the cerebellar molecular layer with increased microglial density, suggesting degenerative remodeling of PF-PC synapses. Conventional electron microscopy showed a slight increase in the PF terminal area in LKB1 cKO mice, whereas three-dimensional reconstructions revealed no significant differences in bouton morphology except for an increased mitochondrial volume ratio. In contrast, the proportion of PF boutons forming multiple synapses with PC spines was higher in LKB1 cKO mice than in controls, potentially altering synaptic inputs to PCs and contributing to downstream changes in cerebellar output and reduced presynaptic occupancy at neuromuscular junctions. These findings highlight the importance of LKB1 in GCs for maintaining PF-PC synaptic remodeling and cerebellar circuit integrity, which may contribute to motor coordination.

items.title: A plasma proteomic atlas of rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorders reveals convergent molecular signatures, neurodegenerative overlap, and a cross-disorder severity index
items.abstract: Rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorders are individually too small for well-powered biomarker studies, and each is typically studied alone. We present a harmonized plasma proteomic resource that treats them together: over 10,000 proteins measured across 27 rare genetic neurodevelopmental disorders and unaffected family members, 26 of them with enough participants for differential abundance analysis, paired with standardized adaptive behaviour phenotypes and released with the full analysis pipeline. Aggregating across disorders makes shared biology visible that single-disorder studies cannot resolve. Genetically distinct disorders converge onto two proteomic clusters separated along a single dominant axis, distinguishing cytoskeletal and vesicle-trafficking proteins from metabolic and hepatic ones; the grouping is independent of gene function and of clinical classification, indicating convergence on shared downstream biology rather than gene-specific pathology. Epilepsy leaves a reproducible plasma signature detectable across disorders and largely independent of genotype, identifying candidate markers of seizure burden that are shared rather than syndrome specific. These proteomes also overlap those of adult neurodegenerative disease: most disorders are enriched against at least one signature of Alzheimer disease, Parkinson disease, frontotemporal dementia or amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, more often inversely than concordantly, placing early-life monogenic disorders on a shared axis with late-onset degeneration. A multivariate severity index built from plasma proteins tracks adaptive communication ability in disorders held out entirely from model training and distinguishes severity among individuals who share a diagnosis rather than only separating disorders from one another. Twenty-four of the prioritised cross-disorder proteins have a recorded drug interaction, several with agents already approved for other indications. Recruitment was concentrated at single sites for a subset of disorders, and results for those disorders are reported separately and descriptively throughout. Collectively, these findings support a shift from single-gene to pathway-based, cross-disorder trial strategies that leverage convergent biomarker panels and mechanistically informed, potentially repurposed interventions.

items.title: CAS-X: A Probabilistic Multi-Tissue eQTL Framework for Prioritizing Candidate Effector Genes at Type 2 Diabetes Risk Loci
items.corresponding_institution: A.V. College of Arts, Science & Commerce (Autonomous), Osmania University
items.abstract: The genetic etiology of Type 2 Diabetes (T2D) involves regulatory mechanisms operating across multiple metabolic tissues. However, candidate effector gene prioritization can be limited by approaches that focus predominantly on pancreatic transcriptomics. To address this limitation, we developed CAS-X, a computational multi-tissue functional genomics framework for prioritizing candidate effector genes at T2D susceptibility loci. CAS-X integrates fine-mapped Posterior Inclusion Probabilities (PIP) and allelic fold changes (aFC) across five tissues: pancreas, skeletal muscle, subcutaneous adipose, visceral adipose, and whole blood. In the reported analysis, multi-tissue integration identified 28 candidate genes meeting the selected prioritization threshold, compared with 12 under the pancreas-only baseline, representing a 133.3% increase in candidate coverage. Prioritized candidates included JAZF1, FTO, GRB14, and CDKN2B. Framework robustness was examined through Leave-One-Tissue-Out sensitivity analysis and comparisons with non-metabolic GTEx Brain Cortex controls. Pathway enrichment analysis highlighted associations with insulin resistance, adipocytokine signaling, and lipolysis regulation. The analysis also incorporated phenome-wide associations and computational assessments of therapeutic tractability. CAS-X provides a computational approach for integrating regulatory evidence across metabolic tissues to support candidate effector gene prioritization in T2D research.

items.title: Electrophysiological correlates of placebo hypoalgesia and nocebo hyperalgesia during the anticipation and delivery of pain
items.abstract: Positive and negative expectations can substantially shape pain and analgesic treatment outcomes, highlighting the need to elucidate neural mechanisms underlying placebo hypoalgesia and nocebo hyperalgesia. The primary aim of this feasibility study was to assess adaptations to an established placebo-nocebo conditioning pain paradigm in the context of electroencephalography (EEG). The secondary aim was to assess EEG correlates of placebo hypoalgesia and nocebo hyperalgesia during the anticipation and delivery of experimental heat pain in healthy volunteers. Placebo hypoalgesia and nocebo hyperalgesia were induced in a within-subjects design in 20 young adults through verbal instructions, a conditioning procedure and (sham) transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation while EEG was recorded. Placebo and nocebo effects as well as positive and negative pain expectations were successfully established, demonstrating paradigm effectiveness. EEG results showed increased theta, alpha and beta power in the placebo compared to the control condition during pain delivery, and in the nocebo compared to the control condition during pain anticipation and delivery. Additionally, gamma-band power was increased in the nocebo compared to the placebo condition as a function of a higher perceived pain intensity. Taken together, feasibility of the EEG-compatible placebo-nocebo conditioning pain paradigm was demonstrated. Furthermore, our EEG results are in line with previous findings that, in the context of placebo hypoalgesia and nocebo hyperalgesia, link theta-, alpha- and beta-band activity to top-down processing, and gamma-band activity to expectation-modulated sensory processing.

items.title: Implication of the amyloid precursor protein expressed in GABAergic interneurons for CA3 neuronal dynamics
items.corresponding_institution: Interdisciplinary Institute for Neuroscience, Univ Bordeaux, CNRS
items.abstract: The amyloid precursor protein (APP), a key player in Alzheimers' disease (AD, is ubiquitously expressed in a large majority of neurons, including GABAergic interneurons (INTs) in the hippocampus. INT dysfunction and subsequent abnormalities in neural circuits have emerged as potential mechanisms of cognitive decline in AD. How APP expressed in selective classes of hippocampal INTs controls local neuronal activity and thereby influences brain rhythms remains unclear. We investigated the physiological function of APP in GABAergic INTs with regard to intrinsic excitability, synaptic properties and circuit activity in the hippocampal CA3 region. We selectively deleted APP, and its homolog APLP2 to prevent compensatory mechanisms, in CA3 INTs. We categorized INTs into different clusters based on morphological and electrophysiological properties, and detected only subtle differences in intrinsic excitability and dendritic complexity between control and conditional KO INTs. In contrast, the selective deletion of APP/APLP2 in CA3 INTs impaired the amplitude and kinetics of spontaneous inhibitory currents in CA3 pyramidal cells (PCs). We further performed in vivo silicon probe recordings within CA3 in head-fixed awake mice to investigate the impact of APP/APLP2 deletion on CA3 circuit activity. By analysing oscillations and the spiking activity of putative CA3 PCs and INTs we revealed alterations in the cross-frequency coupling at oscillatory frequencies in the low gamma range, as well as in the strength of connections specifically between INTs. Our work helps better understand the physiological contribution of APP to network activity and to excitatory/inhibitory balance within hippocampal circuits, which are impaired in AD.

items.title: Probe-assisted Structural Topography Reveals In-tissue Lesion Heterogeneity in Alzheimer's Disease
items.abstract: Disease lesions are typically defined by morphology, yet this classification often masks underlying structural heterogeneity. In Alzheimer's disease (AD), amyloid-{beta} (A{beta}) plaques appear as featureless deposits under conventional microscopy, obscuring distinct sub-regions with divergent packing, maturation, and pathological potential. Here, we present Probe-Assisted Structural Topography of Amyloid (PASTA), a single-staining framework that combines a novel pan-A{beta} probe (NapIM) with fluorescence lifetime-resolved detection and super-resolution microscopy to unmask this hidden complexity. Leveraging PASTA, we quantify plaque maturity via the Protofibril Index (PFI) at sub-lesion level, and resolve the three-dimensional (3D) in-tissue architecture of A{beta} plaques at ~30 nm resolution, identifying radially extended A{beta} branches as fundamental structural units. PASTA enables structural mapping across plaque developmental stages to reconstruct their dynamic growth trajectories, resolving two distinct assembly lineages (dense and loose) with divergent growth paths that converge to a mixed terminal subtype and share a common transition point. We further applied PASTA for mapping microglial engagement, linking interdigitated microglial contacts to dense plaque compaction and uncontacted fibril branches to loose morphology. Together, PASTA provides an unprecedented framework for understanding A{beta} heterogeneity, nanoscale architecture, and microglial-mediated remodeling in AD.

items.title: Switch from inflammatory signaling to excessive extracellular matrix remodeling in fibrotic fibroblasts attenuates monocyte tissue infiltration
items.abstract: Tissue damage induces infiltration of monocytes that differentiate into macrophages and cooperate with fibroblasts in tissue repair. If repair fails and tissue stress persists, a feedforward loop involving high contractility of activated fibroblasts, extracellular matrix (ECM) stiffening, and TGF-{beta}1 signaling can lead to chronic fibrosis characterized by hypertrophic scarring. In advanced fibrotic tissues areas devoid of immune infiltration have been detected but how the interplay between chemotactic signals versus ECM remodeling impacts monocyte infiltration and spatial positioning in such late-stage fibrotic tissues is unresolved. To address this, we designed a series of 3D co-culture formats incorporating fibrillar collagen I-based ECM, human fibroblasts, and primary human monocytes. RNA-seq, secretome analysis, and confocal microscopy showed that collagen-embedded fibroblasts strongly upregulated inflammatory signaling compared to 2D fibroblast cultures. Incorporation of fibroblasts enhanced collagen fiber network porosity and stimulated monocyte entry into collagen hydrogels and their migration within the collagen network. TGF-{beta}1 activation of collagen-embedded fibroblasts caused a striking switch from inflammatory signaling to an ECM remodeling signature, which was accompanied by local ECM accumulation around fibroblasts and a pronounced increase in collagen fiber network pore size. This did not affect overall fibroblast-stimulated monocyte migration through the ECM, but it prevented monocytes from crossing liquid-hydrogel barriers to penetrate the collagen network. Moreover, it caused excessive ECM remodeling near clusters of fibroblasts, which locally arrested monocyte migration. These findings indicate that excessive fibroblast activation in fibrotic tissues can shift the balance from chemotactic cues toward biomechanical constraints, which limits monocyte infiltration and locally restricts monocyte migration.

items.title: Domain-informed effector gene assignment exposes training-data dependence of drug target prioritisation from GWAS
items.corresponding_institution: Health Data Modelling, Berlin Institute of Health at Charité - Universitätsmedizin Berlin, Germany
items.abstract: About 90% of trait-associated lead variants lie outside protein-coding regions, so nominating the effector gene at genome-wide association study (GWAS) loci remains the principal bottleneck in translating associations into biological insight. Since no experimentally resolved ground truth exists at scale, every method rests on quasi-true-positive sets dominated by a single line of evidence. Here, we benchmarked established prioritisation methods across three independent evaluation sets, trained five models each informed by a different biological domain, and annotated lead variants for six common diseases. Performance did not transfer across domains (AUPRC 0.91 to 0.46 for the same method), and we traced this to how differently models weight the distance between variant and gene (p<5.3x10-123), not to how they were built. Curation assumptions propagated into predictions and can become self-confirming, such as druggability in the Open Targets-informed model. The five models shared only 17.1% to 31.8% of effector gene assignments, converging on established disease biology but diverging where GWAS are expected to yield novel insight. Recovery of 340 approved drug targets differed markedly between models, and no way of combining them, by averaging scores (38.8%) or training on all curations jointly (36.5%), approached the 52.1% recovered across all five together. Our workflow matched Open Targets L2G across three annotation sets without prior biological knowledge and exceeded it where curated knowledge already linked gene and disease. We provide the Domain-informed EFfector gene Assignment framework (DEFA; https://github.com/lkohleick/DEFA), which reports rather than hides the curation assumption behind each gene assignment so that it can be examined and tested.

items.title: Single-dose neonatal gene therapy preserves motor coordination and extends survival of Polg-deficient mice
items.abstract: POLG mutations are the most common single nuclear gene cause of mitochondrial disease. POLG disease spans a spectrum of clinical presentations with variable age of onset and severity. Early-onset disease is often severe and fatal (e.g., Alpers syndrome, myocerebrohepatopathy), while late-onset disease can be relatively mild (e.g., progressive external ophthalmoplegia). POLG disease is incurable, with few symptomatic treatments available, none of which can prevent its progression. Gene replacement therapy has the potential to halt or prevent POLG disease, but its development has been hindered by the large size of the POLG cDNA and the scarcity of suitable mouse models. Here, we developed a bespoke Polg knockout (KO) mouse model by inactivating the Polg locus in parvalbumin-expressing neurons (e.g., Purkinje cells) and fast-twitch skeletal muscle fibers. KO mice developed progressive motor coordination deficits, respiratory chain deficiency in Purkinje cells and skeletal muscle, and died prematurely. We also developed nine AAV-based gene therapy vectors and confirmed their ability to deliver and express the human POL{gamma}A protein in different mouse tissues. A single high-dose administration of either of two lead candidates into Polg KO neonates preserved respiratory chain activity in Purkinje cells and skeletal muscle, delayed the onset of motor coordination deficits, and extended lifespan. Thus, our work provides preclinical proof of concept for gene replacement therapy for POLG disease, establishing the feasibility of this approach and laying the foundation for further development in the field.

items.title: QuadSeq: A duplicated-duplex DNA-synthesis technology for high-fidelity nanopore sequencing of linear DNA amplicons
items.corresponding_institution: The Department of Molecular Biosciences, The Wenner-Gren Institute, Stockholm University
items.abstract: Long-read nanopore sequencing is a highly versatile technology that is currently constrained by high error-rates, which can impair accurate genotyping of complex DNA samples. Common mitigation strategies based on creating consensus sequences from tandem duplications synthesized by rolling-circle or multiple-displacement amplification are prone to create both chimeric DNA molecules and require an initial DNA-circularization. Here we present QuadSeq, a three-step DNA-synthesis technology that can convert linear DNA amplicons into duplicated DNA duplexes that encode two forward and two reverse strand copies of a sequence-of-interest. Intramolecular consensus sequences generated from QuadSeq duplicated DNA duplexes yielded a median single-amplicon accuracy of up to 0.9992 (Q31), without requiring a cumbersome DNA-circularization of the amplicon-of-interest. We can also show that the primary bottleneck for achieving accurate nanopore amplicon sequencing is not the mutation rate of the initial PCR-amplification, but the fidelity of the nanopore sequencing. QuadSeq consensus sequences generated from amplicons synthesized by a low-fidelity DNA polymerase (Taq) had a 6.6-fold lower median error-rate compared to amplicon simplex reads synthesized by a high-fidelity DNA polymerase (Phusion U). Going forward, we predict that the QuadSeq DNA-synthesis technology will enable the use of almost any low-fidelity DNA polymerase for high-fidelity nanopore amplicon sequencing.

items.title: No detectable DNA methylation in the kelps (Laminariales): a conversion-free test of a predicted loss
items.abstract: Kelps (Laminariales) dominate temperate and polar rocky coasts and support a fast-growing aquaculture sector. Breeding and restoration programs need to know whether a line's performance follows its genotype or its culture history. DNA methylation has been reported in kelps, with differences by life stage, thermal history and population of origin now underpinning a literature on conditioning and priming in seaweed breeding. Recent comparative genomics work predicts otherwise, because brown algae lack the canonical DNA methyltransferases and should therefore carry little or no DNA methylation. We tested the prediction with native-DNA nanopore sequencing, which requires neither bisulfite conversion nor methylation-dependent digestion, in seven kelp datasets spanning three genera, four species and four S. latissima life stages. Nuclear 5-methylcytosine stayed at the measurement background in every sequence context (CG 0.021-0.034% of sites, against 0.023% on PCR copies that carry no methyl group by construction), while the same pipeline returned 58% of CG sites methylated in a diatom and recovered the transposon-targeted distribution a functioning system predicts. In native reads, thirteen of the fourteen best-covered chloroplast positions that bisulfite sequencing placed above 2% carry at most one methylated call, and those published levels track each library's conversion efficiency rather than its tissue. Gene content and direct measurement agree, so the heritable effects reported in cultivated kelp require a carrier other than DNA methylation: chromatin modifications or non-coding RNA.

items.title: Robust Cluster Typing, a computationally accessible tool for species designation from whole genome data, exemplified with the genus Campylobacter
items.corresponding_institution: University of East Anglia, Norwich & SequenceAnalysis.co.uk
items.abstract: Bacterial genomic analysis is a cornerstone of modern epidemiology. Many genomic typing methods exist, and most are designed to work within a given species in a hierarchical fashion. However, designation of bacterial species can be problematic, making the higher resolution level of hierarchical typing difficult. Using the universally present ribosomal proteins, we have developed a pipeline for a robust typing system which can be used to assign an unknown organism to a species-level cluster or, sometimes, a sub-species cluster.
