As proof of principle, we have used bacterial genomes from the genus Campylobacter, the most common cause of human bacterial gastroenteritis within which new strains, and new species (C. infantis), are reported. Species assignment, of all but the two most common species C. jejuni and C. coli, is beyond the ability of most microbiology laboratories. Outbreak investigation, even with genomic data, is difficult and so a robust typing scheme would be useful. Using available sequence-based typing schemes, we attempted to differentiate between 39 published Campylobacter species; we determined that the ribosomal 16S sequence typing and SNP typing did not discriminate all 39 but a single gene phylogeny method (GyrA), BUSCO, Mash, Panaroo and use of the Hugg proteins differentiated all 39. We assessed computational accessibility (important for implementation) and biological applicability (one universal typing scheme is easier to validate). The application of Hugg proteins proved computationally efficient and should be widely applicable. We developed a workflow in snakemake and Python, capable of clustering thousands of bacterial genomes. This Robust Cluster (RC) typing workflow was made accessible via the Terra platform, with usage instructions provided through an online training course on YouTube. Ninety-eight Campylobacter isolates from Bangladesh were sequenced and analysed using the Terra workflow, resulting in the identification of several novel clusters not previously found among publicly available genomes. Our work establishes the availability of RC typing and demonstrates its capacity to identify new Campylobacter lineages, thereby facilitating reporting and supporting future research initiatives.

items.title: Accurate and interpretable protein complex stoichiometry prediction through agentic AI with StoiAgent
items.abstract: Accurate protein complex structure modeling requires knowledge of complex stoichiometry, yet the copy numbers of individual subunits are often unknown. Consequently, predicting protein complex stoichiometry has emerged as a major challenge in recent years. Here, we present StoiAgent, a large language model (LLM)-powered AI agent that automates the retrieval and integration of sequence, structural, and literature evidence to predict stoichiometry while preserving interpretable reasoning traces (chain of thoughts) of its evidence assessment and ranking decision. An open-weight LLM model, Qwen3.6-27B, is used by StoiAgent as the LLM backbone to combine sequences, structural templates, AlphaFold3 structure predictions, and literature evidence, and perform stoichiometry candidate generation and ranking. On 56 CASP17 protein complex targets, it achieves top-1 accuracy of 75.0%, which represents a 23.2 percentage-point improvement over PreStoi with AlphaFold3 ranking (51.8%) and matches the top-1 accuracy of StoPred. Moreover, StoiAgent has a higher top-3 and top-5 accuracy than StoPred (85.7% versus 80.4% and 87.5% versus 85.7%, respectively). Furthermore, it outperforms general-purpose frontier LLMs, including ChatGPT and Gemini, in stoichiometry prediction. Case studies further illustrate how StoiAgent evaluates competing assembly hypotheses by integrating complementary evidence, with recorded reasoning traces documenting its decision-making process. Overall, StoiAgent demonstrates the potential of LLM-powered AI agents to improve protein complex stoichiometry prediction through the automated integration of diverse sources of evidence while providing interpretable explanations to guide downstream structure modeling.

items.title: GENECraft: A Function- and Prior-Constrained Discrete Dynamical System for Controllable Regulatory DNA Design
items.abstract: Designing regulatory DNA requires reconciling two complementary modeling paradigms: genomic language models (gLMs) capture evolutionary syntax without guaranteeing targeted regulatory activity, whereas sequence-to-function predictors provide explicit functional supervision without enforcing native-like sequence plausibility. We introduce GENECraft, a training-free Function- and Prior-Constrained Discrete Dynamical System (FP-DDS) that couples a genomic language model (Carbon) and a functional oracle (AlphaGenome) during inference-time optimization to balance predicted regulatory activity and consistency with genomic sequence priors. GENECraft evolves continuous latent nucleotide logits while evaluating strictly decoded discrete DNA sequences under a time-dependent composite vector field that fuses normalized functional utility, bidirectional contextual prior guidance, and compositional quality penalties, followed by feasibility-first trajectory readout. Across 2,185 loci spanning promoters, multi-constraint enhancers, and 18 transcription factors (TFs), GENECraft achieves full-joint success rates of 62.70%, 65.23%, and 94.56% (macro-averaged), substantially outperforming seven optimization, evolutionary, and generative baselines (which reach at most 2.15% on enhancers). In matched 336-locus ablations, in-loop Carbon guidance reduces native-relative dinucleotide divergence by 7.8--11.5%, enhancer context sensitivity by 10.5%, and TF mutation sensitivity by 11.0%, establishing FP-DDS as a principled framework for controllable regulatory DNA design.

items.title: scUNVEIL: Learning scRNA-seq Cell Embeddings Through Measurement Enrichment
items.corresponding_institution: University of West Bohemia in Pilsen
items.abstract: Large-scale pretraining can improve scRNA-seq representations through measurement enrichment: estimating what the same measurement would reveal at greater UMI depth under the same measurement process. We introduce scUNVEIL, a self-supervised model trained through next-UMI prediction. We show that the Bayes-optimal next-UMI predictor is the posterior mean of the transcriptome composition that arbitrarily deep sequencing would reveal. Because UMI identities are exchangeable conditional on transcriptome composition, scUNVEIL operates directly on count vectors using a residual multilayer perceptron, without attention over gene tokens. The measurement-enriched transcriptome composition is predicted from a single low-dimensional hidden state, which therefore serves naturally as the cell embedding. The same model provides both reusable cell representations and measurement-enriched gene-expression estimates. scUNVEIL was pretrained without labels or auxiliary metadata on approximately 92 million human cells spanning diverse tissues. Under linear evaluation on fine-grained cell-type annotation, its zero-shot representations achieved the best performance among the evaluated methods, while providing over 1000-fold faster inference than the strongest evaluated transformer-based foundation model and matching that model's predictive performance using 88% fewer input UMIs per cell. Further evaluations show that these representations improve prediction of tumor reactivity, mitochondrial membrane potential, cell morphology, and lineage-associated treatment outcomes.

items.title: BI-SCUDO Regression - A novel algorithm to infer clinical variables from omics datasets
items.abstract: Regression analysis of high-throughput omics data is often made difficult by noise, batch effects, and the loss of information resulting from the discretization of continuous variables. Existing machine learning algorithms often struggle to extract stable biological signals under these heterogeneous conditions. We introduce BI-SCUDO Regression, a rank-based regression framework designed for omics data analysis. By leveraging within-sample rankings and network-based predictions, BI-SCUDO Regression bypasses the need for complex normalization and provides robust, interpretable results. In synthetic benchmarks, BI-SCUDO Regression demonstrated strong resilience to noise, maintaining predictive and feature-selection stability under conditions in which standard models exhibited performance degradation. When applied to cohorts from TCGA datasets, BI-SCUDO Regression consistently outperformed LASSO, Random Forest Regression, and XGBoost in predicting survival, with an average increase in Ratio of Performance to Deviation ranging from 43% to 86%, depending on the comparator. Furthermore, the algorithm consistently identified parsimonious, statistically significant, and biologically relevant biomarkers, with enrichment for cancer-related terms across all stage stratifications. Although BI-SCUDO Regression incurs higher training times due to its genetic optimization strategy, it offers a robust and interpretable approach to outcome prediction and biomarker discovery, with potential applications in precision medicine, where noisy data compromise the performance of conventional regression methods.

items.title: Elflow: Automated Quality Control and Self-Supervised Representation Learning for High-Dimensional Cytometry
items.abstract: High-dimensional flow and mass cytometry are foundational technologies for clinical immunophenotyping and hematological diagnostics, yet computational data analysis remains bottlenecked by operator-subjective manual gating. While computational tools have emerged, they remain fragmented across isolated tasks such as quality control or discrete clustering, leaving an unmet need for integrated, modular workflows that resolve continuous biological variation without manual supervision. Here, we introduce Elflow, a modular, self-supervised framework that links automated quality control, single-cell representation learning, and patient-level modeling without manual gating at inference. Elflow couples automated machine-learning quality control with Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularization (VICReg) to learn continuous, batch-resilient single-cell representations without negative pairs or hand-labeled training sets. Across four diverse public benchmarks, Elflow adapts to distinct biological panels and clinical objectives. On 22-channel spectral flow cytometry (OMIP-030), self-supervised embeddings preserve fine functional T-cell gradations and outperform classical baselines in unsupervised clustering, while an anchor-guided extension accurately reproduces canonical manual gating hierarchies. On hand-curated CyTOF panels (Levine-13), linear PCA matches deep models, establishing an empirical boundary condition where linear methods suffice. Across multi-center clinical cohorts (FlowCAP-II), Elflow representations achieve high diagnostic sensitivity for acute myeloid leukemia across heterogeneous instruments despite severe class imbalance. In longitudinal immune monitoring (FlowCAP-IV), patient mean embeddings and micro-cluster differential histograms preserve rare antigen-specific responses, yielding significant AIDS-free survival stratification. By uniting automated quality control, self-supervised representation learning, and multi-scale patient aggregation, Elflow provides a modular, reproducibly benchmarked framework for high-parameter and multi-center translational cytometry.

items.title: Vocabulary recurrence, rather than biological grounding, explains tokenization transfer in protein function prediction.
items.abstract: Sequence-based protein function prediction requires a choice of tokenization. K-mers, the common default, correspond to no biological unit; enzymatic digestion offers a principled alternative, since tryptic peptides are the fragments proteases generate and mass spectrometry measures. We asked whether this grounding improves transfer to unseen proteins. Using six Gene Ontology terms and 23,723 UniProt proteins, we compared tryptic peptides, peptide topics (groups of related peptides), 3-mers, and amino- acid composition, with ESM-2 embeddings and homology transfer as reference points. Peptide performance followed vocabulary coverage: 92.2% of peptide tokens in test proteins were never seen in training, whereas almost every 3-mer had been seen. As a result, 38.9% of test proteins contained no peptide the model had seen, and with nothing to work from, the classifier gave all of them the same answer. The remaining 61.1% of proteins were classified almost perfectly with a random forest; however, because of this uncovered fraction, tryptic peptides scored lower overall than 3-mers under all three classifiers tested (macro-F1 0.640 against 0.690). These results suggest that vocabulary recurrence matters more than biological grounding for tokenization transfer.

items.title: Optoretinographic measurements of cone photoreceptor function in disease-affected retinas
items.abstract: Optoretinography (ORG) provides a noninvasive approach for measuring stimulus-evoked photoreceptor responses in the living human retina, but its application to retinal disease using clinically translatable imaging systems remains limited. Here, we applied velocity-based ORG using a clinical-grade swept-source optical coherence tomography (OCT) system to assess photoreceptor function in disease-affected human retinas and healthy controls. Following pupil dilation and dark adaptation, repeated B-scans were acquired at 400 Hz during visible-light stimulation using a phase-sensitive 100-kHz, 1060-nm swept-source OCT system. Stimulus-evoked optical path length changes between the inner segment/outer segment junction (IS/OS) and cone outer segment tips (COST) were used to quantify cone outer-segment responses. Healthy retinas exhibited rapid and reproducible responses characterized by an initial outer-segment contraction followed by elongation, whereas disease-affected retinas exhibited quantitatively reduced or altered response amplitudes and temporal dynamics. ORG also detected functional improvement following treatment in a vitamin-A-deficient retina. These findings demonstrate the ability of velocity-based ORG to quantitatively detect photoreceptor dysfunction and functional change using a clinically compatible OCT platform, supporting its potential as a noninvasive functional biomarker for retinal disease and therapeutic response.

items.title: Beyond morphometry: Adolescent brain microarchitecture reflects sex differences in pubertal timing and hormones
items.abstract: Puberty is a sensitive neurodevelopmental period characterized by dramatic increases in adrenal and gonadal hormones, yet how these changes relate to human brain microarchitecture remains unclear. Here, we used restriction spectrum imaging (RSI) to link peripubertal hormone levels to individual differences in brain microarchitecture (i.e., cellular and neurite density) in 7,457 youth (ages 9 to 13 years) from the ABCD Study. Sex- and age-stratified multi-task regression analyses identified microarchitecture patterns jointly associated with physical pubertal maturation and each dehydroepiandrosterone (DHEA), testosterone, estradiol (in female youth), in turn, combining repeated cross-validation with permutation-based feature importance. At ages 9 to 11 years, microarchitecture differences explained 11-13% of pubertal hormone variability in female youth and 4-6% in male youth. Further, microarchitecture features were differentially associated with pubertal hormones. Younger male youth exhibited widespread pubertal hormone-related differences in neurite density that consolidated into fewer, stronger associations with age, while female youth exhibited age-related expansion in pubertal cellular density differences. Anatomically, hormone-relevant microarchitecture consistently included reward processing hubs (e.g., pallidum, accumbens, orbitofrontal cortex). Because animal models suggest that DHEA and testosterone metabolites have opposing effects on GABAergic signaling, we hypothesize that future research should investigate gray matter microarchitecture for insight into pubertal hormone contributions to adolescent refinement of excitatory-inhibitory balance. Ultimately, these findings provide a starting point for investigating how pubertal endocrine changes shape reward circuitry and neurotransmitter systems, with potential implications for the pubertal emergence of sex differences in adolescent psychopathology.

items.title: Multistage gradient-based whole-cortex modeling for joint inference of regional circuit heterogeneity and interregional structural connectivity
items.abstract: Current non-invasive neuroimaging methods cannot directly resolve regional circuit heterogeneity and interregional structural connectivity, limiting mechanistic understanding of brain structure-function relationships and accurate whole-brain modeling. Here we introduce StaGIC (Staged Gradient-based Inference of Circuitry), a method that jointly infers regional circuit heterogeneity and model-constrained structural connectivity (SC) from resting-state functional connectivity (FC) and functional connectivity dynamics (FCD). Ablation and synthetic-recovery experiments show that staged optimization improves fits to functional data and ground-truth parameter recovery, with inferred SC remaining highly consistent across retained solutions from independent optimization runs. In human data, freely optimized regional parameters exhibit consistent relationships with cortical hierarchy across parcellations, while SC inference substantially improves FC reconstruction. In macaque and marmoset data, inferred SC shows stronger correlation with tracer-derived projections than diffusion MRI estimates, particularly for long-range connections. As a proof of concept in computational psychiatry, group-level models of major depressive disorder (MDD) reproduce MDD-associated FC differences and generate exploratory hypotheses about hierarchical differentiation and interregional projection organization. StaGIC thus provides a differentiable framework for inferring multiscale cortical organization from non-invasive functional imaging.

items.title: Stage-Dependent Requirement for SETX in Human Motor Neuron Maturation and Survival
items.abstract: Senataxin (SETX) is an RNA/DNA helicase involved in transcription, RNA processing, R-loop resolution, and genome maintenance. Mutations in SETX cause neurological disorders, but its role in human motor neuron (MN) development remains unclear. Here, we examined SETX function using isogenic SETX knockout (KO) human induced pluripotent stem cells (hiPSCs), shRNA-mediated knockdown, and direct conversion of fibroblasts into MNs. SETX expression increased during differentiation from hiPSCs to neural progenitor cells (NPCs) and MNs. SETX loss slowed hiPSC and NPC proliferation without preventing MN generation. However, SETX-deficient MNs developed shorter neurites, dystrophic swellings, and progressive neuronal loss. MEA recordings showed reduced firing and burst activity and almost no synchronized network bursts. RNA hybrid accumulation increased after SETX loss, with the largest relative increase in MNs among the cell types examined. RNA-seq revealed altered neurodevelopmental gene expression at the NPC stage and during MN differentiation, together with increased expression of stress- and apoptosis-associated genes. Proteomic analysis identified changes in proteins involved in neuronal structure, synaptic function, RNA regulation, and cellular homeostasis. Concordant decreases in selected RNAs and proteins supported disruption of neuronal structural and synaptic programs. Together, these findings reveal a stage-dependent requirement for SETX and identify SETX as an important regulator of transcriptional programs governing human MN maturation, function, and survival, providing a mechanistic framework for understanding the selective MN vulnerability associated with SETX-linked neurological diseases.

items.title: Biological Embedding of Social Experience Over Genomic and Neural Time Scales
items.abstract: The "Neurons for Today, Genes for Tomorrow model" (NTGT) predicts how the brain's neural and molecular control systems interact to regulate biological embedding, whereby social experience alters the brain to shape future behavior. We report here on the first test of this model, using honey bee queen retinue pheromone (QRP) and behavioral, single-nucleus transcriptomic, and electrophysiological analyses. Consistent with theory, weaker exposure triggered a simple attraction response and transcriptomic changes primarily in the antennal lobes (AL), whereas stronger exposure induced transcriptomic changes in the mushroom bodies, a brain region affecting more complex behavior. In addition, AL electrophysiological responses to QRP were enhanced after stronger exposure, also consistent with theory. We also showed how individual differences in biological embedding can be explained by NTGT, with individual differences in brain gene regulatory network topology, especially in specific sensory cell clusters, supporting a new mechanistic framework for behavioral regulation.

items.title: Modeling CNS inflammatory demyelination using myelin-directed CAR T cells
items.abstract: Multiple sclerosis therapies remain confined to immunomodulatory agents that reduce inflammatory activity; none restores lost myelin, and disability can continue to accumulate independently of relapses. Development of remyelinating therapies has been hindered by models that incompletely reproduce the persistently inflamed lesions in which remyelination fails. Here we show that chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells targeting myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) build such lesions on demand. Human CD4+ CAR T cells transferred into immunodeficient mice infiltrated the brain, spinal cord, and optic nerve, producing perivascular demyelinating lesions, with reproducible optic nerve involvement. Within these discrete optic nerve lesions, treatment with the remyelinating compound clemastine reduced lesion size and improved optic nerve conduction, despite persistent inflammation. Thus, this MOG CAR T model reproduces key features of inflammatory demyelinating disease and enables testing of remyelinating therapies; more broadly, it introduces CAR T cells as programmable perturbative agents for building defined pathology in vivo.

items.title: Two co-occurring dynamics explain the organization of a natural movement repertoire
items.abstract: Natural movements vary across multiple kinematic features, making it difficult to identify the dynamics shared across movements that generate a behavioral repertoire. Here, we provide a low-dimensional, interpretable generative account of the larval zebrafish hunting repertoire that links tail dynamics to behavioral outcomes. Analysis of thousands of movements spanning classically defined bout types revealed that repertoire diversity arises from continuous combinations of two simultaneously expressed dynamics: a slow, non-oscillatory bending component and a fast, oscillatory undulatory component. An analytical model captured these dynamics with six interpretable parameters and accurately reconstructed movements across the full repertoire and at two developmental stages. Different parameters predicted distinct aspects of movement outcome: maximum tail bend predicted change in heading angle, maximum tail curvature and movement duration predicted distance traveled, and oscillatory asymmetry predicted displacement direction. Relationships among the dynamical parameters constrained the movements and outcomes available to the animal. Key parameters could also be recovered directly from empirical tail kinematics, establishing them as experimentally accessible movement variables rather than model-dependent latent dimensions. Together, these results explain both the diversity and limits of a natural movement repertoire through constrained combinations of co-occurring dynamics.

items.title: Shared-Encoder Residual Task-Bridging Network for Motor Execution to Motor Imagery EEG Transfer in Brain-Computer Interfaces
items.abstract: Motor-imagery brain-computer interfaces (MI-BCIs) hold promising application prospects in the fields of limb motor rehabilitation and human-computer interaction. However, the reliability of MI calibration data is limited by the difficulty of verifying participants' engagement during motor imagerywhereas motor execution (ME) provides a more readily supervised source of motor-related information.To investigate the potential of ME-derived knowledge for assisting MI decoding, we propose a Shared-Encoder Residual Task-Bridge Network (SE-RTBNet) to achieve accurate intra-subject cross-task knowledge transfer from ME to MI. The proposed framework consists of two major components: a shared encoder and a residual task-bridge module. The shared encoder extracts stable general motor representations from multi-band EEG signals and explores the shared feature patterns underlying ME and MI tasks. The residual task-bridge module is equipped with a performance-aware routing mechanism. It adaptively compensates for task-specific discrepancies between the two tasks, enabling precise cross-task feature alignment and knowledge transfer. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed model, experiments are conducted on three public datasets. The proposed method achieves average classification accuracies of 69.39%, 74.61%, and 98.94%, respectively, and outperforms existing transfer-learning algorithms in overall performance. Our model provides an effective strategy for reducing dependence on extensive MI calibration data through intra-subject cross-task knowledge transfer.The source code of the proposed SE-RTBNet is publicly available at https://github.com/Daisyzyx2002/SE-RTBNet

items.title: TDP2 couples PKA-CREB signalling to genome stability in human cerebellar development
items.corresponding_institution: Interdisciplinary Research Center on Biology and Chemistry, Shanghai Institute of Organic Chemistry, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Shanghai 200032, China
items.abstract: Transcription and neuronal activity in the central nervous system generate abundant DNA damage, particularly DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs), rendering neural cells - and cerebellar neurons especially - vulnerable to genome instability. Tyrosyl-DNA phosphodiesterase 2 (TDP2, also known as TTRAP) resolves topoisomerase-2-linked DSBs, and biallelic TDP2 mutations cause spinocerebellar ataxia autosomal recessive 23 (SCAR23), yet how DNA repair shapes human cerebellar development is unknown. Here we model SCAR23 in cerebellar organoids derived from patient induced pluripotent stem cells carrying TDP2 c.650del and from prime-edited isogenic TDP2 c.400C>T lines. TDP2 inactivation caused organoid hypoplasia during FGF8b-dependent cerebellar specification, which was reversed by TDP2 complementation. Single-nucleus transcriptomics across three developmental stages revealed early dysregulation of ribosome biogenesis, attenuated CREB1 regulon activity and a subsequent failure of Purkinje cell maturation. TDP2 inactivation upregulated PKIB, a cerebellum-enriched inhibitor of protein kinase A, lowering PKA and CREB phosphorylation. Whole-genome sequencing showed excess de novo deletions in mutant organoids, enriched at candidate cis-regulatory elements of neurodevelopmental genes. Pharmacological activation of the cAMP-PKA cascade restored CREB phosphorylation, reduced DNA damage and rescued organoid growth. These findings link developmental signalling to genome maintenance in the human cerebellum and identify the cAMP-PKA-CREB axis as a candidate therapeutic target in DNA-repair-deficient cerebellar disease.

items.title: Measuring the information budget of cross-target antibody affinity generalization: a robust cross-target wall, and why structure reaches developability but not affinity
items.abstract: Structure-based machine learning is widely expected to advance antibody engineering, yet it is unclear how far affinity predictions transfer to new targets, and why. We introduce a noise-corrected, censoring-aware estimator of the cross-target transfer ceiling, {rho}max = {surd}(T/(T+I)), which separates a transferable antibody-intrinsic component (T) from a non-transferable target-specific interaction (I). On deterministic synthetic ground truth the estimator recovers the noise-free ceiling to {+/-} 0.0003, whereas the naive sum-of-squares estimator is biased downward by measurement noise. Applying it from synthetic to real systems, the transferable budget is small, and on real neutralization panels it is not an artefact: the target-specific interaction survives noise and censoring correction. It is strongly regime-dependent, with a two-tier structure: predicting a novel antibody from sequence alone (the design setting) reaches a lower ceiling ({rho} {approx} 0.44 on real breadth data) than ranking a characterized one ({rho} {approx} 0.59), even with a strong protein language model. Synthetic oracles also overstate transferability: an oracle scored on real predicted structures carries about half the budget of a matched synthetic lattice (0.45 vs. 0.81), and real neutralization and escape panels sit well below the synthetic ceiling (0.32-0.68). Under leakage-free antigen-cluster splits, cross-target affinity ranking across every method family collapses to this budget, while within a sampled target a structure-based graph network ranks affinity above off-the-shelf FoldX and GearBind (within-complex Spearman 0.55), and structural surface descriptors predict a surface-driven developability property (hydrophobic aggregation) where sequence-dominated properties (humanness, charge-driven self-association) do not benefit. A controlled ablation attributes the residual within-target signal to the antibody alone: dropping the antigen from the structural model leaves it essentially unchanged (interface {Delta} {rho} between -0.01 and +0.02 across four panels), so for this model the paratope-epitope interface adds no ranking signal over the antibody alone. Models climb toward the budget within a target -- via a measure-then-rank operating mode that recovers top binders 6-8 times more efficiently than random once a target has been sampled -- but none crosses it.

items.title: De novo Genome Assembly and Annotation of the Seep Tubeworm Lamellibrachia satsuma using Oxford Nanopore Sequencing
items.corresponding_institution: National Marine Biodiversity Institute of Korea, Seocheon, South Korea
items.abstract: The tubeworm Lamelllibrachia satsuma inhabits seep region by forming a mutualistic symbiotic relationship with chemosynthetic bacteria residing in its trophosome. Genomic and symbiotic studies have been extensively conducted, primarily from a bacterial perspective. But rarely vice versa. Here we present a high-quality draft genome assembly of L. satsuma and its tissue-specific transcriptome data. This genome will be valuable for further understanding the mechanisms of adaptation in cold seep environments, host-microbe interactions, as well as genome variation among tubeworms. We generated ~103 Gb of genomic sequencing data using Illumina and Oxford Nanopore platforms, which assembled in a 665 Mb draft genome. The assembled genome consisted of 6,320 scaffolds with 95.7% genome completeness. Among 32,394 predicted protein-coding genes, 1,063 gene families have expanded, and 1,385 gene families were contracted. Among the expanded gene families, multiple copies of leukocyte elastase inhibitor, reverse transcriptase, arylesterase, and xanthine dehydrogenase/oxidase genes were found. Molecular clock analysis based on the phylogenomic dataset revealed that L. sastuma and L. luymesi were diverged from their common ancestor during the Early Cenozoic era, approximately 13 million years ago.

items.title: FULL-seq reveals isoform-specific regulatory architecture in single cells
items.corresponding_institution: Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School; Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard; Ragon Institute of Mass General Brigham, MIT and Harvard
items.abstract: Gene regulation is commonly modeled at the gene level, yet genes express multiple isoforms from distinct transcription start sites whose regulatory architecture is not resolved by current approaches. Here we introduce FULL-seq, a scalable single-cell multiomic platform that jointly profiles chromatin accessibility and full-length transcript coverage from the same cell, enabling direct coupling of regulatory elements to alternative first exon (AFE) usage. FULL-seq achieves high sensitivity for both transcriptome and chromatin accessibility while providing transcript-wide coverage across mRNAs up to 15 kb with precise exon-level mapping. We uncover diverse promoter-AFE regulatory architectures, revealing distinct transcription factor programs across alternative first exons of the same gene, and show that gene-level annotation frameworks can obscure regulatory relationships in multi-promoter genes. Applying FULL-seq to human cancer cells further reveals metastasis-associated AFE programs that are not apparent from gene-level expression. These AFE programs were reproduced in independent colorectal cancer cell-line datasets, and CALB1 AFE activation was observed in a subset of liver metastases from an independent patient cohort. Furthermore, CRISPRi-mediated repression of metastasis-associated CALB1 AFEs reduced colorectal cancer cell migration. Together, our findings establish alternative promoter and first-exon usage as a functionally relevant layer of gene regulation and demonstrate that FULL-seq enables regulatory relationships and cellular phenotypes to be connected at the promoter-isoform level.

items.title: Fine-tuned DNA sequence language models for predicting gene expression in admixed population: A comparison with variant-based methods
items.abstract: Predicting gene expression from whole genome sequencing data is essential for elucidating regulatory mechanisms and interpreting functional consequences of non-coding variants to complex diseases. While traditional approaches rely on variant-based linear models, DNA sequence-based language models have gained increasing popularity for their ability to learn regulatory features directly from whole genome sequence data. Previous studies have evaluated models such as Enformer, but newer sequence-to-function models, including Borzoi and AlphaGenome, remain less well characterized for individual-level gene expression prediction, particularly in non-European and admixed populations. Here, we evaluated and fine-tuned Borzoi and AlphaGenome using personal genomes paired with whole-blood RNA-seq data from the Hispanic Community Health Study/Study of Latinos (HCHS/SOL). Fine-tuning substantially improved the performance of both sequence-based models compared with their pretrained versions; however, their performances remained similar to that of the variant-based linear models. Leveraging the ancestral diversity of HCHS/SOL, we found that Borzoi and AlphaGenome showed similar performance across Amerindian-, European-, and African-enriched groups. Fine-tuned Borzoi, fine-tuned AlphaGenome and elastic net performed modestly better when trained and evaluated in the same ancestry-enriched group. Finally, we explored strategies to improve prediction performance and found that incorporating predicted epigenetic features improved prediction near the promoter region. Significant progress remains needed before the full potential of sequence-based models is attained. Incorporating more biology-guided training approaches could be helpful to achieving better performance.

items.title: DRAFT: graph-recurrent learning of dynamic gene regulatory networks along single-cell multi-omics trajectories
items.corresponding_institution: Centre for organismal Studies (COS), Heidelberg University
items.abstract: Single-cell multi-omics data offer an opportunity to resolve how gene regulatory networks (GRNs) are rewired during cell-fate transitions, but most existing methods infer static snapshots, ignore temporal dependencies or assume linear regulation. Here we present DRAFT, a deep learning framework that combines graph attention with recurrent temporal memory to infer dynamic GRNs from time-resolved single-cell multi-omics data. On simulated data, DRAFT outperforms existing methods in accuracy and temporal smoothness. In mouse cellular reprogramming and Drosophila adult spermatogenesis, it recovers interactions supported by independent ChIP-seq, perturbation and Hi-C data, together with known stage-specific regulators. By inferring regulatory activity from dynamic network structure rather than expression alone, DRAFT identifies regulators whose activity precedes their transcriptional peak, including the candidate early germline regulator Mondo. Germline-specific Mondo knockdown alters germline stem cell number and expression of the predicted targets kuz and mamo. DRAFT also enables nonlinear alignment of co-developing lineages and reveals stage-specific cell-cell communication.

items.title: Sc-HistoMorphomics: A General Framework for High-throughput, Multimodal Profiling of Nuclear Morphology in Tissues.
items.abstract: Quantitative cellular morphology provides a rich but underutilized window into cell identity and state. We introduce sc-HistoMorphomics, a scalable framework for profiling nuclear morphology in whole-slide H&E images and correlating these measurements with spatial transcriptomics data. Our pipeline combines deep-learning based segmentation with 194 interpretable morphometric features capturing nuclear shape, eosin and hematoxylin texture, and neighbourhood architecture, enabling high-throughput, multimodal characterization of tissue organization. Applied to endometrium, breast cancer tissue, and pancreas, sc-HistoMorphomics revealed conserved high-dimensional feature structure across tissues and reproducible association between morphology and gene expression. Eosin-based texture features were associated with senescence signatures in endometrium, and morphology-based clustering recapitulated broad stromal, lymphocyte, and epithelial tumor cell classes in breast cancer. In pancreas, negative correlations between CDKN1A and multiple morphological features were consistent across cell types and donors. Together, these results establish sc-HistoMorphomics as a generalizable and interpretable tool for linking morphology with spatially resolved molecular state across diverse tissues.

items.title: Robustness of cortical distortion metrics to unmodelled OPM errors
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Imaging Neuroscience, UCL Queen Square Institute of Neurology, University College London, WC1N 3AR, London, UK
items.abstract: The estimate of cortical current flow from magnetic fields measured outside the head is an ill-posed problem. Recent work using head casts to minimise co-registration errors in conventional cryogenic magnetoencephalography (MEG) has shown that ground truth anatomy can be used to judge between different inversion schemes and metrics. Inversion algorithms or metrics that are insensitive to anatomical distortion are unlikely to reflect correct assumptions about the underlying current distribution. Here we aim to identify constraints when using this approach to validate current flow estimated from recordings made with optically pumped MEG (OP-MEG). To do so, we used simulations contaminated by different sources of (typically unmodelled) error. For example: error in the estimate of the true sensor positions or orientations and the effects of unmodelled gain changes. In accordance with previous work, with no unmodelled errors, distortion was minimized when the simulation and the inversion assumptions matched. We then quantified the amount of error (in mm) relative to the true cortical mesh that one might expect in empirical recordings (given gain, position and orientation errors). We found that the approach was tolerant to independent sensor position errors of less than 2 mm (per axis); orientation errors of less than 5 degrees; fixed array displacements of less than 10 degrees and to random sensor gain errors of less than 10%. Additionally, we tested this approach using two empirical OPM datasets. We found that source reconstructions based on both minimum norm and beamformer assumptions were sensitive to the underlying anatomy.

items.title: False-negative assessment of NanoNewron's NewroBus blood-brain barrier delivery platform in the JAX apical-domain-humanized TfR1 mouse
items.abstract: Humanized transferrin receptor 1 (TfR1) mice are frequently used to evaluate blood-brain barrier (BBB) delivery, yet available strains differ in the extent and design of receptor humanization. We compared two NanoNewron NewroBus-based anti-TNF constructs, NN-841 (D3 TfR1-binding module) and NN-843 (A2 module), in JAX #038212 (humanized apical domain), Cyagen C001584 (human extracellular-domain CDS model), Cyagen C001860 (human extracellular-domain genomic replacement model), and wild-type controls. Thirty mice received intravenous injections and were evaluated 24 h later. Brain parenchymal-fraction signals were reported in all 12 Cyagen mice, but in none of six JAX or 12 wild-type animals. Serum concentrations were measurable in every group and followed the same rank order for both constructs: Cyagen-CDS>Cyagen-HU>wild type >JAX. Mean CDS-to-JAX serum ratios were approximately 13--fold for both constructs. Compared with the Cyagen-HU strain, the CDS strain showed higher parenchymal concentrations; the ratio of mean parenchymal to mean serum concentration increased prominently for NN-841, but only modestly for NN-843. These findings indicate that model choice influences 24-h circulating concentrations and apparent BBB delivery. Circulating soluble human TfR1-mediated stabilization and endothelial TfR1-dependent transport are plausible, untested explanations for strain-dependent differences. A negative brain-delivery result in JAX #038212 alone cannot be taken as evidence that NewroBus lacks BBB delivery activity

items.title: Children become accurate years before they become fast: electroencephalography dates the separate maturation of decision components
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Biomedical Engineering, College of Engineering, Shantou University, Shantou, Guangdong, China
items.abstract: Perceptual decisions, a hallmark of cognitive development, become faster and more accurate from early childhood to adulthood, but whether the underlying components mature together, as a single global gain in processing speed would predict, or on separate timetables remains unclear. Behaviour alone cannot distinguish whether age-related improvement reflects clearer sensory encoding, more efficient evidence accumulation, fewer attention lapses or shorter non-decision processes, and prior direct measurements have typically come from small samples spanning limited age ranges. We analysed electroencephalography from 1,534 participants aged 5 to 21 years in the Healthy Brain Network during a contrast-change discrimination task. On the same trials, we measured the visual response and an evidence-accumulation signal, while a decision model estimated accumulation efficiency, attention lapses and non-decision time. We found that the visual response did not grow with age and retained 77% of its strength on missed targets. Instead, accuracy improved through fewer lapses and more efficient accumulation, both reaching half of their developmental change by about 9 years, whereas speed improved later: non-decision time shortened between 11 and 14 years and was longer in children whose accumulation signal rose later. These findings show that perceptual decision-making matures through dissociable stages rather than a single global increase in processing speed: mechanisms supporting accuracy mature in middle childhood, whereas those supporting the fastest responses continue to develop into early adolescence. This framework links developmental theories of processing speed to neural mechanisms of decision-making and provides a reference for identifying which component is disrupted in children who struggle.

items.title: Heterogeneous short-term plasticity reformats latent temporal information into an explicit population clock
items.abstract: Short-term plasticity (STP) supports diverse synaptic-level computations, but how its organization across a circuit shapes emergent, network-level dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we first characterize STP across sparse inputs to Kenyon cells in the Drosophila mushroom body, revealing an unstructured and near-random organization that could not be explained by either pre- or postsynaptic cell identity. Rather than representing biological noise, an experimentally constrained network model instead shows how this heterogeneous organization reformats temporal information embedded in presynaptic spike rate trajectories into a behaviorally relevant population clock. Although an ideal observer could recover the same degree of temporal information from most alternative models, only the STP-mediated transformation made that information accessible to a biologically realistic decoder. Together, our results identify heterogeneous STP as a distributed biophysical mechanism that collectively functions as a temporal basis set to support circuit computations across variable input statistics.

items.title: Altered age-dependent somatic mutational trajectories in ALS motor cortex neurons
items.corresponding_institution: Department of translational neuroscience, UMC Utrecht, Utrecht, NL
items.abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease in which disease onset is influenced by genetic, age-associated and environmental factors. Somatic mutations accumulate throughout life and may provide a molecular link between aging and neuronal vulnerability. Here, we investigated neuronal somatic mutational patterns in ALS and control motor cortex using three previously generated 10X single-nucleus RNA and ATAC sequencing datasets. Within the genomic regions accessible to 10X sequencing, variant calls showed established features of neuronal somatic mutagenesis, including neuronal enrichment, age-associated accumulation and recovery of the clock-like SBS5 mutational signature. ALS was associated with a disease-specific age-dependent trajectory of neuronal somatic mutation burden, with higher burden in younger ALS donors and a decreasing difference with age. SBS5 represented the largest fitted mutational component and showed a corresponding age-dependent difference. A similar pattern was observed in an independent single-cell whole-genome sequencing dataset. These findings support age-dependent alterations in neuronal somatic mutational patterns in ALS.

items.title: Regulatory grammar design of tissue-specific enhancers across species
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Microbial Sciences in Health, Cleveland Clinic Research, Cleveland Clinic, 9500 Euclid Avenue, Cleveland, OH 44195, USA
items.abstract: Enhancers encode tissue-specific gene expression through the combinatorial identity, number, and arrangement of transcription factor motifs, collectively known as regulatory grammar. However, existing deep-learning methods directly optimize nucleotide sequences, leaving enhancer regulatory grammar implicit. Here we introduce REgulatory Grammar Architecture via reinforcement Learning (REGAL), a framework that explicitly programs enhancer grammar under sequence-to-function oracles. REGAL generated tissue-specific enhancers across species using the same placement architecture with interchangeable oracles and motif vocabularies. Experimental validation and perturbation revealed that tissue specificity requires coordinated target-tissue activation and off-target repression, depends on both motif composition and spatial organization, and employs distinct regulatory strategies across tissues. REGAL-designed enhancers drove predicted lineage-specific expression in transgenic mouse embryos, outperformed a nucleotide-level optimizer in human cells, and matched or exceeded leading designs in zebrafish and Drosophila at notably shorter length. Together, these findings establish regulatory grammar as a programmable and experimentally testable substrate underlying enhancer design and specificity.

items.title: A de novo reference genome of the red seaweed Furcellaria lumbricalis
items.abstract: Furcellaria lumbricalis is a red seaweed that occurs across a broad salinity gradient, ranging from the saline waters of the NE Atlantic to the brackish Baltic Sea. In the Baltic Sea, natural populations of F. lumbricalis are harvested commercially, primarily for furcellaran extraction, a sulphated polysaccharide used as a stabilizing, thickening, and gelling agent. Genomic resources for this species remain absent, constraining evolutionary, ecological, and applied research. Here, we present a de novo reference genome assembly of the seaweed Furcellaria lumbricalis using PacBio Hifi and Oxford Nanopore Technologies long-read sequencing. The final assembly, consisting of 149 contigs spanning 918.2 Mb, contains a high proportion of repetitive elements (90.5%), and has an N50 of 15,5 Mb. We further integrated RNA-seq data, protein homology evidence, and ab initio gene prediction to build a genome annotation comprising 6100 genes, of which 82.6% has a functional annotation. This genomic evidence contributes to a steadily growing body of genomic resources of red algae, with often expanded and highly repetitive genomes, and helps facilitate the study of genetic adaptation to their unique environments.

items.title: BiomedCAT: Biomedical Context Analysis Tool for Supporting Mechanistic Hypothesis Generation via User-defined Contextual Subgraph Extraction
items.corresponding_institution: Univ. Grenoble Alpes, CNRS, Grenoble INP, LIG, 38000 Grenoble, France
items.abstract: Researchers formulate mechanistic hypotheses in slides and figures long before they write them as text, yet knowledge-graph (KG) tools expect a query in the vocabulary of the graph. We present BiomedCAT, an open-source workflow that turns biomedical slides into a subgraph of the RTX-KG2c knowledge graph shaped by the user's research profile, on a laptop and without sending the documents out. A small vision-language model describes each slide; a 4-billion-parameter agent types the terms into the classes of the Biolink model; an existence gate removes invented entities; identifiers are retrieved from Translator services or from a local table and selected, never generated, by a judge model; and a profile-weighted two-hop expansion builds the context graph. On a synthetic Biolink typing benchmark whose labels were audited by an expert, the local agent reaches 0.71 accuracy on 517 non-ambiguous mentions, 4 points below Claude Opus 5 (0.75), level with DeepSeek-V4-Flash (0.69) and above open-weight models of 24 and 31 billion parameters; the audit also showed that 55\% of the generated labels were wrong or ambiguous. On expert-annotated slide decks, the reading stage recovers 81 to 94\% of the explicit terms of the English deck, less on French decks, and linking assigns the expert identifier to 65\% of the found terms online and 26\% in the fully local mode. A one-slide run takes 33 to 42 minutes, with peaks of 9.8~GB of system RAM above idle and 5.3~GB of GPU memory. In a facioscapulohumeral muscular dystrophy (FSHD) case, three slides that each draw one pathway from DUX4 at a different biological scale give graphs that overlap by 7 to 15\% of their nodes, each recovering its own pathway's expected nodes, and expose sourced paths from DUX4, such as a DUX4--HMGB1 interaction from IntAct. Of 21 compounds tested in FSHD, seven, including every agent that targets DUX4, are absent from RTX-KG2c, which bounds what a graph-based approach can propose. BiomedCAT lets a researcher set a working hypothesis against curated knowledge, with every edge traceable to its source.

items.title: Systematic evaluation using SigMatch reveals how sample tissues shape transcriptomic disease relationships
items.abstract: Motivation Diseases often share underlying molecular characteristics captured by transcriptional responses. Leveraging this knowledge transfer can aid in uncovering novel disease biology and drug repurposing. Large-scale transcriptomic datasets and disease signatures provide an opportunity to computationally identify these shared disease relationships based on shared genome-wide gene expression changes. However, disease signatures are strongly influenced by sample tissue, making it difficult to distinguish shared disease biology from shared tissue origin. Despite this challenge, existing computational approaches do not systematically take into account or evaluate the impact of tissue on their predictions. Results We present SigMatch, a systematic evaluation of the impact of sample tissue on transcriptomic-based disease relationship prioritization. We evaluate this impact on existing correlation- and rank-based methods, and on an alternative family called reconstruction-based methods. In particular, we examine (i) mechanistic disease relationships given the context of sample tissues and (ii) prediction agreement with external evidence of disease relatedness based on shared genes, symptoms, drugs, and comorbidities. We found that predicted disease relationships by all the methods are heavily influenced by sample tissue. Tissue-specific genes are not the sole driver of the prediction scores. Across methods, removal of tissue-specific genes did not reduce the observed tissue-dependent patterns or improve recovery of evidence-supported disease pairs. This work demonstrates substantial sample-tissue influence in transcriptomic similarities between diseases and that sample tissue should be considered when identifying and interpreting inferred transcriptomic disease relationships.

items.title: XAMPGen: An Interpretable Super Intelligence Pipeline For Novel Antimicrobial Peptide Discovery
items.abstract: Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) are short peptides with a broad spectrum of activity against bacterial pathogens, representing a promising avenue for combating the growing threat of antibiotic resistance. This study focuses on two main components: 1) generative super intelligence (GenSI) and 2) utilizing explainable super intelligence (XSI). We fine-tuned ProGen, a decoder-only protein language model, on known AMPs to generate novel peptide sequences with strong antimicrobial properties. Generated candidates were screened with an AMP classifier and filtered based on predicted minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC), along with human insights into AMP structure and activity in bacterial membranes. A final set of peptides was selected for synthesis and experimental testing. Biological assays confirmed antimicrobial activity in all generated and tested peptides, while fluorescence and circular dichroism measurements characterized membrane binding and peptide structure. We then applied XSI techniques to interpret the generative model and derive biological insights. Specifically, layer probing was used to identify cornerstone layers that encode functionally critical information. Self-attention analysis within these layers revealed residue-level interdependencies and patterns underlying antimicrobial functions, which we evaluated against well-characterized AMPs from the literature. We further examined associations between amino acid sequence patterns and binding properties in bacterial membrane mimics, relating these observations to biological activities in cell-based assays. These analyses provide insight into the model's decision-making process. This builds confidence that the learned amino acid interdependencies have physico-chemical significance, as applied to AMPs, and may facilitate the discovery of novel AMPs with therapeutic potential. This work demonstrates that interpretable generative language models can support rational AMP discovery.

items.title: ARGeement: sequence-based, versioned mapping of antimicrobial resistance gene databases
items.corresponding_institution: Centre for Bioinformatics, University of Veterinary Medicine, Budapest, 1078, Hungary
items.abstract: Genomic studies of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) rely on several independently curated reference databases, which describe the same genes under different names, in different structures and with different classifications. This makes results obtained with different databases difficult to compare. ARGeement maps the entries of AMRFinderPlus, the Comprehensive Antibiotic Resistance Database (CARD) and ResFinder/DisinFinder to each other by protein sequence, independently of their names. It characterises every link by its relation type, difference count and coverage, tracks the database versions, and produces a documented, immutable mapping for every release. The 17,920 entries of the release described here encode 17,959 protein sequences, corresponding to 9,337 unique proteins. For 64.4% of the cross-database entry pairs that encode the same protein, the names differ even when letter case is ignored, and 447 pairs show a genuine naming conflict. Conversely, 2.0% of the pairs with the same allele name do not encode the same protein. For synthetic variants created with known modifications, the original protein was among the best hits in 99.6% of the cases. In 100 complete RefSeq genomes annotated with AMRFinderPlus, the Resistance Gene Identifier (RGI) and ResFinder, the gene names agreed at 55.3%-75.6% of the loci called by both tools of a pair, whereas after mapping the two reference proteins were identical, near-identical or length variants at 89.6%-94.2%. These results show that name-based comparison is unreliable even for identical sequences, and that a sequence-based, versioned mapping is needed.

items.title: Most substitutions need more than one base change and an exact test tells which deposited scans measure the route
items.abstract: Design methods that reach a target through an intermediate take two substitutions at one position, and no deep mutational scan built from a single parental sequence reports the second. The detour is common, since 230 of the 380 ordered pairs of amino acids are more than one base change apart. Both substitutions are nevertheless present in the public record wherever one protein has been scanned on two parental backgrounds that differ at a position. We assemble every such comparison in MaveDB, 102,421 complete two-step routes over 65 protein clusters. The difference between a route and its two legs is a double difference, which is the epistasis between the tested position and the other positions at which the two backgrounds differ. Where the backgrounds differ nowhere else, that quantity is zero by construction. The rank correlation over the target residues must then return one, on any scale and against no null, which makes the comparison an exact test. Over the 741 qualifying pairs across 46 proteins the median is 0.965, and 34 of the 46 proteins return a median at or above 0.9. The arithmetic therefore holds across the population the record supplies, short natural domains drawn from families of near-identical sequences. Which pairs fail is not written in the record, since pairs drawn from one experiment set return 0.34 and pairs from unrelated submissions 0.97. The null such comparisons are read against fails the same test, returning +0.227 where it must return zero, more than the shift the comparison reports. Matching the control positions on the dispersion of the effects ranked halves that bias to +0.104. Two deposits of one protein agree at 0.642 where both score the same position. That bounds any predictor tested against one deposit at 0.80 for a position drawn at random, and at 0.90 and 0.98 where positions are scored more reliably. The test costs one correlation and settles, before any analysis, whether two deposits can be compared.

items.title: Overcoming subtype-specific immune resistance in small cell lung cancer through RNA-based immunotherapy
items.corresponding_institution: TRON - Translational Oncology at the University Medical Center of the Johannes Gutenberg University gGmbH; Freiligrathstraße 12, 55131 Mainz, Germany
items.abstract: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) comprises neuroendocrine (NE) and non-neuroendocrine (non-NE) subtypes with distinct immune landscapes and responses to therapy. Here, we established murine experimental metastases models to investigate RNA vaccination across SCLC subtypes. These exhibited distinct organotrophic properties and differ in both the magnitude and kinetics of interferon-induced MHC-I upregulation. Vaccination controlled non-NE tumors but provided limited survival benefit against NE tumors established in the lung or liver. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing and chromatin accessibility profiling revealed inflammation-associated programs following vaccination shared between organs. To overcome the limited survival benefit of vaccination in NE SCLC, we combined RNA vaccination with liver-targeted RNA-encoded cytokines. This combination markedly prolonged survival of NE tumor-bearing mice and enhanced inflammatory immune activity within the tumor microenvironment. Together, these findings identify vaccination-associated inflammatory programs of potential clinical relevance and warrant further investigation of cytokine combination therapy as strategy to improve immunotherapy in NE SCLC.

items.title: Computable Genomes: A Layered Computational Framework for Non-Coding DNA and Cellular Behavior
items.abstract: Genome-wide association studies have catalogued tens of thousands of trait-associated loci, most of them in non-coding DNA, yet for most loci the path from nucleotide to phenotype remains correlational. We propose a layered computational decomposition of the genome as a complement to data-driven approaches: sequence as formal language, sequence as information-bearing signal, mobile elements as runtime, compilation to interaction networks through thermodynamic and rule-based models, and execution as cellular and multicellular dynamics. Each layer is defined by its inputs, outputs and formalisms, and we set out where the frame breaks down, including the looseness of algorithmic-information estimates, the triviality of universality results and the failure of string grammars at the chromatin level. Synthetic-biology platforms serve as tests of whether the layers compose, and genomic foundation models and the AlphaGenome Atlas, which predicts effects for all nine billion possible single-nucleotide variants, serve as oracles whose coverage and limits we map onto the framework. We state five falsifiable predictions and test the first, that sequence compressibility carries information about regulatory function beyond composition and conservation, on 38,556 single-nucleotide variants from a saturation-mutagenesis reporter assay of 21 regulatory elements. In a pooled model, local compressibility is associated with measured effect size (standardized {beta} = -0.030, p = 0.0014). The association roughly halves under full control for base composition, loses significance when composition, motif and noise adjustments are combined under locus-level inference (wild cluster bootstrap p = 0.11), and averages zero within loci (random-effects {beta} = -0.0003, p = 0.90). The prediction is therefore not supported at the variant level in these data, which bound the effect a genome-wide test should expect. The argument is not that the genome "is" a program, but that treating it as one supplies formal tools whose predictions can be checked.

items.title: Spatiotemporal profiling reveals emergence of cell type-specific molecular aging and senescence programs in the spinal cord
items.corresponding_institution: Center for Genomics of Neurodegenerative Disease, New York Genome Center, 101 Avenue of the Americas, New York, NY 10013; Department of Neurology, Columbia Univ
items.abstract: The spinal cord is the primary relay center between the periphery and the brain, playing a critical role in sensory, motor and autonomic function. Despite its functional importance, the cellular and molecular changes underlying spinal cord aging and their relationship to cellular senescence - a hallmark associated with aging - remain incompletely understood. Here, we generated a cross-species, multi-omic atlas of spinal cord aging in mice and humans by integrating a combination of liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, Visium spatial transcriptomics, single-nucleus RNA-sequencing, and multiplexed immunofluorescence imaging. We identified converging age-associated increases in fibrinogen, laminin, and immune activation-associated proteins across the mouse and human spinal cord. Over the mouse lifespan, we further identified distinct spatiotemporal patterns of aging. Downregulated transcriptional programs, including synaptic signaling, mitochondrion organization, and autophagy, were most highly expressed in grey matter regions and in neurons. Upregulated transcriptional programs, including vascular and immune processes, were enriched in white matter regions and in endothelial cells and microglia, respectively. Notably, these increasing spatial modules were also enriched for senescence-associated genes. In the human spinal cord, endothelial cells and microglia were also most enriched for canonical senescence markers CDKN1A and CDKN2A, respectively. Overall, this study defines the shared, spatially-resolved, cell type-specific features associated with aging and senescence in the mouse and human spinal cord.

items.title: Genome assembly for Amanita muscaria var. muscaria
items.abstract: Amanita muscaria is a charismatic and widely distributed mushroom-forming fungus. Amanita muscaria comprises a species complex, and genomic resources are unevenly distributed, which may bias genetic and genomic study of the species complex. This study produces a high quality hybrid genome assembly of a specimen from New Zealand. Phylogenetic analysis shows that this belongs to Amanita muscaria var. muscaria.

items.title: ChIMe-seq enables multimodal epigenetic profiling in single molecules and single cells
items.abstract: Recent advances in single-cell and single-molecule sequencing have enabled high-resolution characterization of epigenetic states. However, methods that jointly measure multiple layers of epigenetic regulation within the same molecules and cells remain limited. Here, we developed Chromatin Immuno-Methylation sequencing (ChIMe-seq), a multimodal approach that simultaneously profiles histone modifications, DNA methylation, and nucleosome positioning genome-wide in single molecules and single cells. In contrast to recent approaches that rely on enzymatic fragmentation, ChIMe-seq preserves long DNA molecules by using a methyltransferase to deposit exogenous methylation marks that report on proximal histone modifications. This enables integration of multiple epigenetic features within individual molecules and supports short-read, long-read, and single-cell sequencing. These multimodal measurements are integrated into a novel mathematical framework that captures the coupling between nucleosome positioning, histone modifications, and DNA methylation. Both single-molecule and single-cell analyses reveal that DNA methylation is linked to nucleosome density in a manner modulated by local histone modifications, whilst differences in nucleosome:DNA structures are observed depending on epigenetic context and cell-type. Together, these results establish ChIMe-seq as a framework to investigate multifaceted epigenetic coordination across scales, from single-nucleotide resolution to long-range chromatin organization in single molecules and single cells.

items.title: Target-enrichment sequencing reveals intergenotypic reassortment of infectious salmon anaemia virus in Atlantic Canada
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Pathobiology and Population Sciences, Royal Veterinary College, University of London, Hatfield, Hertfordshire AL9 7TA, UK
items.abstract: Infectious salmon anaemia virus (ISAV) causes severe disease and substantial economic losses in farmed Atlantic salmon (Salmo salar). The virus has an eight-segment, negative-sense single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) genome and is divided into European and North American genotypes. Despite their co-circulation in locations such as the Atlantic coast of Canada, reassortment between these genotypes has never been observed. However, routine diagnostic and sequence-based surveillance often target individual genome segments and may therefore fail to identify reassortant viruses or accurately resolve their genomic ancestry. In this study, we developed a probe panel targeting both genotypes and applied Oxford Nanopore sequencing to 37 ISAV-positive samples collected from 14 farm sites in the Bay of Fundy, New Brunswick, Canada. Twenty-seven samples yielded 29 consensus genomes, including separate viral consensuses recovered from two mixed infections. Segment-specific phylogenies identified 24 viruses with a previously unreported intergenotypic genomic constellation comprising a European-genotype segment 3 and North American-genotype segments 1, 2 and 4 - 8. Their consistent monophyletic clustering across segment-specific phylogenies supports a single ancestral reassortment event followed by onward circulation of the reassortant lineage. A time-scaled phylogeny of segment 3 estimated the posterior mean time to the most recent common ancestor (tMRCA) of the sampled reassortant cluster as September 2016 (95% HPD: March 2013-June 2019), indicating that this segment 3 lineage pre-dated its first sampling in 2021. Five additional viruses represented several distinct EU-genotype lineages. To our knowledge, this is the first documented reassortment between the European and North American ISAV genotypes. These findings identify an intergenotypic reassortant lineage detected across multiple farms in the Bay of Fundy and demonstrate the value of whole-genome sequencing for detecting reassortment, mixed infections and epidemiologically relevant viral diversity.

items.title: CIRCA learns identifiable cell- and niche-level programs and their interactions with tissue pathology from spatial transcriptomics
items.corresponding_institution: The University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston
items.abstract: Interactions among cells and their local microenvironments shape tissue organization and function, while their dysregulation can contribute to disease. In Alzheimer's disease (AD), the complex responses of glial cells and neurons to amyloid-{beta} pathology can both mitigate and exacerbate neuronal injury. Spatial transcriptomics enables investigation of these relationships in situ, but recovering interpretable transcriptional programs and their interactions from spatial transcriptomics remains challenging, in part because conventional nonlinear models are non-identifiable. Here we present CIRCA (Causal Interaction Representation for Cellular Architectures), a self-supervised causal representation learning framework that jointly learns identifiable cell- and neighborhood-level transcriptional programs and the directed interactions among them under explicit assumptions. It can also be extended to incorporate additional modalities such as pathology. Benchmarked against five existing methods across seven cell-resolution datasets, CIRCA achieved the highest biological accuracy in six and the highest overall score in all five multi-section datasets, while recovering higher-order anatomical organization. In an AD mouse model, incorporating amyloid-{beta} pathology revealed four region-specific plaque niches enriched for microglia. Plaque-associated microglia shared a core disease-associated response whose strength varied by region, and AD genetic risk was preferentially enriched in hippocampal and cortical plaque-associated microglia. Reproducible latent factors linked to cell-level amyloid burden separated phagocytic from inflammatory microglial programs. Applied to a human colorectal cancer dataset, CIRCA resolved patient-specific tumor niches, conserved stromal remodeling niches, and distinct macrophage states, highlighting its versatility. Together, these results establish CIRCA as a methodological advance over existing approaches, enabling deeper insights into tissue organization and the molecular dependencies linking cells to their local environments.

items.title: Evaluation depth reshapes method rankings in proteomic co-abundance network inference
items.corresponding_institution: Section Computational Pathology Heidelberg, Institute of Pathology Heidelberg, University Hospital Heidelberg, University of Heidelberg, Heidelberg, Germany.
items.abstract: Network inference from quantitative proteomics is usually benchmarked at a single, arbitrarily chosen number of top-ranked edges, so the influence of evaluation depth has not, to our knowledge, been systematically tested. We compared five strategies (random forest with bootstrap selection-frequency filtering, WGCNA, GENIE3, Spearman correlation and context likelihood of relatedness) across seven proteomic datasets from four quantification platforms, using harmonised preprocessing and Precision@K, the fraction of a method's K top-ranked protein pairs present in a pooled reference of curated protein associations (STRING, BioGRID and CORUM). Method rankings changed with depth. In all six datasets that allow an equal-depth comparison, the leading method at K = 50 differed from the leader at K = 2,000, and 18 of 24 pairwise comparisons involving the filtered random forest reversed somewhere along the depth range, although seven of these reversals rested on differences of at most 0.02 in precision and each network was inferred only once. No method dominated. Relative to the same random forest without filtering, the selection-frequency filter was associated with small differences (+0.006 to +0.036 in Precision@500 in six of six equal-depth datasets; mixed at shallower depths) that cannot be separated from its 20- to 50-fold greater number of fitted trees. Prospective testing on independent datasets gave one qualified replication, one non-replication and one non-evaluable dataset. We recommend reporting precision trajectories across depths rather than single-threshold comparisons.

items.title: Breedbase: An Integrated Breeding Informatics System with Statistical Analysis and Decision-Support Tools
items.corresponding_institution: Boyce Thompson Institute, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14853, USA
items.abstract: Breeding programs are becoming increasingly data-intensive, digital and collaborative. One-stop digital breeding ecosystems, in which data storage, field workflow tools, statistical analysis and breeding decision-support tools are seamlessly integrated, are increasingly important. Breedbase (https://breedbase.org) is one of the few open-source platforms that integrate these functionalities within a single system. It provides tools for phenotypic data quality control, descriptive, inferential and predictive statistical analyses. Integrated into the database are tools for single-trial analysis of variance (ANOVA), linear mixed modeling, stability analysis, correlation analysis, principal component analysis, k-means and hierarchical clustering, kinship and inbreeding analysis, genome-wide association study (GWAS), and genomic prediction. Input data and outputs from these analysis tools are visualized in interactive plots and are also available in text files for downloading and sharing. By persisting analysis datasets in the database and applying standardized and automated data preprocessing and analysis workflows, Breedbase is designed to improve efficiency, help maintain data integrity, and support reproducible analyses that can be readily shared among collaborators. Breedbase is open-source software, containerized using Docker, and available for self-hosting or cloud hosting and management by the Mueller lab.

items.title: SPIDER: Contextualizing Biomedical Knowledge for Evidence-Grounded Scientific Reasoning
items.abstract: Aggregated relations in biomedical knowledge graphs can obscure evidence and study conditions, complicating the distinction between scientific disagreement and contextual differences. Here we introduce SPIDER, a multi-agent framework grounding biomedical relations in literature evidence and extracting study conditions for interpretation. Applied to a graph integrating 48 databases and ontologies, SPIDER analyzed 1.95 million PubMed abstracts, adding 2.31 million previously unrepresented, literature-supported entity pairs to construct SPIDER-KG. Daily updates incorporate relations and evidence from newly indexed PubMed records. Across 89,937 evidence-supported comparisons of potentially incompatible relations, SPIDER classified 79.0% as contextual differences, and 6.1% as genuine disagreement, achieving 80.3% macro-F1 averaged across both categories against expert annotations. On SPIDER-Bench and four biomedical reasoning benchmarks, SPIDER-KG improved large language models' interpretation of evidence-supported biomedical relationships. Retrospective analysis of newly reported gene--disease relationships further demonstrated how evidence-linked knowledge can contextualize emerging discoveries. SPIDER-KG provides a reusable, incrementally extensible evidence layer for biomedical reasoning.

items.title: HARICOT: De Novo Assembly of Raw Nanopore Signals using Fuzzy de Bruijn Graphs
items.abstract: Nanopore sequencing enables reading long nucleotide sequences by measuring characteristic changes in ionic current as molecules pass through a nanopore. These current measurements, known as raw signals, can be analyzed without translating them into bases (i.e., without basecalling), which provides fast and resource-efficient genome analysis. Prior work, Rawsamble, enables finding overlaps between raw nanopore signals, without basecalling them, and generating assemblies from these overlaps with off-the-shelf assemblers such as miniasm. Constructing assemblies directly from raw signals can substantially reduce redundancy and fragmentation in signal datasets, which is useful for many downstream tasks such as constructing non-redundant and accurate basecalled reads from assembled signals. However, existing overlap-based signal assembly strategies suffer from limited scalability and resolution mainly due to using off-the-shelf assemblers (e.g., miniasm) that are designed for basecalled sequences. While scalability and performance limitations can be addressed by existing de Bruijn graph approaches to assembly, their reliance on exact matches makes these methods too sensitive to the inherently noisy raw nanopore signals. To improve assembly of raw signals using de Bruijn graph approaches, we present HARICOT, a mechanism that constructs assemblies from raw nanopore signals by utilizing fuzzy de Bruijn graphs and Hough-transform-based overlap detection to robustly tolerate errors and noise in raw nanopore signals. Our evaluations on various genomes of different sizes show that HARICOT significantly improves assembly contiguity and quality compared to Rawsamble, helping close the gap to popular assembly tools such as Flye or wtdbg2 operating on nucleotide sequences. At the same time, performance remains comparable to these assemblers, without requiring additional basecalling. We discuss that assembling raw nanopore signals before basecalling enables future work in various ways such as building these de Bruijn graphs in a streaming way and assembly-aware basecalling techniques that can basecall assembly graphs for accurate and redundancy-resolved basecalling.
