HARICOT is available at https://github.com/STORMgroup/HARICOT . We also provide the scripts to fully reproduce our results on our GitHub page.

items.title: Timing and meaning in spoken thought relate to distinct patterns of brain dynamics
items.corresponding_institution: University of Science and Technology of China
items.abstract: When people think aloud, their reports vary in duration and in how closely successive thoughts are related in meaning. We asked whether these two dimensions relate to distinct patterns of brain dynamics. Using 10-minute think-aloud fMRI scans from 75 adults, we quantified timing as variability in sentence-event duration and semantic continuity as similarity between adjacent grouped thoughts. In models including both measures, greater duration variability was associated with lower relative brain entropy (BEN), estimated from BOLD time series, in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (voxel wise FDR q < 0.05). This association persisted after adjustment for speech coverage, pause duration, articulation rate and event count. Semantic continuity was associated with differences in BOLD amplitude and synchrony across bilateral sensorimotor regions. These voxel wise associations fell below the FDR threshold after adjustment for speech coverage or pause duration. In a secondary atlas-based analysis, semantic continuity remained positively associated with local synchrony in Default C after adjustment for speech timing ({beta} = 0.517, P = 0.003). These findings link the timing of spoken reports to dorsolateral prefrontal brain activity irregularity and show how the sensorimotor correlates of semantic continuity covary with speech timing.

items.title: Stability and flexibility in the Wisconsin Card Sorting Task emerge from goal-directed inference and planning under the free-energy principle
items.abstract: In goal-directed behavior, the brain has to balance stability and flexibility. Stability means keeping the current recognition of environmental context, whereas flexibility means switching to a new one. The Wisconsin Card Sorting Task (WCST) is a standard task for studying this balance. In this task, stability is keeping the category estimate after correct feedback, and flexibility is switching it after incorrect feedback. Computational models have been proposed to elucidate the mechanism behind this balance. However, most models are given a variable for each category in advance, and every model treats correct feedback as desirable from the start. These models cover neither the category learning process nor the goal-directed process that adjusts the card selection to get correct feedback. To explain both processes under one principle, we modeled the WCST with a hierarchical recurrent neural network based on the Free Energy Principle (FEP). The model first infers the environment from observations and then plans the card selection to reach the goal. In both steps, the model minimizes prediction error based on the FEP. For inference, the error lies between the predicted signals and the received signals. For planning, it lies between the predicted feedback and the correct feedback. As a result, the latent states formed category-related clusters during learning. In the testing phase, the model kept the estimate after correct feedback and switched it after incorrect feedback. Removing the goal-directed process degraded the keeping and the switching. This implies that the two processes and this balance emerge from the FEP.

items.title: Spectral and complexity-based signatures of advanced concentration absorption meditation: A high-density EEG study of jhana
items.corresponding_institution: Meditation Research Program, Department of Psychiatry, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, USA
items.abstract: Advanced meditation provides structured and reproducible alterations of consciousness that are increasingly used as model states for the neuroscience of consciousness. Jhana-type advanced concentration absorption meditation (ACAM-J) consists of eight progressively deepening absorption states (ACAM-J1-8) in which sensory and self-referential content gradually attenuate. We applied high-density EEG and a comprehensive multidimensional battery of spectral and complexity measures to characterize each ACAM-J state individually in 20 advanced meditators, together with phenomenological ratings. ACAM-J produced widespread posterior-central reductions in oscillatory and aperiodic power, posterior aperiodic flattening across all eight states, and convergent increases in entropy-based complexity over the posterior cortex, with power effects strengthening with phenomenological depth. Crucially, neural complexity remained elevated even in the late, most minimal and unified states, in opposition to the prevailing account that links higher neural entropy to richer phenomenal content. Between practitioners, lower power and higher entropy accompanied more visual and auditory but less bodily content, a redistribution rather than an enrichment of experience; within practitioners, only reduced low-frequency power tracked wider attention and less narrative thought. ACAM-J thus emerges as a non-pharmacological model state at the high-complexity end of the spectrum of altered consciousness, and reveals a previously unquantified dissociation between neural complexity and experiential richness for specific ACAM-J states.

items.title: Distinct developmental organization of intrinsic brain dynamics supports different components of inhibitory control during adolescence
items.corresponding_institution: University of Science and Technology of China
items.abstract: Adolescent inhibitory control develops within a changing organization of intrinsic brain activity, yet the signal properties and cortical systems associated with different control demands remain unclear. We studied 101 youths aged 8-18 years using brain entropy (BEN), amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF), fractional ALFF (fALFF), and regional homogeneity (ReHo) derived from resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Voxelwise and seven-network models evaluated age associations and task-by-age interactions while adjusting for sex, head motion, and gray-matter anatomy. Spatially standardized ALFF showed age associations in somatomotor and salience/ventral-attention networks. Contextual control, assessed with the AX Continuous Performance Task (AX-CPT), showed the broadest age-dependent coupling: all four spatially standardized measures yielded voxelwise interactions surviving permutation-based cluster false discovery rate correction, and the frontoparietal BEN interaction survived network correction. Better action cancellation was associated with higher frontoparietal BEN without a corrected network age interaction. Independent cortical references further differentiated these patterns: raw BEN age-effect evidence was stronger toward association cortex, whereas the ALFF-AX-CPT age interaction was stronger toward sensorimotor cortex. Additional task interactions aligned with the second and third connectivity gradients. Core voxelwise AX-CPT findings persisted after age trimming. These findings link the differentiation of inhibitory-control demands to the developmental organization of complementary intrinsic signal properties across cortical systems, highlighting contextual control as a prominent locus of age-dependent brain-behavior coupling.

items.title: Neuronal activity regulates glycolysis to sculpt synaptic transmission
items.abstract: Neuronal computation imposes rapid, localized changes in energy consumption, yet how energy production is regulated at such fine spatiotemporal scales is incompletely understood. Using two photon imaging of neuronal activity and energy metabolism in Drosophila , we show that neurons recruit glycolysis in less than a second, with cell-type and subcellular specificity. This coupling scales with neuronal activity and is regulated by AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK). Activity-induced glycolysis is tightly correlated with presynaptic sites in cholinergic neurons, and is required for cholinergic but not glutamatergic neurotransmission. In cholinergic neurons, glycolysis supports both energetic demand and acetylcholine biosynthesis, with ATP citrate lyase linking these functions by both activating acetylcholine biosynthesis and disinhibiting glycolytic flux. These findings establish glycolysis as a previously unrecognized regulator of cell-type specific computation.

items.title: Oligodendrocyte Development and Myelination in the 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome
items.abstract: The 22q11.2 deletion syndrome is associated with a high risk of neurodevelopmental disorders, including a 25% chance of developing schizophrenia (SCZ). SCZ is prevalent in 0.4-0.7% of the population. Evidence suggests that the cognitive deficits of SCZ may be caused by neurodevelopmental disconnection due to impaired oligodendrocyte (OL) maturation and myelination. We hypothesized that the 22q11.2 deletion syndrome impairs OL life cycle progression, halting oligodendrocytes in their immature phase and preventing advancement to the mature stage. This in turn creates myelination changes, demonstrated by a decrease in myelin. To test this, we utilized a 22q11.2 deletion mouse model focusing on the prefrontal cortex (PFC), a late-myelinating brain region. We evaluated PFC regions (mPFC, dlPFC, mOFC, lOFC) in adolescent (P14 and P28) mutant mice and controls. Additionally, we examined the two-hit hypothesis of schizophrenia using a maternal separation model. At P28, mutant mice displayed a significant increase in immature OLs and mature OLs in the PFC, and a decrease in myelination and myelin process length compared to controls. At P14, mutant mice showed subtle reductions in oligodendrocyte precursor cells and subtle myelination alterations in the mPFC. When considering the two-hit hypothesis, we saw equivalent reductions in myelination in the genetic-only, environmental-only, and two-hit groups. Together, these data demonstrate that the 22q11.2 deletion impairs OL maturation and functional myelination between P14 to P28, a critical window for neurodevelopment. Examining the impact of SCZ on OLs could reveal key intervention targets before SCZ symptom onset, and may determine the role of OLs and the 22q11.2 deletion in neural disconnectivity in schizophrenia.

items.title: Drastic improvement in MHC class I epitope prediction through training data augmentation, generative adversarial network modeling of selfness, and consideration of homology to class II epitopes.
items.abstract: Accurate identification of immunogenic neoantigens is critical for personalized cancer vaccines but remains hindered by the high false-positive rates of current predictors. Here, we present DeepOmicsNeo, a modular deep learning framework that harmonizes three biological determinants of immunogenicity. The first module, DeepOmicsNeo-Binding, overcomes data scarcity in non-9mer peptide-Class I Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) binding prediction via a novel augmentation strategy that synthesizes pseudo-binders and non-binders by editing non-anchor residues, outperforming its competitors. The second module, DeepOmicsNeo-Selfness, addresses the paucity of negative training data for immunogenicity prediction by utilizing a Generative Adversarial Network trained on around 60 million human self-peptides. This unsupervised approach quantifies selfness to detect immunogenic peptides and the resulting score correlated with IFN-{gamma} secretion by T-cells. The third module, DeepOmicsNeo-H2, exploits the central-region homology between known HLA Class-I and Class-II restricted epitopes. The integrated model, DeepOmicsNeo-Immunogenicity, outperforms state-of-the-art predictors on the TESLA, HiTIDE, and TiTANIAN benchmark datasets.[2.1] Top20 precision, the most important benchmark for clinical utility in personalized cancer vaccine design, was drastically improved over other predictors. Together, these findings indicate that jointly modeling the three complementary features captures biologically meaningful determinants of immunogenicity, supporting DeepOmicsNeo as a robust computational framework for neoantigen prioritization in personalized cancer immunotherapy.

items.title: GRABS: a content-addressed antibody-antigen binding-affinity dataset with predicted structures and a leak-free benchmark
items.abstract: Machine-learning prediction of antibody-antigen binding affinity depends as much on the training data as on the model, yet public affinity measurements are scattered across databases with incompatible formats, mix genuine dissociation constants with censored or predicted values, and concentrate most of their label mass on a few heavily mutated targets. We present GRABS (Geometric Resource for Antibody Binding Studies), a curated, content-addressed, structure-ready dataset that consolidates nine public sources, of which the seven with redistributable licenses yield 4,380 canonical antibody-antigen records} (median-collapsed from 4,761 raw measurements), each with an experimentally measured dissociation constant (Kd), paired heavy and light variable regions (VH, VL), and an antigen sequence, covering 2,015 distinct antigen sequences. Every structure, graph, and feature is addressed by a content key, md5(VH+VL+antigen)[:10], and verified non-circularly: each graph's node features are decoded back to sequence and re-hashed, matching the content key for 4,282/4,282 (100%) structure-backed records. This integrity is load-bearing: an alignment ablation shows that a previously-reported strong cross-target result (R2 {approx} 0.415) was a misalignment-mediated source/batch leak that content-key regeneration dissolves. On the resulting leak-free, antigen-cluster-grouped benchmark, cross-target ranking of variants of a held-out antigen collapses to the noise floor (within-held-out-antigen Spearman {rho} {approx} 0 for every model family: sequence, structure, and folding-confidence), with structure giving no advantage, a rigorously leakage-controlled quantification of the limited reach of current methods. GRABS ships model-ready artifacts (Boltz-2 predicted complexes, per-residue ESM-2 embeddings, geometric graphs, feature vectors) with antigen-stratified splits, and is intended for leakage-free benchmarking and within-target affinity ranking (measure-then-rank), not zero-shot prediction for antigens absent from training.

items.title: Systematic prediction of genetic variance in a line development program
items.abstract: To date, predicting the genetic variance (VG) in biparental crosses has been unreliable. My objective was to determine if predicting VG via tabular analysis, which was developed assuming free recombination and having known VG in founder crosses, is effective even if these unrealistic assumptions are unmet. With line X being developed from the P1/P2 cross, the VG in X/Y was predicted as VX/Y = {lambda}1VP1/Y + {lambda}2VP2/Y, where {lambda}1 was the parental contribution of P1 to X and {lambda}2 was the parental contribution of P2 to X. Simulations involved four founder lines with biallelic marker loci and multiple alleles at quantitative trait loci. The VG in each founder cross was estimated from simulated phenotypic values of N lines under varying heritability (h2). Non-founder lines were developed successively from the founders. Among the 774 non-founder crosses, the mean correlation between the true VG and predicted VG ranged from 0.49 (N = 50 and h2 = 0.20) to 0.70 (N = 400 to 1000 and h2 [≥] 0.50). The mean regression of predicted VG on true VG was 0.51-0.52. Having N = 100-200 lines was sufficient for estimating VG. Free recombination increased the regression of predicted VG on true VG to 0.87 and the correlation between the two to 0.64-0.93. Overall, the results suggested that tabular analysis is currently the most effective method for predicting VG. Further research is needed on combining VG estimates in both founder and non-founder crosses when conducting tabular analysis in a breeding program.

items.title: Multimodal Structural and Regulatory Architecture of Coding and Non-Coding Variants Across the Orofacial Clefting TP63-IRF6-GRHL3 Network
items.corresponding_institution: Centro Universitário de Belo Horizonte (UniBH), Belo Horizonte, Minas Gerais, Brazil
items.abstract: Pathogenic variation across the TP63-IRF6-GRHL3 transcriptional network causes syndromic and nonsyndromic orofacial clefts (OFCs), yet scalar sequence predictors collapse distinct failure modes and leave isoform-specific coding variants, splice-altering indels, and distal enhancer alleles unresolved. Here, we integrate 29 AlphaFold 3 (AF3) assemblies (10 wild-type, 19 mutant), thermodynamic stability ({Delta}{Delta}G) calculations, and AlphaGenome regulatory modeling across clinical, saturation-mutagenesis, and reporter benchmarks. In strict leave-one-gene-out (LOGO) coding benchmarks, replacing paralog crystal templates with full-length human AF3 structures improves IRF6 classification (biophysical AUROC rising from 0.7844 to 0.8967; {Delta}{Delta}G from 0.6461 to 0.8516) and resolves canonical isoform gaps in the 602-residue MANE Select GRHL3 homodimer. Projecting IRF6 missense variants onto a two-dimensional stability-versus-interface phase plane separates dominant-negative popliteal pterygium syndrome (PPS) poisons from haploinsufficient Van der Woude syndrome (VWS1) alleles (VWS1-versus-PPS Quadrant I odds ratio [OR] = 0.0263 [reciprocal OR = 38.0], p = 4.652 x 10-3) and distinguishes DNA-contact poisons from dimer-unfolding alleles across 12 zebrafish in vivo assays. Atomistic base-readout contacts in the AF3 TP63-MCS9.7 tetramer mirror loss-of-function profiles in MaveDB ({rho} = 0.6048, p = 6.52 x 10-4) and AlphaGenome keratinocyte DNase predictions ({rho} = 0.6040, p = 6.65 x 10-4). Across non-coding benchmarks, AlphaGenome splicing tracks reach an AUROC of 0.9876 while prioritizing cryptic splice variants of uncertain significance, and epithelial chromatin tracks capture enhancer grammar, plasmid-cloning artifacts, and context-dependent ARHGAP29, FOXE1, and local 8q24 chromatin effects within AlphaGenome's 1.049-Mb horizon.

items.title: Comparative metagenomics reveals diversity and metabolic heterogeneity of sediment microbes from the Great Barrier Reef
items.corresponding_institution: The University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia
items.abstract: Microbial communities in coral reefs are highly connected through benthic-pelagic coupling. Pelagic and host-associated microbiomes have recently been characterised via genome-resolved metagenomics. However, similar characterisation of sediment communities has lagged behind due to their higher complexity. Here, using short- and long-read shotgun sequence data, we characterised sediment microbial communities of Australia's Great Barrier Reef. From 191 samples across 48 broadly distributed sites, we recovered 2,698 prokaryotic metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) representing 1,201 species-level clusters, most of which are novel. Compared against their sympatric counterparts in seawater, sediment MAGs exhibited greater phylogenetic diversity and flexibility in metabolic potential, implicating diverse respiration strategies and cycling of nitrogen, sulphur, and hydrogen. They also encode more abundant and novel biosynthetic capabilities, likely reflecting competition and adaptation to intermittent fluctuations in nutrient regimes, and between oxic and anoxic conditions. Our results provide foundational genomic resources for reef sediment microbes, uncovering biodiversity and function that together with planktonic microbes shape the ecological success and stability of coral reef ecosystems.

items.title: MARRI: Mechanism-Aware Learning of RNA-RNA Interactions with Foundation Models
items.abstract: RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) are central to post-transcriptional regulation, yet their prediction requires accounting for structural accessibility and intermolecular base pairing beyond sequence complementarity. Pretrained RNA foundation models provide representations of individual RNAs, but translating these representations into interaction predictions requires mechanistic knowledge of interaction recognition. Here, we introduce MARRI, a mechanism-aware multimodal framework that couples pretrained representations with domain knowledge by embedding learned opening penalties and hybridization gains into bidirectional cross-RNA attention. MARRI improves ROC--AUC and PR--AUC over the strongest baseline by 12.20\% and 10.25\%, respectively, and maintains strong discrimination for unseen RNA partnerships and interaction regions. Perturbation and repeat-context analyses identify prediction-relevant sequence regions. Integrating MARRI-derived interaction propensities with disease-associated expression profiles links molecular prediction to systems-level models of disease progression and network remodeling. MARRI thus illustrates a knowledge-guided strategy for coupling molecular foundation models with domain knowledge to support grounded prediction, interpretation and systems-level hypothesis generation.

items.title: LipidRT: leveraging retention time coherence for robust lipid annotation in reversed-phase LC-MS-based lipidomics
items.abstract: MS/MS data alone is often insufficient for confident lipid identification, while existing retention time (RT)-based methods, despite their promise, have limited applicability. We present LipidRT, an R-based Shiny application that uses RT coherence to validate, refine and expand lipid annotations in untargeted RPLC-HRMS lipidomics in a dataset-specific, software-agnostic manner. By exploiting conserved chromatographic elution relationships as structural constraints and excluding RT-inconsistent annotations from model fitting, LipidRT improves annotation confidence, coverage and consistency while minimizing manual curation.

items.title: spicyR enables robust, well-powered co-localisation tests in large spatial omics cohorts
items.abstract: Spatial omics technologies can now profile finely resolved cell populations in patient tissue at scale, offering a way to link their arrangement to outcomes. Yet images often differ in size, shape and cell content, and existing tests between patient groups mistake these differences for co-localisation or weight every image equally. We present spicyR v2, which avoids both problems with a fast, permutation-free test that accounts for these differences and weights each image by how precisely it measures co-localisation. In simulations and 74 analyses of 42 public datasets, it controlled false discoveries, had more power than spicyR v1 and was robust to tears, holes and differences in cell number that misled other methods. These analyses also revealed that many studies relating co-localisation to clinical outcomes are underpowered, and spicyR v2 can estimate the number of patients a new study needs. spicyR v2 analyses 100 million cells in minutes, making robust, well-powered tests of co-localisation practical for large spatial omics cohorts.

items.title: Quantifying Homology and Length Bias in Antimicrobial Peptide Prediction
items.corresponding_institution: Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University
items.abstract: Bacteria are becoming resistant to existing antibiotics faster than new ones are found. Antimicrobial peptides are a promising alternative, but laboratory testing is slow and costly. Candidates are therefore ranked first by a classifier, and published classifiers report near-perfect accuracy. Two controls are missing from the benchmarks behind those numbers. Training and test peptides are not separated by sequence homology. The negative class is not matched to the positive class by length. We propose a controlled evaluation protocol that imposes both, plus a sample-size control that separates matching from the data it removes. We apply it to a four-model ensemble of our own and ten baselines on a benchmark of 16,168 sequences, holding the models fixed. A classifier given nothing but peptide length separates the benchmark far above chance. Homology control costs 0.067 MCC and length matching a further 0.115, taking the reported score from 0.834 to 0.661. Over ten redrawn partitions the length term holds while the homology term shrinks, so length is the effect that survives. The protocol also reorders the methods, and a frozen ESM-2 embedding overtakes the ensemble. Three published benchmarks show the same pattern. We recommend a minimum reporting standard that makes such losses visible.

items.title: Learning spatial cellular state through 3D reconstruction of the cell
items.abstract: Subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics localizes individual RNA transcripts within cells with high-precision. Existing methods for identifying spatially organized cell populations rely on cellular niches defined by neighboring cells, leaving open whether such populations can be identified from individual-cell representations alone. Moreover, representations that jointly capture transcript identity and three-dimensional (3D) spatial organization have not been systematically learned or biologically evaluated. Here we present a representation learning framework that models each cell as a gene-annotated point cloud of transcripts and trains a rotation-equivariant neural network to reconstruct 3D cell shape, yielding spatially informed transcript embeddings. We further aggregate these embeddings into a cell-state representation that summarizes transcript-level spatial patterns. Our framework outperforms existing point-cloud-based 3D reconstruction methods on cell-shape reconstruction. In MERFISH human uterine cancer, combining the learned embeddings with gene expression improved prediction of CD45RO protein intensity over both gene expression alone and niche-based embeddings. Applied to MERFISH human liver cancer and Xenium human lung datasets, our framework identified distinct spatial patterns between cell populations, including spatially organized subpopulations marked by disease-associated gene expression and patterns associated with pathological tissue structures. Together, these results show that learning transcript representations through 3D cell reconstruction provides a novel approach to capture cell-state heterogeneity and biologically relevant spatial organization in subcellular spatial transcriptomics.

items.title: Benchmarking four large language models on generating and selecting hypotheses that match published findings in 50 studies of ageing biology
items.abstract: Objective We asked how often hypotheses generated by large language models for 50 research tasks matched the withheld finding of the published study, and whether model forecasts could identify the matching hypotheses. Methods We built tasks from 50 peer-reviewed studies in ageing biology published after the models' stated training cutoffs; each task gave the background and a research question and withheld the study's finding (the reference finding). GPT-6 Astra, Grok 4.5, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini 4 Argon each generated five hypotheses per task by three methods: a single request, a multistep pipeline, and the Omega Point method without literature search (2997 hypotheses). A hypothesis matched the reference finding if at least two of three judge models from other developers scored it at least 3 (primary threshold) or at least 4 (strict threshold) on a 0 to 5 scale; refusals counted as non-matches. A selection rule, chosen from 112 variants evaluated on the Grok 4.5 hypotheses, kept only the hypotheses for which all four predictor models forecast experimental confirmation; the predictors never saw the published finding. The controls were recorded random answers and each generator's first-listed hypothesis. Confidence intervals (95% CIs) were calculated by cluster bootstrap over tasks. Results Of the hypotheses generated by a single request, 13.2% to 18.0% matched the reference finding, compared with 11.2% to 18.8% for the multistep pipeline and 2.8% to 7.6% for the Omega Point method. With a single request, the hypothesis listed first matched in 37.5% of cases (75/200), and the hypotheses in positions 2 to 5 matched in 10.1% (81/800). Among the hypotheses selected unanimously, the match rate was 73.7% (14/19) for Grok 4.5, 47.4% (9/19) for Gemini 4 Argon, and 63.6% (14/22) for Claude Opus 5.5, compared with 12.1% to 17.9% for the random control and 37.5% to 40.0% for the first-listed hypotheses. The selected lists captured 27.3% to 35.0% of all matching hypotheses. Pooled across the three sets, the match rate among selected hypotheses exceeded that among first-listed hypotheses by 23.2 percentage points (pp; 95% CI [13.0, 32.6]). When Gemini 4 Argon re-extracted the reference findings, the match rate among selected hypotheses was 59.6% (34/57), compared with 61.4% (35/57) against the original reference findings for the same tasks. In a manual audit with the generator, judge scores, and selection status hidden, our classifications agreed with the judges' at the primary threshold in 81/100 cases (Cohen's kappa 0.62). Agreement was 89.7% after weighting the sample strata by their size in the corpus. We classified 19 of 30 sampled selected hypotheses as matches, and the judges classified 20 of 30. Conclusions In the evaluated sets, unanimous selection by the four predictors increased the match rate among selected hypotheses; the resulting match rate depended on the matching threshold. Generators listed a matching hypothesis first more often than in later positions, and 50 of the 60 selected hypotheses were listed first. The advantage over the first-listed hypotheses and over the best single predictor at equal list length was statistically significant for the Grok and Opus hypotheses but not for the Gemini hypotheses, and the pairwise differences of the advantage between generators were not statistically significant (p >= 0.16 after Holm correction). We selected the rule using the Grok hypotheses and evaluated it on the Gemini and Opus hypotheses for the same 50 tasks; it has not been tested on new tasks.

items.title: GenVinci reconstructs 3D molecular tissue scenes from histology to map senescence across aging and disease
items.corresponding_institution: Cutaneous Biology Research Center, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA; Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard, Cambridge, MA, U
items.abstract: Spatial omics has generated measurements at unprecedented scale, yet computational approaches remain largely confined to individual modalities and 2D representations. Here we assemble ImageOmicsNet-300M, a corpus of 300 million single-cell and spatial transcriptomic profiles, including 24.9 million H&E-predicted virtual spatial transcriptomics profiles, and 4,623 H&E sections. Of these H&E sections, we generated 1,782 from aging mouse organs and serially sectioned human skin spanning five decades, with matched spatial transcriptomics and snRNA-seq. Building on this resource, we develop GenVinci, a multimodal tissue foundation model that reconstructs 3D tissue scenes from routine 2D histology. GenVinci predicts spatial gene expression from H&E with zero-shot generalization and maps senescence-associated states across 85.8 million cells, revealing cell-type-specific patterns and disease-associated remodeling. Integration with human genetics implicates suprabasal keratinocytes in atopic dermatitis and keratinocyte carcinomas, linked to higher and lower p16 and p21 expression, respectively. These findings establish GenVinci as a framework mapping senescence in 3D across scales.

items.title: Integrating disease and protein networks expands genetic support for therapeutic targets
items.corresponding_institution: University of  Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center
items.abstract: Human genetics guides therapeutic target selection, but direct genetic support covers few clinically investigated target-indication pairs, each linking a target to a disease. Here we introduce BRIDGE (Biological Relation-Informed Diffusion of Genetic Evidence), which propagates genetic evidence through coupled protein-protein interaction and disease-similarity networks. Each candidate's score is calibrated against scores obtained after randomly substituting similarly connected genes for genes with direct genetic support. In a retrospective benchmark of 13,022 pairs that had reached at least phase I, BRIDGE supported 572 additional pairs, increasing coverage from 5.1% to 9.5%. Among eligible pairs lacking direct genetic support, 25.3% of network-added pairs had reached launch versus 8.6% of remaining candidates (relative success, 2.94; 95% confidence interval, 2.51-3.45). This enrichment extended to 158 pairs involving 101 genes with no direct genetic support in the benchmark. At a matched selection size of 1,310 pairs, BRIDGE ranking captured 265 launched pairs, compared with 223 under a rule transferring support across neighbouring targets or indications. These findings show that coupling disease relationships with protein connectivity expands the reach of human genetics to additional therapeutic targets and indications while retaining clinical relevance.

items.title: Solanaceae-derived spirostane saponins inhibit dengue virus replication and remodel host-cell metabolism
items.abstract: Flaviviruses reprogram host-cell metabolism to support viral replication. In previous work, we showed that Solanaceae-derived spirostane saponins inhibit dengue virus replication and were predicted to interact with viral enzymes. Here, we investigated whether S01, a purified solid from Solanum ovalifolium containing predominantly two characterized spirostane saponins, also modulates host-cell metabolism in association with reduced permissiveness to dengue virus serotype 2 (DENV-2). We performed untargeted GC-QTOF-MS metabolomics in Vero cells under four conditions, including untreated control, S01 treatment, DENV-2 infection, and DENV-2 infection with S01 treatment. Quality-control samples clustered tightly, supporting analytical reproducibility. Principal component analysis revealed separation among experimental groups, and PERMANOVA confirmed significant global metabolic differences (F = 27.567, R{superscript 2} = 0.827, p = 0.001). S01 also retained strong antiviral activity, producing 99.9% inhibition under the metabolomics conditions. DENV-2 infection was associated with alterations metabolites related to amino acid, carbohydrate, lipid, and sphingolipid metabolism. Pathway analysis highlighted glutamate metabolism, arginine and proline metabolism, glycolysis-related pathways, fatty-acid oxidation and carnitine-associated metabolism, phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis, and sphingolipid metabolism. In uninfected cells, S01 induced a distinct metabolic profile (OPLS-DA R{superscript 2}Y = 0.951, Q{superscript 2} = 0.851; permutation p = 0.002), characterized by increased carbohydrate-related metabolites, including the unresolved Talose/D-glucose feature, gluconic acid, 2-keto-L-gulonic acid, and D-mannitol, together with decreased abundance of selected lipid-related metabolites. During infection, S01 induced a distinct metabolic (OPLS-DA R{superscript 2}Y = 0.928, Q{superscript 2} = 0.841), characterized by lower abundance of several fatty-acid-related and organic-acid metabolites and higher abundance of carbohydrate-related metabolites, while modifying selected DENV-2-associated metabolic alterations. These findings associate S01 antiviral activity with substantial remodeling of host-cell metabolism. Together with previous docking predictions of interactions with viral targets, the results support a model in which the antiviral activity of Solanaceae-derived spirostane saponins may involve complementary effects on viral and host-associated processes.

items.title: Precision of sensory representations in cortex is indexed by alpha power and pupil dilation, and tracks the dynamics of correlated noise
items.abstract: Sensory representations fluctuate in precision from moment to moment, shaping the fidelity of perception and memory. Population-coding theory proposes that these fluctuations are constrained by correlated variability within neural populations, yet linking these mechanisms to behaviour and brain state in humans has remained challenging. Here we combined EEG with an encoding-decoding framework to reconstruct orientation-selective population responses and quantify representational precision dynamically over time. Precision predicted subsequent working-memory performance and evolved in close correspondence with the dynamics of correlated variability between decoded orientation channels. Following stimulus onset, correlated variability was selectively suppressed among similarly tuned channels, the pattern predicted to maximise coding fidelity. Prestimulus alpha power and pupil size independently predicted representational precision, linking these dynamics to endogenous cortical and neuromodulatory state. Together, these findings identify candidate mechanisms and accessible physiological markers of representational precision in humans.

items.title: PROGMF: Progressive Multimodal Fusion and Representation Learning for Incomplete Neuroimaging Data
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Computer Science, Georgia State University, Atlanta, GA, United States
items.abstract: Multimodal neuroimaging studies often involve cohorts with partially overlapping data modalities. Many conventional multimodal fusion methods rely on participants with complete observations across the selected modalities. We introduce Progressive Multimodal Fusion (ProgMF), a novel fusion framework for learning multimodal source representations from incomplete neuroimaging data without imputing missing observations. ProgMF integrates modalities sequentially through independent vector analysis (IVA), cross-stage component alignment, and anchor-guided representation transfer, allowing information learned from earlier-stage cohorts to inform subsequent multimodal decompositions. We evaluated ProgMF on four neuroimaging-inspired synthetic modalities, while varying subject overlap, observation noise, modality relatedness, and fusion orders. ProgMF generally achieved lower source-recovery errors than complete-case IVA and the evaluated imputation-based methods, with larger improvements as multimodal subject overlap decreased. We further applied ProgMF to structural MRI gray matter, resting-state functional network connectivity, and 18F-florbetapir (AV45) amyloid positron emission tomography data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. ProgMF achieved higher mean cross-modal fusion scores than the imputation-based baselines and a modest improvement over complete-case IVA. Among the 293 participants with complete multimodal observations, two recovered source component vectors showed significant associations with clinical diagnosis across cognitively normal, mild cognitive impairment, and dementia groups. Both sources were also significantly associated with cognitive performance and dementia severity. The recovered sources exhibited diagnosis-related structural and amyloid PET patterns involving regions such as the hippocampi, precuneus, and cingulate cortices. Our findings support progressive representation transfer as an effective approach for recovering coherent, interpretable multimodal sources from participants with incomplete modality coverage.

items.title: Counterfactual aging in individual digital twin brains uncovers a latent dimension of resilience to aging
items.corresponding_institution: National Center of Neurology and Psychiatry
items.abstract: Cognitive reserve concerns why the same aging causes less decline in some individuals than others, a question that digital twin brains can address by aging each individual in silico. Here we present Brain-VRNN, a connectome-constrained variational recurrent neural network trained on longitudinal multitask functional MRI. Its regenerated brain signals reproduced four functional aging markers of unseen individuals (r = 0.93-0.96) and identified each person (accuracy 0.98). Without cognitive scores, its global latent learned a trait dimension stable within each person, which helped predict future cognition. Crucially, when every individual underwent the same counterfactual aging, those with a lower trait value declined more, yet recovered up to 1.6 times as much with a reduction in body mass index, a modifiable dementia risk factor. Aging single regions showed that different markers decline through different regions, with a lateral temporal-angular region shared by all. Brain-VRNN brings within-person simulation to cognitive reserve.

items.title: Aging remodels the neuronal activity-dependent transcriptome
items.corresponding_institution: Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis
items.abstract: Experience-driven neuronal activity induces coordinated transcriptional programs in neurons and glia that support plasticity and memory. How aging reshapes these activity-regulated gene (ARG) programs, and whether activity mitigates or exacerbates aging phenotypes, remain open questions with implications for cognitive decline. Here, we develop novel-environment and chemogenetic paradigms to characterize age-dependent remodeling of ARG transcriptomes in the mouse hippocampus at single-cell resolution. Aging contracts youthful ARG programs in both gene number and dynamic range, a contraction that persists under controlled chemogenetic stimulation independent of behavior. In parallel, novel experience in older mice reveals a latent transcriptional competence. First, distinct sets of genes respond to neuronal activity selectively in older cells. Second, enhancing activity in older animals partially reverses, or buffers, basal aging-associated changes across the transcriptome. Novel experience counteracts aging-associated changes in the target genes of the memory regulator CREB1 and the ER-stress sensor ATF6 across cell types. These data constitute a resource for neuronal activity-dependent transcription across the lifespan and identify a basis for the benefits of cognitive engagement: novel experience buffers age-related transcriptional drift.

items.title: Thrombin cleavage of circulating osteopontin in the lung drives hippocampal neuroinflammation and acute delirium-like neurologic dysfunction after acute kidney injury
items.corresponding_institution: Division of Nephrology, Department of Medicine, Washington University School of Medicine, St. Louis, MO, USA and VA Saint Louis Health Care System, John Cochran
items.abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common clinical problem with high morbidity and mortality due to frequently occurring secondary organ complications, including acute neurologic dysfunction, such as delirium. Specific mechanisms responsible for this kidney-brain crosstalk are unknown but hypothesized to include uremic toxins and neuroinflammation secondary to systemic inflammation. Here we show that uremic mice with AKI show hippocampal monocytic neuroinflammation associated with acute delirium-like neurologic dysfunction only in the presence of circulating osteopontin fragments. Mechanistically, circulating osteopontin (OPN/Spp1) released by the injured kidney was cleaved by thrombin in the lung into OPN-N and OPN-C-terminal fragments. Both OPN fragments were required to drive upregulation of the monocyte chemoattractant chemokine-ligand-2 (CCL2) in hippocampal endothelial cells. AKI mice lacking OPN or unable to activate OPN by thrombin cleavage showed kidney injury and serum uremic toxin elevations like wt controls but were protected from hippocampal CCL2 upregulation, monocyte recruitment, and delirium-like symptoms. Systemic application of an OPN or CCL2 neutralizing antibody was protective. Our results suggest that a specific kidney-released circulating factor, osteopontin, drives acute neurologic dysfunction after AKI and challenge the widely held hypothesis that uremic toxins play a dominant role. They also identify thrombin cleavage of OPN as a potential therapeutic target and critical switch for the remote functions of circulating OPN.

items.title: Molecular analysis of 55 dopamine transporter variants from psychiatric patients reveals convergent mechanisms of dysfunction
items.abstract: Rare genetic variants are increasingly recognized as contributors to neuropsychiatric disease and may reveal underlying pathobiological mechanisms. The dopamine transporter (DAT), encoded by SLC6A3, regulates dopaminergic neurotransmission through rapid dopamine (DA) reuptake. Although disease-associated DAT variants have been linked to disorders ranging from infantile parkinsonism to neuropsychiatric disease, the molecular basis of DAT dysfunction remains poorly understood. Here, we systematically investigated 55 DAT missense variants identified in the iPSYCH2012-nested case-control cohort. By assessing transport activity, inhibitor binding, cell-surface expression, subcellular localization, amphetamine responsiveness and constitutive DA efflux, we resolved the variants into seven phenotypic classes. These reflected distinct molecular defects, including impaired substrate and ion coupling, destabilized intramolecular interactions, and defective folding, trafficking or surface expression. Molecular dynamics simulations provided structural insight into representative variants. Collectively, our findings reveal mechanistic convergence of genetically diverse DAT variants and establish a framework for interpreting the pathogenicity of newly identified SLC6A3 variants.

items.title: Cask dysfunction in inhibitory neurons reveals distinct synaptic and epileptic phenotypes in mouse models of CASK-related disorder
items.abstract: Epilepsy is a major neurological manifestation of genetic neurodevelopmental disorders, yet how genetic disruptions produce distinct seizure phenotypes remains poorly understood. CASK-related disorder is an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder frequently accompanied by epilepsy. It is caused by pathogenic variants in CASK, which encodes calcium/calmodulin-dependent serine protein kinase, a protein with diverse molecular functions. Here, we establish sex-specific mouse models of CASK-related disorder and identify epileptic phenotypes in both sexes. Cell type-specific Cask deletion identifies inhibitory neurons as a critical cellular locus of distinct forms of epileptic activity. Cask deficiency in parvalbumin- or somatostatin-expressing inhibitory neurons primarily causes spike-wave discharges or motor seizures, accompanied by reduced spontaneous or evoked inhibitory synaptic transmission, respectively. Thus, Cask dysfunction in different inhibitory synapses and circuits produces distinct seizure phenotypes. These findings reveal how cell type-specific synaptic dysfunction shapes epilepsy in CASK-related disorder and may provide insights into diverse neurological phenotypes of neurodevelopmental disorders.

items.title: Modern speech recognition systems exhibit human-like word recognition but superhuman use of statistical dependencies between words
items.abstract: Advances in machine learning have yielded machine systems that approach human performance on real-world perception tasks. For speech recognition, it remains unclear whether such models' behavior resembles that of humans. We addressed this question by measuring word recognition abilities in humans and models across 272 speech distortions, providing a detailed behavioral fingerprint. Three recent industry speech recognition models trained on hundreds of years of speech outperformed humans. However, in conditions where linguistic context was removed, they matched human performance well, suggesting that the models are superhuman in their ability to leverage statistical dependencies between words. Experiments manipulating model training data suggest that training data variability and realism contribute to the match to human perception. Overall, the results show that superhuman performance is now possible with systems that are optimized over enough data and suggest that accurate models of human speech recognition require optimization over appropriate tasks and amounts of speech.

items.title: The assembly and annotation of a new reference genome for the eastern mosquitofish (Gambusia holbrooki) reveal a new sex chromosome system in its invasive range
items.corresponding_institution: MARBEC, Univ Montpellier, CNRS, IFREMER, Montpellier, IRD, France
items.abstract: Gambusia species, especially eastern mosquitofish - Gambusia holbrooki - are of broad relevance to evolutionary biologists aiming at understanding genomic bases of adaptation during biological invasions and rapid response to selection to heterogeneous environments including pollution. Here we used HiFi and HiC to assemble a new, high quality, chromosome scale, genome sequence for G. holbrooki in its invasive range. Both haplotypes of the nuclear genome were assembled, comprising 657.64 Mb and 651.75 Mb respectively, in 24 chromosomes and had N50s of 28.97 Mb and 28.25 Mb. They had 94.87% and 94.29% BUSCO scores, illustrating a high completeness. Genome annotation yielded 25146 genes, which is comparable to other recent genome annotations of poecilid fish species. Repeat content was 25.69%, similar to what was previously reported for this species and for G. affinis. Synteny was highly conserved between the G. holbrooki assembly and the reference genome for G. affinis and Xiphophorus maculatus, shown here to be a genetically close species, with very few inter-chromosomal and little intra-chromosomal rearrangements. Mapping of resequenced males and females to the reference genome provided genomic evidence for a newly evolved homomorphic sex chromosome pair (W and Z, hence with female heterogamety) in G. holbrooki's invaded range, which is unlike the XY system of its native range. Also, the new sex chromosomes are homologous to the ZW sex chromosome pair (chromosome 1) of the sister species G. affinis. This assembly provides a high quality reference genome for Gambusia holbrooki, in its invasive range in Europe, that is serving as a key resource for research on the genomics of invasion and of rapid adaptation to environmental change, pollution adaptation and sex determination evolution.

items.title: Transposase-mediated activity is associated with accessory gene turnover and positive-selection signals in Streptococcus pyogenes
items.abstract: Streptococcus pyogenes causes diseases ranging from mild pharyngitis to life-threatening invasive infection, yet the genomic determinants of this variation remain poorly understood. We analyzed 1,863 publicly available genomes, whose pangenome comprises 6,568 genes (1,392 core and soft-core, 656 shell, and 4,520 cloud), and grouped isolates into 15 genetic groups with FastBAPS. Ten groups were monophyletic on the global phylogeny, and non-monophyly of the remaining five largely reflected the placement of isolates from group 12, which is dispersed across the tree. A GenomegaMap scan identified 163 of 3,147 genes with {omega} > 1. These genes were depleted among core genes and enriched among cloud genes, a pattern consistent with positive selection on recently acquired genes but also with the retention of slightly deleterious variation in young genes. A putative IS transposase (K07497) was the most consistent functional enrichment signal, which led us to analyze insertion sequence (IS) elements directly. In group 12, complete IS copies within genomes were more often near-identical than in other groups (OR = 1.46), consistent with more recent IS activity, and genes with {omega} > 1 were 2.9 times more likely than other accessory genes to lie within 5 kb of an IS element (8.8% vs. 3.0%; permutation p = 0.0006) after excluding IS-encoded genes. We did not detect this association in any other group, and most genes under selection were not IS-proximal.

items.title: A compartmentalised cochlear ageing programme: weak systemic concordance and a distinct macrophage compartment
items.abstract: Whether the ageing cochlea follows the systemic ageing programmes defined by multi-organ atlases is unknown. We integrated single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data for 13,988 mouse cochlear nuclei (3, 12 and 24 months) with the Tabula Muris Senis atlas (16 droplet-based and 12 Smart-seq2 fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS) sources). Cross-organ alignment of ageing programmes was quantified by genome-wide vector correlation, pre-ranked gene-set enrichment and a systemic ageing score. Cochlear ageing showed weak but significant genome-wide concordance with systemic ageing (Spearman rho 0.01-0.12), with lineage-matched pairs ranking among the highest. In contrast, systemic tissue ageing-up signatures, dominated by immune and inflammatory programmes, were depleted from the ageing-up rankings of cochlear non-sensory epithelial cells (normalised enrichment score -1.45, adjusted p = 0.032) and, for the immune-organ signatures, from cochlear macrophages. The cochlear macrophage ageing vector correlated positively with tissue-resident macrophages of peripheral organs (kidney rho = 0.056, 95% confidence interval 0.016-0.063, p = 1.6 x 10^-13; microglia rho = 0.034, p = 1.4 x 10^-6), negatively with bone-marrow and splenic macrophages, and not with lymphocytes. A systemic ageing score increased with age in spiral ganglion neurons, Schwann cells, inner hair cells, epithelial cells, and fibrocytes, but not in cochlear macrophages. These cell-type-resolved analyses support a compartmentalised view of cochlear ageing: non-immune compartments track systemic ageing weakly, the immune arm is reversed, and cochlear macrophages age along a tissue-resident rather than haematopoietic programme.

items.title: The global geometry of optimal neural representations
items.abstract: Efficient coding hypothesizes that neural activity optimally represents information under resource constraints. The global structures of such optimal population codes are difficult to study theoretically, and previous works have usually resorted to either focusing on local properties like fine discrimination or placing restrictions on the parametric forms of neural tuning. We address the general problem by analytically deriving the neural representation that minimizes the all-pairs average classification error of a one-dimensional circular variable under various forms of neural response noise. Our method is based on formulating the space of neural response distributions as a statistical manifold whose geometry can be simplified through a generalized version of variance-stabilizing transformations. The theory fully characterizes the complete family of optimal population codes and allows us to make two novel predictions. First, an optimal code should allow the existence of oppositely peaked bimodal tuning curves. Second, there should be a correlation between spike count variability and tuning sharpness. We validate both of these predictions in the mouse head direction system.

items.title: Region-Specific Changes in the Aging Enteric Nervous System
items.abstract: As human life expectancy increases, understanding the physiological changes that accompany aging becomes increasingly important. Gastrointestinal (GI) dysfunction is common with age, and age-related changes in the enteric nervous system (ENS), which regulates GI motility, may contribute to this decline in function. Studies of the aging ENS have reported contradicting results, potentially reflecting the substantial regional heterogeneity of the ENS and the fact that most studies focus on only one or two areas of the GI tract. Neurons in the myenteric plexus, which regulate intestinal contractions and motility, are organized into ganglia that form circumferential stripes along the length of the gut. Here, we systematically compare neuronal and glial density and organization across all five regions of the small and large intestine in young (3-4 month-old) and aged (22-26 month-old) mice. We find that neuronal density remains unchanged with age across all regions, despite localized changes in ganglia organization. Although the overall stripe-like arrangement is preserved, ganglia are less aligned with stripes in the duodenum and ileum, while those in the ileum and distal colon are smaller, contain fewer neurons, and have a greater proportion of neurons located outside the ganglia. Glial cell numbers vary regionally with age, increasing in the duodenum and distal colon but decreasing in the proximal colon. The proportion of Calretinin+ neurons, meanwhile, remains stable across the small intestine. Together, these findings reveal that aging is associated with selective, region-specific remodeling of myenteric plexus cytoarchitecture rather than uniform structural decline across the GI tract. This comprehensive regional analysis may help reconcile conflicting reports of age-related changes in the ENS.

items.title: LANCE-seq: Live-tissue Analysis via Needle-encoded Capture Extraction for Spatial Transcriptomics
items.corresponding_institution: State Key Laboratory of Digital Medical Engineering, School of Biological Science & Medical Engineering, Southeast University, Nanjing 210096, China
items.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics enables the resolution of spatial heterogeneity in gene expression within tissues, yet most existing sequencing-based methods rely on ex vivo tissue processing, making it difficult to track dynamic molecular changes in the same living individual. We developed LANCE-seq (Live-tissue Analysis via Needle-encoded Capture Extraction sequencing), a live-tissue spatial transcriptomics platform based on encoded microneedle arrays that enables high-density spatial RNA capture through poly(amidoamine) (PAMAM) dendrimer-functionalized interfaces and microfluidic orthogonal combinatorial encoding. In frozen mouse brain tissue, LANCE-seq detected an average of 6,399 genes per spatial spot and reconstructed the spatial distribution of major brain regions and representative marker genes. Furthermore, in the acetaminophen (APAP)-induced acute liver injury model, LANCE-seq enabled repeated sampling from the same living animal at different time points. At 6 h after APAP treatment, injury-related genes such as Hmox1, Ddit3, Atf3, and Fgf21 were significantly elevated, and transcriptional programs associated with stress, inflammation, and cellular injury were broadly enhanced. Meanwhile, liver zonation-related transcriptional signatures were remodeled, with different relative zonation states all exhibiting activation of injury programs. By integrating high-throughput spatial encoding with minimally invasive in vivo sampling, LANCE-seq provides a platform for longitudinal spatial transcriptomic studies of drug responses and disease progression.

items.title: Native architecture of a mitochondrial oxphosome
items.corresponding_institution: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Spitalstrasse 41, CH-4056 Basel, Switzerland
items.abstract: Mitochondrial cristae are the primary bioenergetic units of eukaryotic cells, yet the molecular principles that dictate their morphologies remain largely unknown. Using in situ cryo-electron tomography and integrative modeling, we resolve the native organization of the respiratory machinery in the diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum. Unlike previously studied animals and green algae, diatoms possess tubular crista, a conserved membrane architecture found in diverse and globally relevant species. We identify several native supercomplexes assemblies, including an oxphosome comprising the entire respiratory chain. Our results, together with molecular dynamics analyses, reveal that these supercomplexes assemble through a lipid-mediated mechanism. We propose that tubular cristae are shaped by the interplay between membrane-bending ATP synthase oligomers that bud the hemispherical crista tips and supercomplexes that act as molecular roadblocks to constrain ATP synthase propagation, thereby balancing membrane curvature and allowing cristae body extension. Furthermore, we show that the diatom Complex I retains ancestral subunits related to fatty acid synthase. Beyond illuminating diatom bioenergetics, our findings reveal a fundamental principle of mitochondrial morphogenesis where ATP synthase-driven membrane curvature is spatially fine-tuned by respiratory supercomplexes.

items.title: Metabolic transitions reprogram translation through sequence-dependent regulation
items.abstract: Cells suppress protein synthesis during starvation, but how translation recovers upon nutrient repletion remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we followed translational recovery in budding yeast after repletion of glucose, nitrogen, or phosphate, combining time-resolved metabolomics, structural proteomics, transcriptomics, and spike-in-calibrated ribosome profiling. Nutrient addition rapidly altered ribosome occupancy in distinct, transcript-specific programs. To identify their sequence determinants, we developed RiboNet, a deep learning framework that predicts ribosome load and positions along transcripts from mRNA sequence. RiboNet-guided in silico mutagenesis revealed reduced pausing at serine codons upon glucose repletion and transiently increased pausing at leucine codons following nitrogen repletion. These responses coincided with altered cognate tRNA charging and metabolite-associated structural changes in aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases. RiboNet also identified a conserved 5' UTR motif, GAUY, that increased reporter protein output following glucose repletion. Our findings reveal how metabolic state alters the contributions of mRNA sequence features to translation initiation and elongation.

items.title: A near-infrared fluorescent genetically encoded calcium ion biosensor with a direct response
items.abstract: Near-infrared genetically encoded calcium ion (Ca2+) indicators (NIR GECIs) enable Ca2+ imaging at longer wavelengths than green or red fluorescent GECIs, providing reduced autofluorescence and phototoxicity, and improved compatibility with deep-tissue and multiplexed imaging applications. We have previously reported biliverdin (BV)-binding phytochrome-based NIR GECIs such as NIR-GECO2G that exhibit inverse fluorescence responses. Although inverse response GECIs can effectively report Ca2+ dynamics, their high baseline fluorescence in the resting apo state causes faster photobleaching and substantial out-of-focus background fluorescence, complicating signal interpretation. Here, using the inverse response NIR-GECO2G as the starting scaffold, we developed a direct response Ca2+ indicator, designated dNIR-GECO1.0, through iterative rounds of protein engineering and screening. dNIR-GECO1.0 exhibited greater molecular brightness than NIR-GECO2G, robust fluorescence in mammalian cells without exogenous BV supplementation, and a high dynamic range for reporting Ca2+ changes. A detailed mechanistic investigation identified the key mutations within the Ca2+ binding domain that were necessary to convert the inverse response indicator into a direct response indicator. Resonance Raman spectroscopic analysis provided insight into the specific changes in the BV chromophore resulting from the Ca2+-dependent conformational change.

items.title: The Caenorhabditis elegans pangenome elucidates hyper-divergent region gene content to reveal extensive gene copy-number variation and a novel anthelmintic resistance locus
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Biology, Johns Hopkins University, Baltimore, MD, 21218, USA.
items.abstract: Caenorhabditis elegans has been a keystone model in biological research since the early 1970s, and it was the first metazoan to have its genome sequenced and assembled in 1998. Over the last few decades, the genetic and genomic resources developed for C. elegans made it one of the most powerful models for understanding metazoan biology. Recently, the C. elegans community has collected over 2,000 globally distributed wild strains, which after whole-genome sequencing, were found to contain punctuated regions of extreme genetic variation, called hyper-divergent regions (HDRs). HDRs have been described in organisms across the tree of life, including plants and humans, and genes in HDRs appear to be involved in adaptation, such as environmental response genes, parasitism genes, or immunity genes. However, the extreme genetic divergence at these loci complicates short-read alignments, and the genomic content of these regions in non-reference strains is largely uncharacterized. To define the gene content in HDRs, we de novo assembled and annotated genomes of 140 genetically diverse strains. These data enabled the construction of the first gene-based pangenome for the species. Among these strains, we characterized the landscape of structural variation and developed novel methods to quantify gene content diversity. We found that both variable copy-number and stable-copy environmental response genes were enriched in HDRs. These results further suggest that these regions have an important evolutionary role in adaptation to heterogeneous environments. We leveraged this pangenome to elucidate gene content in previously identified quantitative trait loci associated with adaptive traits. In one HDR, we found large deletions, spanning multiple genes, that are correlated with resistance to the anthelmintic drug abamectin. The C. elegans pangenome provides novel insights into genome and gene family evolution in a genetically diverse animal species, and empowers deeper investigations of genotype-phenotype relationships underlying adaptive traits, particularly in the context of structural and gene copy-number variation.

items.title: Rac1-Abi-1 Signaling Links DNA Repair to Tumorigenesis
items.abstract: The DNA damage response governs genomic integrity, and abnormal DNA repair can drive tumorigenesis. We previously identified a Rac1-Abi-1 signaling pathway in which Rac1 activates protein phosphatase 5, leading to Abi-1-S323 dephosphorylation and enhanced non-homologous end joining (NHEJ). Given the error-prone nature of NHEJ and its potential to promote genomic instability, we sought to determine whether Rac1-Abi-1-mediated regulation of NHEJ contributes to tumorigenesis. Here, we demonstrate the tumorigenic role of Abi-1-S323 dephosphorylation in nonmalignant cell models and multiple tumorigenesis models established using a newly generated genetically engineered Abi-1 mouse model. We first found that the dephospho-mimetic Abi-1-S323A mutant promoted transformation-associated phenotypes in nonmalignant human cells and enhanced orthotopic glioblastoma growth under unperturbed conditions. To further investigate its tumorigenic potential in vivo, we generated CRISPR/Cas9-mediated Abi-1-S296A knock-in mice, in which S296 corresponds to human S323. Abi-1-S296A mouse embryonic fibroblasts exhibited increased proliferation, while mutant mice developed spontaneous tumors involving lymphoid tissues and organs under unperturbed conditions. Furthermore, Abi-1-S296A increased susceptibility to tumorigenesis following DNA damage. In a low-dose whole-body irradiation model, Abi-1-S296A mice showed a trend toward shortened survival and increased tumor development, with lesions including Harderian gland papillary cystadenomas, round-cell neoplasms, and anaplastic sarcomas. In addition, in an azoxymethane/dextran sulfate sodium (AOM/DSS)-induced colorectal tumor model, Abi-1-S296A mice developed significantly more tumors and had a greater tumor burden. These findings identify Abi-1-S323 dephosphorylation as a previously unrecognized regulator of tumorigenesis and establish a new mouse model for investigating the physiological and pathological consequences of constitutive activation of upstream NHEJ-regulatory signaling.

items.title: Prospective multi-omic profiling identifies predictive and genetically supported molecular determinants of incident epilepsy
items.corresponding_institution: Luxembourg Centre for Systems Biomedicine, University of Luxembourg, Esch-Sur-Alzette, Luxembourg
items.abstract: Abstract Epilepsy affects approximately 50 million people worldwide, yet biomarkers capable of identifying individuals at risk before clinical onset are lacking, and the molecular mechanisms preceding disease onset remain poorly understood. Here, we integrated plasma proteomic, metabolomic, and genomic data from the UK Biobank to characterize molecular changes preceding epilepsy and evaluate their predictive and causal relevance. We quantified 2,923 plasma proteins in 53,000 participants and followed incident epilepsy for up to 15 years before epilepsy diagnosis. Cox proportional hazards analyses identified 116 proteins associated with incident epilepsy, led by neurofilament light chain (NEFL; HR=2.03) and growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15; HR=1.73). These proteins were enriched for extracellular signaling, immune regulation, and cell-death pathways and displayed distinct subtype- and age-specific signatures. A proteomic risk score comprising 32 proteins stratified epilepsy risk, with individuals in the highest quintile exhibiting a 3.5-fold greater risk than those in the lowest quintile (AUC=0.70). In parallel, 154 of 249 circulating metabolites were associated with incident epilepsy, with the strongest inverse association observed for citrate (HR=0.72) and positive associations across HDL-related metabolites (HR=1.16-1.21), implicating dysregulated energy and lipoprotein metabolism. A metabolomic risk score showed more modest discrimination (AUC=0.63). Integrating proteomic, metabolomic, polygenic, and demographic information yielded an overall AUC of 0.71 for incident epilepsy; in a separate cross-sectional analysis of individuals with early-onset epilepsy discrimination reached an AUC of 0.79. Proteome-wide cis-pQTL Mendelian randomization identified 12 proteins associated with epilepsy after false discovery rate correction, predominantly for genetic generalized epilepsy. O-GlcNAcase (OGA), a regulator of protein O-GlcNAcylation with established roles in neuronal function and synaptic plasticity, showed the strongest protective association (OR=0.71, FDR=2.7 e-8). Serine protease 53 (PRSS53), a poorly characterized serine protease, showed strong evidence for a potential shared causal variant with epilepsy (colocalization PP.H4=0.95). Together, these findings demonstrate that circulating molecular alterations precede epilepsy diagnosis by years and reveal complementary proteomic, metabolic, and genetic determinants of disease susceptibility, providing a framework for biologically informed risk stratification and therapeutic target prioritization.

items.title: Traumatic microbleeds are associated with unfavorable outcome out to 1 year after mild traumatic brain injury
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Neurological Surgery, University of California, San Francisco, CA
items.abstract: Importance: Traumatic microbleeds (TMB) are commonly observed in mild TBI (mTBI). However, questions remain regarding their long-term prognostic significance. Objective: Determine whether traumatic microbleeds predict unfavorable outcome after mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) Design: The prospective longitudinal observational Transforming Research and Clinical Knowledge in Traumatic Brain Injury (TRACK-TBI) study enrolled acute TBI patients presenting to Emergency Departments (ED) at 18 U.S. Level 1 trauma centers between 2/26/2014-08/08/2018. CT and MRI were evaluated using the National Institutes of Health National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke (NIH NINDS) TBI Common Data Elements. Outcome was assessed using the Glasgow Outcome Scale Extended (GOSE-TBI) at 2 weeks and 3, 6, and 12 months post-injury. Setting: 18 U.S. Level 1 trauma centers Participants: 929 GCS 13-15 patients at least 17 years of age (38.5 +/- 16.5 years, 66% male) who underwent clinical head CT =5) at 2 weeks and 3, 6, and 12 months Results: Generalized estimating equation models showed that TMBs and/or IVH were strongly associated with unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI =5) at 3, 6, and 12 months post-injury, but not with incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI =5 TMBs surpassed the importance of all demographic and baseline clinical predictors throughout the 1-year follow-up period. For prediction of incomplete recovery (GOSE-TBI <8 vs. =8), brain contusions, subarachnoid hemorrhage, and subdural hematoma were more important throughout the 12-month follow-up period. Conclusions and Relevance: Traumatic microbleeds (TMB) are common in mTBI. The presence of 4 or more TMBs and/or IVH is strongly associated with unfavorable outcome (GOSE-TBI <5) after mTBI out to at least 1 year, even after controlling for other neuroimaging abnormalities and demographic and clinical predictors. Better understanding of the implications of TMBs for long-term functional outcome may inform rehabilitation planning.

items.title: Central motor cortical repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation at 5 Hz or 10 Hz combined with cerebellar 1 Hz stimulation for ataxia in multiple system atrophy of the cerebellar type: a retrospective cohort study of efficacy and predictors of response
items.corresponding_institution: Sanbo Brain Hospital, Capital Medical University
items.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the efficacy of central motor cortical repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) at different frequencies (5 Hz and 10 Hz) combined with cerebellar 1 Hz stimulation on the core domains of ataxia in patients with multiple system atrophy of the cerebellar type (MSA-C), and to explore the independent predictors of the response. Methods: In this retrospective study, 48 patients with a confirmed diagnosis of MSA-C were included. All patients received bilateral cerebellar hemispheric 1 Hz rTMS as background therapy and were divided according to the frequency of central cortical stimulation into a control group (cerebellar 1 Hz stimulation only, n=15), a 5 Hz combination group (n=16) and a 10 Hz combination group (n=17). Ataxia severity before and after treatment was assessed with the International Cooperative Ataxia Rating Scale (ICARS); absolute improvements and improvement rates were calculated for each subscore and for the total score. Continuous variables were described as mean +/- standard deviation (SD) or median (interquartile range) according to normality; within-group pre-post comparisons used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test, and between-group comparisons used one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) or the Kruskal-Wallis H test with Bonferroni correction. Clinical response was defined by an absolute improvement threshold (delta-ICARS total score >= 8 points), and independent influencing factors were analysed by Firth-penalised logistic regression; sensitivity analyses were performed with a total-score improvement rate >= 20% (and with >= 15% and >= 30% as alternative thresholds), and robustness results are reported for the delta-ICARS >= 10-point criterion. Missing cognitive and mood scale scores were imputed by multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE; m=5; the mean of the five imputations constituted the analysis dataset) and then included in the analysis. Subgroup and interaction analyses were performed according to the median disease duration (2 years) and median age (57 years). Results: After treatment, the ICARS total score in the overall cohort was significantly lower than at baseline (median difference 7.0 points, P = 20% was used to define clinically significant efficacy, the response rates of the three groups were 6.7%, 50.0% and 58.8% (P=0.006), and both the 10 Hz and 5 Hz groups were significantly better than the control group (Bonferroni-corrected P=0.006 and P=0.040), with no statistically significant difference between the two frequencies. Domain-specific comparison showed statistically significant between-group differences in both the absolute improvement and the improvement rate of limb kinetic function (P=0.013 and P=0.005), with the 10 Hz group significantly better than the control group. When clinical response was defined as delta-ICARS >= 8 points, the response rates of the three groups were 20.0%, 56.2% and 64.7% (P=0.029); Firth-penalised multivariable regression showed that baseline ICARS total score was an independent predictor of clinical response (OR=1.076, 95% CI 1.013-1.143, P=0.017), whereas 5 Hz (OR=4.298, 95% CI 0.757-24.412, P=0.100) and 10 Hz (OR=5.847, 95% CI 0.885-38.640, P=0.067) stimulation did not reach independent statistical significance after adjustment. When response was defined as delta-ICARS >= 10 points, the response rates were 0%, 43.8% and 47.1% (P=0.007), and there were no responders in the control group. Subgroup analysis showed a significant group-by-age interaction (P=0.020); the clinical response rate of patients aged >= 57 years receiving 10 Hz stimulation was 85.7% (exploratory finding; small subgroup sample). The group-by-duration interaction was not statistically significant (P=0.210). Conclusions: Central 5 Hz and 10 Hz rTMS combined with cerebellar 1 Hz stimulation both significantly improved the symptoms of ataxia in patients with MSA-C, and the efficacy was domain-specific, with the greatest improvement in the limb kinetic domain; sensitivity analyses across multiple criteria (delta-ICARS >= 8 points, improvement rate >= 20%, delta-ICARS >= 10 points) consistently supported the efficacy benefit of high-frequency stimulation in the same direction, but stimulation frequency did not reach independent predictive statistical significance after adjustment, and baseline ICARS total score was significantly associated with absolute improvement. Age may have a modifying effect on the efficacy of stimulation frequency (exploratory finding; small sample). This study provides preliminary support for the efficacy of the central 10 Hz combined with cerebellar 1 Hz regimen; the optimal stimulation parameters and independent predictors remain to be verified in larger prospective studies.

items.title: Adverse Events and Baseline Psychological Distress Among Dementia Family Care Partners in the Tele-STELLA Study
items.abstract: Background: Adverse event (AE) narratives may reveal physical and psychological challenges experienced by family care partners of people living with Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. Objective: To characterize care partner AEs during the national Tele-STELLA study and explore differences in baseline psychological characteristics by AE category and subcategory. Methods: This descriptive, exploratory analysis included 43 AEs reported by 36 care partners. Narratives were classified as Physical, Psychological, or Random/Other. Baseline depressive symptoms, grief, and behavioral reactivity were compared between care partners with and without each AE type within this sample. Results: Physcial events accounted for 48.8% of AEs, Psychological events for 39.5%, and Random/Other events for 11.6%. Infections predominated among Physical events; stress/distress accounted for half of the Psychological events. Psychological AEs were associated with higher baseline grief and behavioral reactivity. Stress/distress-related AEs were associated with higher depressive symptoms and reactivity, whereas aggression-related Aes were associated with greater grief.
