Conclusions: Care partner AE narratives captured heterogeneous physical and psychological experiences. Classification may complement conventional assessments of care partner health and distress. These exploratory findings do not establish causality or predictive validity and warrant prospective study.

items.title: Evaluating the Clinical Utility of a Brief Remote Speech Assessment for Screening and Triage of Speech Disorders
items.abstract: Purpose: Speech abnormalities can often be early or clinically important manifestations of neurologic disease, yet access to clinicians with specialized expertise required for comprehensive motor speech evaluation may limit timely assessment. Brief remote speech assessment could provide a scalable approach for identifying patients who warrant more comprehensive evaluation, but its utility across heterogeneous speech presentations remains unclear. This study evaluated the validity and clinical utility of the Mayo Speech Test (MST), a brief (~5-minute) audio-recorded remote speech assessment, relative to a comprehensive in-person motor speech examination (~1-hour). Specifically, we examined whether MST could support clinically meaningful screening and triage decisions by distinguishing normal from abnormal speech and identifying the presence of a speech disorder. Method: One hundred participants completed a comprehensive in-person speech evaluation and a remote MST. Participants were excluded when the interval between assessments exceeded 90 days (n = 13) or either rater judged audio quality insufficient for diagnostic interpretation (n = 6), with overlapping exclusions resulting in a final analytic sample of 82 participants. Remote recordings were independently evaluated by two speech-language pathologists (SLPs) who were blinded to participant identity. In-person evaluation classifications served as the clinical reference standard and were grouped as normal (n = 33), dysphonia only (n = 5), or speech disorder (n = 43). One participant could not be classified. Performance was evaluated for two clinically motivated binary decisions: distinguishing normal from abnormal (such as dysphonia or speech disorder; Tier 0) and identifying normal speech or dysphonia only versus speech disorder (Tier 1). Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values, agreement, and error patterns were examined. Results: Both remote raters demonstrated similar overall performance despite differing error profiles. For Tier 0 screening, Rater 1 demonstrated 93.6% sensitivity and 71.9% specificity for identifying abnormal voice/speech, whereas Rater 2 demonstrated 78.7% sensitivity and 93.9% specificity. For Tier 1 identification of speech disorder, sensitivity and specificity were 83.3% and 86.5%, respectively, for Rater 1 and 71.4% and 97.4% for Rater 2. Interrater agreement was 79.7% for Tier 0 ({kappa} = 0.60) and 86.1% for Tier 1 ({kappa} = 0.72). Missed speech disorders represented an important source of error, with differences between raters indicating distinct thresholds for assigning abnormality and speech-disorder classifications. Conclusions: A brief remote speech assessment showed promising performance for broad clinical classification, particularly when used to address screening and triage questions rather than reproduce the diagnostic granularity of a comprehensive examination. Similar overall performance across raters masked meaningful sensitivity-specificity tradeoffs, highlighting the importance of examining error profiles in addition to aggregate accuracy. MST may therefore have clinical utility for identifying patients who warrant comprehensive motor speech evaluation, but should not be considered a substitute for a full diagnostic assessment.

items.title: Transparent Implementation and Benchmarking of ACMG/AMP Variant Classification in fastVEP
items.corresponding_institution: Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai
items.abstract: Background: The ACMG/AMP framework is the standard for germline sequence variant interpretation, but applying it in scalable automated software requires operational choices that the original framework and later ClinGen guidance do not always specify. We implemented an ACMG/AMP classification engine within fastVEP and evaluated which implementation choices improved agreement with expert-curated classifications without increasing concerning opposite-direction calls. Methods: The classifier implements all 28 ACMG/AMP criteria and can evaluate 15 from a sites-only VCF using nine public evidence sources. For selecting the optimal classifier, we compared symmetric and hybrid evidence-combining schemes, pathogenic class cutoffs, population-frequency thresholds, and benign-evidence thresholds against 673,660 ClinVar variants with review status of two stars or higher from April 2026. Clinical geneticists reviewed opposite-direction calls. We then applied the selected final classifier unchanged to 116,078 variants that newly reached the two-star threshold in the October 2026 ClinVar release. Results: The final fastVEP ACMG/AMP classifier uses the Tavtigian point scale on the pathogenic side and the 2015 ACMG/AMP combining table on the benign side. Using the 2015 table on both sides reduced pathogenic-side recall from 62.5 to 57.1 percent and lost 4,900 same-direction calls while avoiding 10 opposite-direction pathogenic calls. Using points on both sides increased benign-side recall from 66.4 to 77.0 percent, but increased opposite-direction benign calls from 27 to 399 and reduced recall of ClinVar uncertain variants from 97.1 to 69.5 percent. The 6-point Likely pathogenic cutoff was retained because lowering it to 5 points increased pathogenic-side recall to 73.9 percent but also classified 6,003 additional ClinVar uncertain variants and 17 additional ClinVar benign-side variants as pathogenic-side. The final classifier reproduced ClinVar's exact five-tier class for 431,727 variants or 64.1 percent and its pathogenic, benign, or uncertain direction for 534,335 variants or 79.3 percent. Only 51 calls or 0.0076 percent were opposite in direction to ClinVar. On the later variants, same-direction agreement was 72.6 percent and 20 calls were opposite in direction. Conclusions: The rules used to combine evidence affected classification more than several individual numeric thresholds. The hybrid scheme increased pathogenic-side recall while preventing a single Supporting benign criterion from producing a directional call. This conservative operating profile is suited to large-scale variant triage because it makes high-confidence calls while leaving variants uncertain when the available evidence does not support expert-level resolution. fastVEP is a research and decision-support tool and does not replace case-specific expert review.

items.title: Modifiable and Context-Specific Factors Associated with Dementia in the Democratic Republic of the Congo: A Community-Derived Cross-Sectional Study
items.corresponding_institution: Emory University School of Medicine, Department of Rehabilitation Medicine, Atlanta, GA 30322, USA; University of Kinshasa and Catholic University of Congo, Sch
items.abstract: Background: Evidence linking social, behavioral, and environmental factors to dementia in Central Africa remains limited. Objective: To examine associations between 16 factors and dementia status in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), and quantify incremental model fit beyond age and sex. Methods: This cross sectional analysis included 721 participants (232 cognitively unimpaired; 489 with dementia, including 247 with suspected Alzheimers disease). Logistic regression jointly modeled 16 factors, age, sex, and missing-category indicators. Continuous covariates with missing values were mean-imputed and standardized. Model fit was assessed using Nagelkerke pseudo R squared, likelihood-ratio testing, and 1,000 bootstrap replicates. Results: Nagelkerke pseudo-R2 increased from 0.106 with age and sex to 0.368 after adding the factors (change in R2 = 0.262; bootstrap 95% CI: 0.241-0.371; chi-square(27) = 163.62, p < 0.001). Poverty (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] = 2.34, 95% CI: 1.52-3.60), low resilience (aOR = 1.84, 95% CI: 1.18-2.86), and depression (aOR = 1.53, 95% CI: 1.02-2.31) were associated with higher dementia odds. Higher education (aOR = 0.51, 95% CI: 0.39-0.66, per standard deviation increase) and obesity (aOR = 0.31, 95% CI: 0.10-0.90) showed inverse associations; obesity data were 79.9% missing. Alcohol consumption and PM2.5 exposure were not significantly associated with dementia. Conclusions: Poverty, lower resilience, depression, and education were associated with dementia status in this nonrepresentative cohort. Incremental model fit does not quantify preventable dementia burden, and causality cannot be inferred from these cross-sectional data.

items.title: α-synuclein seed amplification assay positivity is associated with motor progression in the prodromal stage independent of phenoconversion
items.corresponding_institution: National Neuroscience Institute, Department of Research and Innovation, Singapore.
items.abstract: Abstract Background: -Synuclein seed amplification assay (Syn-SAA) has emerged as a promising biomarker for detecting underlying -synuclein pathology and predicting phenoconversion in prodromal Parkinson's disease (PD). However, its association with longitudinal clinical progression during the prodromal stage remains unclear. We investigated whether baseline Syn-SAA status and kinetic parameters were associated with motor and cognitive progression and subsequent phenoconversion in prodromal individuals. Methods: Clinical progression was assessed using the Movement Disorder Society-Sponsored Revision of the Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale (MDS-UPDRS) Part III motor scores, Hoehn and Yahr (H&Y) stage, and Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores. Linear mixed-effects models were utilized to examine the associations between baseline Syn-SAA status, kinetic parameters, and longitudinal changes in these clinical measures. Additionally, time-to-event analyses were performed to assess the associations between SAA measurements and phenoconversion to PD or dementia with Lewy bodies. Results: We identified 2,532 participants with available baseline Syn-SAA status in the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) prodromal cohort. This longitudinal study, which included up to 12 years of follow-up, comprised 1,714 Syn-SAA-positive and 818 Syn-SAA-negative individuals. Over the follow-up period, Syn-SAA-positive participants exhibited significantly faster motor progression measured by MDS-UPDRS Part III motor score than Syn-SAA-negative participants (0.611 vs. 0.139 points/year; P<0.001). This association persisted after excluding phenoconverters (0.430 vs. 0.202 points/year; P=0.014) and restricting follow-up to seven years (0.588 vs. 0.137 points/year; P<0.001). Among the 1,796 participants included in the time-to-event analyses, 181 phenoconversion events occurred. Baseline Syn-SAA positivity was associated with a significantly higher hazard of phenoconversion (adjusted hazard ratio 5.72, 95% confidence interval 3.78-8.68; P<0.001), whereas kinetic parameters showed no significant associations with phenoconversion risk. Conclusions: Baseline Syn-SAA positivity was associated with accelerated motor progression during the prodromal stage independent of phenoconversion. These findings support the potential utility of Syn-SAA positivity as a prognostic biomarker for motor progression and phenoconversion, with implications for risk stratification and participant selection in future disease-modifying trials.

items.title: Maternal vitamin D status during pregnancy is associated with reduced DNA methylation entropy and hypomethylation of regulatory regions related to immune tolerance
items.abstract: Background Vitamin D is crucial to maternal immune system function during pregnancy, acting via the vitamin D receptor (VDR). Yet, there is widespread vitamin D insufficiency among pregnant women. The Vitamin D Antenatal Asthma Reduction Trial investigated the effect of maternal vitamin D on offspring asthma/wheeze. Pregnant women were randomized to a vitamin D supplementation or placebo group, and maternal blood samples were collected at 10-18 and 32-38 weeks of gestation. This analysis aims to identify associations between 25-hydroxyvitamin-D3 (25OHD) and DNA methylation (DNAm). DNAm data were obtained with Illumina Infinium Methylation EPICv2 array. Linear mixed effects models assessed DNAm-25OHD associations, adjusting for demographic and clinical factors. Probe-level results were aggregated to identify differentially methylated regions (DMRs), which were annotated to genes via proximity to promoters or enhancers. In addition, DNAm entropy was investigated for associations with 25OHD. Results Hypomethylated (meso-/hyper-methylated) DMRs showed negative (positive) DNAm-25OHD associations. DMRs overlapped with vitamin D-sensitive topologically associating domains and open chromatin. Annotated genes were primarily enriched for pathways related to antigen processing/presentation. Using paired RNA-seq data, the expression of 59 annotated genes was significantly associated with DNAm of its corresponding DMR. These included IKBKB, a kinase with suppressive effects on the NF-kappa-B pathway. Furthermore, DMRs showed negative entropy-25OHD associations, suggesting a more homogeneous immune methylome in women with higher 25OHD levels. Conclusions Our findings suggest that increased vitamin D may promote methylome stability in genomic regions associated with antigen presentation and immune tolerance, conveying a complex regulatory landscape of the vitamin D-associated methylome during pregnancy.

items.title: Mapping Gene-by-Environment Interactions via the Plasma Exposome at Cell-Type Resolution
items.corresponding_institution: Department of Genetics, Stanford University, Stanford, CA, 94305, USA .	Department of Biomedical Data Science, Stanford, CA, 94305, USA
items.abstract: Gene-by-environment (GxE) interactions inform where genetics and environment converge to impact human health and disease. However, systematically mapping GxE interactions has been challenging due to the diversity of testable exposures and a lack of scalable approaches to measure the environments cells experience in vivo. Here, we identified modules of correlated plasma metabolites and proteins and used them as quantitative proxies for environmental exposures experienced by circulating leukocytes. We demonstrated that these proxies are associated with environmentally modifiable clinical traits such as diet and infection and support broad mapping of geneby environment (GxE) interactions affecting gene expression and CpG methylation in leukocytes. We identified significant interactions for 95.2% of tested genes and 5.9% of tested methylation sites. These GxE interactions showed specificity to exposures and cell type. Colocalization analysis further provided links between interactions and complex trait and disease loci. Finally, we expanded GxE interaction mapping to unexplored cell types using a zero-shot transfer model to predict GxE interactions in held-out cell types, demonstrating how plasma metabolomics and proteomics can enhance the discovery of GxE interactions across the body. Altogether, this work provides a systematic multi-omic framework to study how gene regulation is shaped by both the genome and the molecular environments cells experience in vivo.

items.title: Combined genome-wide association studies in humans and cattle: Cross-species genetic insights into dizygotic twinning
items.corresponding_institution: National Centre for Registry Based Research, Aarhus University, Aarhus, Denmark; The SMARTBiomed Pioneer Centre, Aarhus University, Aarhus, Denmark
items.abstract: To leverage independent genetic evidence from multiple species, we developed a cross-species gene-based GWAS meta-analysis framework and applied this to Dizygotic Twinning (DZT) in humans and cattle. After meta-analysis within species, we converted human and cattle GWAS summary statistics to gene-level association signals within each species, mapped genes across species through human-cattle orthology, and then combined gene-level evidence for orthologous genes across the two species. DZT is defined as giving birth to multiple offspring after a single pregnancy resulting from spontaneous multiple ovulation. In humans, DZT occurs in about 1% of pregnancies with heritability estimates of 20% to 30% whilst in cattle DZT occurs in 1-5% of pregnancies and heritability is estimated at about 11%. Here, we present the largest human GWAS meta-analysis including data from 1,395,285 participants. We identified 16 genetic regions of interest, including 12 independent loci from the SNP based analyses and 4 genes identified in the gene-based MAGMA analyses. Among the prioritized genes are follicle stimulation hormone receptor (FSHR) and growth differentiation factor 9 (GDF9), that both are involved in ovarian folliculogenesis. Cattle GWAS summary statistics were based on data from 2,656 Irish Holstein bulls with estimated breeding values for predisposition to twinning based on 2,238,936 birth records, and 86,391 German Holstein dams. After combining the gene-level analyses for 13,225 genes mapped as orthologous across the human and cattle data we identify FSHR as a central locus for DZT in both humans and cattle. We find evidence of additional associations, including ACVR2A, which plays a role in embryonic implantation and TUFM, which has previously been implicated in premature ovarian insufficiency. Our approach provides a promising framework for future cross-species comparative GWAS studies. It shows benefits for gene discovery and gene prioritization and in our application expands available functional follow-up data, allowing us to leverage cattle eQTL data to resolve human GWAS loci. The method and underlying philosophy presented here are transferable to other shared phenotypes across several species.
